jobs.title: PhD Position in Planning Climate Resilient Mobility Networks
jobs.description_html:
Planning climate resilient mobility networks.

Job description

What is CLIMACT?

CLIMACT (Climate Adaptation through Collaborative Transferability) is a four-year Horizon Europe project coordinated by Dr. Shadi Sharif Azadeh, involving 17 partners across eight European countries. The project develops a transferable framework to assess the effectiveness, limitations, and long-term resilience of climate adaptation strategies across mobility, water-health systems, and agriculture. In the mobility domain, case studies in Lisbon and Greater Manchester examine how flooding and heatwaves affect public transport networks, and how infrastructure, operational decisions, and governance can strengthen resilience. CLIMACT aims to identify adaptation pathways that remain effective under future climate conditions and can be transferred across regions and sectors.

PhD Position

The aim is to develop advanced modelling and optimization methods to improve the resilience of public transport and urban mobility networks under increasing climate risks, particularly flooding and extreme heat. The research will integrate climate projections, transport network simulation, and behavioral modelling to assess how infrastructure vulnerabilities, operational disruptions, and travelers’ responses affect mobility system performance. A central objective is to develop optimization-based decision support methods that identify when existing adaptation measures reach their limits and determine robust adaptation strategies under evolving climate conditions.

The PhD researcher will develop and test these methods through case studies, examining the effectiveness and transferability of adaptation strategies across different infrastructure, operational, and governance contexts. The ideal candidate has a strong background in operations research, mathematical optimization, and stochastic modelling. Experience with simulation, machine learning, or transport demand modelling is a plus.

The Department of Transport & Planning (T&P) of Delft University of Technology is coordinating this project. T&P is composed of 12 research labs addressing various transport challenges. The researcher will be associated with the SUM Lab at CEG and ORBIT Lab at TPM (SUM Lab (tudelft.nl)).

Job requirements
  • A Master's degree in a relevant field, i.e., Applied Mathematics, Operations Research, Computer Science and related topics.
  • Familiarities with climate adaptation, transport networks, and behavioral science are highly valued.
  • Strong programming skills.
  • Ability to work both in a project team, but also independently and take leadership and responsibility for research tasks.
  • Willingness and ability to communicate with other scientific partners, companies, and cities.
  • Willingness to contribute to a stimulating research environment and interactions with project partners and stakeholders.
  • Passionate about scientific excellence and impactful research.
  • Excellent communication skills in English, both written and oral.

If your native language is not English and you do not hold a degree from an institution in which English is the language of instruction, you must submit proof of English proficiency from either TOEFL (minimum total score of 100) or IELTS (minimum total score of 7.0). Proof of English language proficiency certificates older than two years are not accepted.

TU Delft (Delft University of Technology)
Working at TU Delft means contributing to solutions that really make a difference.

For over 180 years, we have been training engineers who make an impact worldwide in companies, government bodies, or as entrepreneurs. Our alumni turn knowledge into concrete solutions for the challenges of today and tomorrow. These challenges are changing rapidly. That is why we focus on themes such as energy, climate, digitalisation, artificial intelligence (AI), and smart mobility every day. Our education and research are directly aligned with what society needs now and in the future.

At TU Delft, our people make the difference. With their knowledge and curiosity, our staff provide a high-quality education and conduct pioneering research that extends beyond the campus. You will have the opportunity to take the initiative, work with others, and grow as a professional. Working at TU Delft means join an international community of professionals and students. Together, we create knowledge, innovations, and solutions that help move the world forward.

Faculty of Civil Engineering and Geosciences
The Faculty of Civil Engineering & Geosciences (CEG) is committed to outstanding international research and education in the field of civil engineering, applied earth sciences, traffic and transport, water technology, and delta technology. Our research feeds into our educational programmes and covers societal challenges such as climate change, energy transition, resource availability, urbanisation and clean water. Our research projects are conducted in close cooperation with a wide range of research institutions. CEG is convinced of the importance of open science and supports its scientists in integrating open science in their research practice. The Faculty of CEG comprises 28 research groups in the following seven departments: Materials Mechanics Management & Design, Engineering Structures, Geoscience and Engineering, Geoscience and Remote Sensing, Transport & Planning, Hydraulic Engineering and Water Management.

Click here to go to the website of the Faculty of Civil Engineering & Geosciences.

Conditions of employment
Doctoral candidates will be offered a 4-year period of employment in principle, but in the form of 2 employment contracts. An initial 1,5 year contract with an official go/no go progress assessment within 15 months. Followed by an additional contract for the remaining 2,5 years assuming everything goes well and performance requirements are met.

Salary and benefits are in accordance with the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities, increasing from €3204 - €4051 gross per month, from the first year to the fourth year based on a fulltime contract (38 hours), plus 8% holiday allowance and an end-of-year bonus of 8.3%.

As a PhD candidate you will be enrolled in the TU Delft Graduate School. The TU Delft Graduate School provides an inspiring research environment with an excellent team of supervisors, academic staff and a mentor. The Doctoral Education Programme is aimed at developing your transferable, discipline-related and research skills.

The TU Delft offers a customisable compensation package, discounts on health insurance, and a monthly work costs contribution. Flexible work schedules can be arranged.

Will you need to relocate to the Netherlands for this job? TU Delft is committed to make your move as smooth as possible! The HR unit, Coming to Delft Service, offers information on their website to help you prepare your relocation. In addition, Coming to Delft Service organises events to help you settle in the Netherlands, and expand your (social) network in Delft. A Dual Career Programme is available, to support your accompanying partner with their job search in the Netherlands.

Additional information
For more information about this vacancy, please contact Dr. Shadi Sharif Azadeh, email: s.sharifazadeh@tudelft.nl, stating the vacancy title and code in the email title.

Application procedure
Are you interested in this vacancy? Please apply no later than 8 December 2026 via the application button and upload the following documents:
  • CV

You can address your application to Shadi Sharif Azadeh.

jobs.title: Promovendus passende zorg in de wijkverpleging
jobs.description_html:
Om passende zorg te realiseren, is het belangrijk dat cliënten en burgers betrokken zijn bij onderzoek en kennisontwikkeling. Binnen academische werkplaatsen wijkverpleging gebeurt dit op verschillende manieren, bijvoorbeeld via projectgroepen en adviesraden. Maar hoe zorg je ervoor dat participatie een structurele en betekenisvolle plek krijgt binnen een organisatie? En wat is ervoor nodig om de ervaringen en perspectieven van cliënten en burgers daadwerkelijk te benutten bij het ontwikkelen en verbeteren van zorg?

In dit promotieonderzoek onderzoek je hoe academische werkplaatsen cliënt- en burgerparticipatie kunnen versterken en duurzaam kunnen verankeren. Je brengt in kaart welke factoren participatie bevorderen of belemmeren en ontwikkelt samen met betrokkenen praktische manieren om participatie inzichtelijk te maken, te evalueren en te verbeteren. Dit doe je binnen de Academische Werkplaatsen Wijkverpleging en in samenwerking met de Academische Werkplaats Huisartsen. Een onderdeel van het onderzoek is de ontwikkeling en het testen van een participatiethermometer die academische werkplaatsen helpt om van hun ervaringen te leren en participatie verder te ontwikkelen. De resultaten worden vertaald naar praktische hulpmiddelen en een handreiking die ook voor andere academische werkplaatsen bruikbaar zijn.

Wil je alvast meer weten over de verschillende fases binnen het PhD-traject? Op deze pagina lees je hierover meer informatie.

Als promovendus ben je verantwoordelijk voor het (verder) uitdenken en opzetten van afzonderlijke studies. Daarbij is er ruimte voor eigen inbreng en initiatief. Je doet literatuuronderzoek en documentanalyses en brengt ervaringen en perspectieven in kaart via interviews, focusgroepen en observaties. Je werkt in co-creatie met cliënten, burgers, projectleiders, coördinatoren en onderzoekers aan de ontwikkeling en het testen van praktische hulpmiddelen. Je voert een pilotstudie uit in academische werkplaatsen wijkverpleging, analyseert de resultaten en bespreekt deze samen met betrokkenen om tot concrete verbeteracties te komen. Je verwerkt de onderzoeksresultaten in wetenschappelijke artikelen en draagt bij aan een hulpmiddelen waarmee academische werkplaatsen participatie kunnen monitoren, evalueren en borgen.

Tijdens je promotietraject werk je aan je professionele ontwikkeling, bijvoorbeeld door cursussen te volgen aan de Graduate School; ook lever je een bijdrage aan onderwijs (o.a. medical humanities) in de opleiding Geneeskunde (UMC Utrecht).

jobs.title: Promovendus duurzame en klimaatbestendige zorgsystemen
jobs.description_html:
Je voert een vierjarig promotieonderzoek uit binnen GOV4CARE, een vijfjarig Europees onderzoeksproject dat wordt gecoördineerd door de onderzoeksgroep Health Systems and Services Research van Amsterdam UMC in samenwerking met het Centrum voor Duurzame Zorg. Het project onderzoekt hoe Europese zorgsystemen hun ecologische duurzaamheid en klimaatbestendigheid kunnen verbeteren en hoe deze doelstellingen kunnen worden verankerd in beleid, de aansturing en organisatie van zorgsystemen en de dagelijkse zorgpraktijk.

Jouw promotieonderzoek richt zich op de vraag waarom en in welke mate Europese zorgsystemen verschillen in ecologische duurzaamheid en klimaatbestendigheid. Je vergelijkt 31 Europese landen en onderzoekt hoe beleidskeuzes, financiering, de organisatie en aansturing van zorgsystemen en bredere maatschappelijke omstandigheden samenhangen met hun prestaties. Daarbij kijk je naar het beperken van de klimaatimpact van de zorg (mitigatie), de paraatheid voor klimaatgerelateerde verstoringen en de aanpassing aan klimaatverandering (adaptatie).

Ook onderzoek je hoe ecologische duurzaamheid en klimaatbestendigheid samenhangen met andere belangrijke doelen van zorgsystemen, zoals kwaliteit, toegankelijkheid, gelijkheid en doelmatigheid. Met dit onderzoek draag je bij aan wetenschappelijke kennis over de factoren die verschillen tussen zorgsystemen verklaren en bied je aanknopingspunten voor verbetering van beleid, organisatie en zorgpraktijk.

Wil je alvast meer weten over de verschillende fases binnen het PhD-traject? Op deze pagina lees je hierover meer informatie.

Je voert internationaal vergelijkend onderzoek uit in samenwerking met onderzoekers en andere partners binnen het GOV4CARE-consortium.

Je werkzaamheden bestaan onder andere uit:
  • Het systematisch in kaart brengen en vergelijken van nationale strategieën, beleidsmaatregelen en instrumenten voor ecologische duurzaamheid en klimaatbestendigheid van zorgsystemen in 31 Europese landen.
  • Bijdragen aan de uitvoering van vergelijkende case-studies op verschillende specifieke onderwerpen met betrekking tot de implementatie van klimaatmitigatiemaatregelen in zorginstellingen door heel Europa.
  • Het analyseren van internationale verschillen en patronen in de prestaties van zorgsystemen, op basis van bestaande en binnen GOV4CARE ontwikkelde indicatoren en datasets.
  • Het onderzoeken in welke mate beleidskeuzes, financiering, de organisatie en aansturing van zorgsystemen en bredere contextuele factoren verschillen in prestaties tussen landen kunnen verklaren.
  • Het analyseren van synergieën en mogelijke spanningen tussen ecologische duurzaamheid, klimaatbestendigheid en andere doelen van zorgsystemen.
  • Het ontwikkelen van typologieën van Europese zorgsystemen op basis van overeenkomsten en verschillen in beleid, prestaties en onderliggende verklarende factoren, en het vertalen van deze inzichten naar aanbevelingen voor beleid en implicaties voor de organisatie en praktijk van zorg, en input voor de scenariomodellering binnen GOV4CARE.
  • Het schrijven en publiceren van circa vijf wetenschappelijke peer-reviewed artikelen, die gezamenlijk de basis vormen voor je proefschrift, en het presenteren van onderzoeksresultaten op nationale en internationale congressen en bijeenkomsten.
  • Het samenwerken met onderzoekers, beleidsmakers en andere internationale partners binnen het GOV4CARE-consortium.
  • Het bijdragen aan onderwijs binnen de afdeling Public and Occupational Health.

jobs.title: PhD position: Spectroscopic optical coherence tomography for non-invasive blood analysis
jobs.description_html:
Project background

Anemia is a frequently occurring condition in hospitalized patients, requiring regular invasive sampling for the analysis of blood hemoglobin (Hb) levels to prevent complications or to initiate therapy. Invasive hemoglobin analysis is associated with adverse complications, including iatrogenic blood loss and delayed decision making. This is particularly problematic for vulnerable patients such as premature newborns and surgical patients. Non-invasive alternatives exist, but are not sufficiently reliable to replace invasive sampling.

Spectroscopic optical coherence tomography (sOCT) offers a novel approach to non-invasive hemoglobin analysis. Whereas conventional non-invasive approaches suffer from signal crosstalk from an unknown amount of non-vascular tissue, sOCT uniquely images microvascular skin anatomy and subsequently confines the Hb determination to vascular tissue exclusively. By excluding the non-vascular component, this approach provides a direct, one-on-one comparison to the current gold standard of invasive blood analysis.

Our aim is to develop sOCT-Hb determinations for both newborn and adult anemic patients with clinically relevant accuracy and precision.

The PhD project
In this PhD project, you will develop and apply a spectroscopic optical coherence tomography system for non-invasive hemoglobin analysis in newborns and adults.

The project contains technological elements (development of sOCT signal analysis models), experimental elements (model validation), engineering elements (clinical sOCT system development) and clinical elements (application on patients).You will be a member of the Biomedical Photonic Imaging group of the University of Twente and will collaborate closely with engineers, clinicians and scientists. During this four-year project, you will conduct research leading to a PhD dissertation. As part of your PhD training, you will also complete approximately 30 EC of courses and professional development activities.

jobs.title: PhD position: developing a genuine multi-scale rational design strategy for soft electronics
jobs.description_html:
Key responsibilities
The response of internal and emergent functions to chemical or structural modification of molecular constituents is often very non-linear - sometimes even disruptive - and remains poorly understood, rendering the design of soft electronic materials with precise properties across different (correlated) scales a significant challenge. On the computational side, there is a historic separation between methods and scientific communities dealing with electronic function and with materials. In particular, quantum/function and classical modelling/materials differ in so many aspects that the community has thus far completely failed to bridge quantum and classical in a practical multi-scale approach. Here, we plan to benefit from the unique expertise available in our group with molecular optimisation, (hybrid) modelling at the quantum, atomistic and mesoscopic level, and with visual workflows for FAIR simulation. In particular, the candidate will extend an existing rational design strategy framework for coarse-grained molecular optimisation named EvoMD into a nested version for structure and function design across multiple scales. In this PhD project, we will focus on two aspects, namely:1) Retaining protein functions like proton pumping upon embedding in a designer mixed lipid/polymer membrane: how does the protein conformational sampling (and thus function) respond to embedding in a structured matrix and vice versa? 2) Evaluating quantum sensitivity: can we mitigate issues of sensitivity at the smallest scale in optimisation schemes? The PhD candidate will have the opportunity to work at the forefront of software development, multiscale simulation, machine learning for multi-objective optimisation, and workflow automation.

This project is part of a larger effort to develop schemes for the automated simulation of transition-metal containing molecules across the QM/classical boundary, for instance focussing on WALP-based metallopeptide insertion into lipid membranes for the purpose of charge transfer like in natural photosynthesis. Funding for other aspects of this development is currently actively sought.

The PhD candidate will be placed in the Leiden Institute of Chemistry research group of Agur Sevink, which is part of the Metals in Catalysis, Biomimetics & Inorganic Materials (MCBIM) group, providing a direct link to experimental research. We are looking for an enthusiastic, motivated and friendly PhD candidate with a multi-disciplinary background that is eager to collaborate, learn and try new things. The philosophy of the group is to select tools (simulation methodology) for a given challenge, not to seek challenges for a given tool. The visual workflow development is carried out in collaboration with dr. Xinmeng Li of BoundaryComputing (Salpa, salpa.app).

Selection Criteria
  • Highly qualified and motivated graduates holding a master’s degree (or equivalent) in physical chemistry, physics, or related areas, with excellent grades.
  • Experience with data-driven methods and optimization.
  • Experience in modern simulation techniques at the quantum, atomistic and coarse-grained scale.
  • No distinct preference for simulation techniques at either the quantum or classical domain, since they will be both equally important for the project.
  • Good communication skills and good to excellent proficiency in English.
  • A keen interest in carrying out research at the frontier of chemistry, physics and biology in a multidisciplinary environment.

Our organisation
The Faculty of Science is a world-class faculty where staff and students work together in a dynamic international environment. It is a faculty where personal and academic development are top priorities. Our people are committed to expand fundamental knowledge by curiosity and to look beyond the borders of their own discipline; their aim is to benefit science, and to make a contribution to addressing the major societal challenges of the future.

The research carried out at the Faculty of Science is very diverse, ranging from mathematics, information science, astronomy, physics, chemistry and bio-pharmaceutical sciences to biology and environmental sciences. The research activities are organised in eight institutes. These institutes offer eight bachelor’s and twelve master’s programmes. The faculty has grown strongly in recent years and now has more than 2.200 staff and almost 4,200 students. We are located at the heart of Leiden’s Bio Science Park, one of Europe’s biggest science parks, where university and business life come together.

The chemistry and life science research in the Leiden Institute of Chemistry (LIC) is organized around two major research areas: ‘Chemical Biology’ and ‘Energy & Sustainability’. The institute’s research themes illustrate the central position of chemistry between biology, medicine and physics. The various research topics carried out within these themes are ideal for executing interdisciplinary research.

For more information, see www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/science and http://workingat.leiden.edu/

Terms and conditions
We offer a full-time position for initially one year. After a positive evaluation of the progress of the thesis, personal capabilities and compatibility the appointment will be extended by a further three years. Salary range from € 3.204 to € 4.051 gross per month (pay scale P in accordance with the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities).

Leiden University offers an attractive benefits package with additional holiday (8%) and end-of-year bonuses(8.3 %), training and career development and sabbatical leave. Our individual choices model gives you some freedom to assemble your own set of terms and conditions. Candidates from outside the Netherlands may be eligible for a substantial tax break.

For more information about employment conditions, see https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/working-at/job-application-procedure-and-employment-conditions

All our PhD students are embedded in the Leiden University Graduate School of Science www.graduateschools.leidenuniv.nl. Our graduate school offers several PhD training courses at three levels: professional courses, skills training and personal effectiveness.

Diversity
Leiden University is strongly committed to diversity within its community and especially welcomes applications from members of underrepresented groups.

Applications
If you want to apply straight away, click the application button.

If you would like more information about what the job entails, please contact Agur Sevink, at a.sevink@lic.leidenuniv.nl. You can apply until 15 December 2026; You will receive a response to your application no later than two weeks after the vacancy closing date.

Please ensure that you upload the following additional documents quoting the vacancy number:
  • Letter of motivation, including a statement why you are suited for this position;

  • Three references, including names, affiliations and email addresses.

To help us get to know each other better, we follow a number of steps in the application procedure. For more information, see https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/working-at/job-application-procedure-and-employment-conditions
  • In choosing between candidates, in case of equal suitability, preference will be given to internal candidates, women, the occupationally disabled and employees with a migration background.

We also believe it is important for international staff to have a good level of Dutch: they are expected to have at least C1 level of Dutch proficiency. Other staff who have the prospect of a permanent position are expected to have at least a passive understanding of Dutch.

jobs.title: PhD Candidate in Paediatric Mucosal Immunology
jobs.description_html:
Job description
Understanding mucosal immune protection against respiratory infections in children
Are you interested in understanding how the immune system protects children against respiratory infections?

Respiratory tract infections are among the most common causes of illness in children worldwide. While most children recover without complications, some experience frequent or severe infections. Why are certain children more susceptible than others, and how can we improve protection against respiratory pathogens?

Most immunological research and diagnostic approaches focus on immune responses measured in blood. Yet respiratory pathogens first encounter the immune system at the mucosal surfaces of the airways. Understanding immune protection at these surfaces may offer new opportunities for preventing and treating respiratory infections.

The Paediatric Respiratory Infection & Immunity Group at Radboudumc is looking for an enthusiastic and curious PhD candidate. Our ambition is to unravel the mechanisms underlying mucosal immune protection and translate these insights into new strategies to prevent respiratory infections in children.

Your research
We investigate how mucosal antibodies protect against respiratory pathogens and how local immune cells, including innate lymphoid cells, contribute to the generation and maintenance of these antibodies.

As a PhD candidate, you will contribute to understanding why mucosal antibody responses differ between children and how these differences relate to susceptibility to respiratory infections.

Your work will include:
  • Characterising mucosal antibody responses in children with recurrent respiratory tract infections and healthy controls.
  • Investigating the diversity and polyreactivity of mucosal IgA and IgG.
  • Studying associations between mucosal immune characteristics and clinical susceptibility to respiratory infections.
  • Exploring the cellular and tissue environments that support mucosal antibody production.
  • Integrating immunological, clinical and, where applicable, multi-omics data to identify the mechanisms underlying mucosal immune protection.

You will work with well-characterised paediatric cohorts and biological samples collected through established research collaborations in the Netherlands, South Africa and the Dutch Caribbean.

The project combines clinically relevant research questions with advanced immunological approaches and offers opportunities to develop expertise in mucosal immunology, translational research and quantitative data analysis.

What we offer
  • A PhD position within a funded research programme at Radboudumc.
  • A stimulating and supportive multidisciplinary research environment.
  • Close supervision and opportunities for scientific and professional development.
  • Access to established clinical cohorts and advanced immunological research infrastructure.
  • Opportunities for international collaboration and, where relevant, research visits to partner institutions.
  • The opportunity to contribute to research connecting fundamental immunology with clinical challenges in paediatric respiratory infections.

jobs.title: PhD in Dynamic CO₂ Capture and Conversion with Intermittent Renewable Power
jobs.description_html:
Can you help turn CO₂ from the air into a renewable carbon resource? Join us to develop electrically heated reactors that combine direct air capture with CO₂ conversion—and work effectively with a fluctuating renewable electricity supply.

Information
Europe’s ambition for a fossil-fuel-free chemical industry calls for new ways to produce chemicals and fuels from circular carbon and green hydrogen. Renewable electricity creates exciting opportunities for electrification, but its intermittency challenges conventional process design. Within CO2URAGE, universities and industrial partners will develop intensified, electrified processes to produce syngas, methane, or methanol from CO₂ captured from air, biomass, or other circular sources.

This PhD position focuses on designing and operating electrified, structured packed-bed reactors for direct air capture and integrated CO₂ conversion under changing renewable power availability. Your central challenge is to maintain efficient capture, sorbent regeneration, and heat recovery as the available electrical power varies. Capturing CO₂ from air requires processing large air volumes, while regenerating the sorbent requires efficient heat supply. How can we design compact reactors that combine low pressure drop, rapid heating and cooling, and effective heat recovery?

You will investigate how 3D-printed reactor structures and resistive or inductive heating can improve heat management and reduce the electricity required to release captured CO₂. You will then explore the integration of sorbent regeneration with CO₂ hydrogenation to methane or syngas. Combining capture and conversion offers opportunities to use reaction heat, simplify processing, and improve overall energy efficiency.

You will combine reactor modeling and laboratory experiments to:
  • Design and test 3D-printed, electrically heated reactors for direct air capture.
  • Optimize capture cycles and heat recovery under fluctuating electricity supply and ambient conditions.
  • Explore integrated CO₂ capture and hydrogenation through modelling and proof-of-concept experiments.

The central scientific challenge is to understand how reactor structure, local heat supply and dynamic operation interact—and use that understanding to design energy-efficient capture and conversion processes.

You will pursue your PhD at Eindhoven University of Technology under the supervision of Prof. Martin van Sint Annaland. Within CO2URAGE’s work package Electrification of Direct Air Capture and Conversion, you will collaborate with researchers at the University of Twente and Delft University of Technology, as well as industrial partners. Your reactor research will connect directly with program activities in process control, system integration, and techno-economic and environmental assessment.

jobs.title: PhD Researcher in Legal and ethical perspectives in data-driven technologies in healthcare
jobs.description_html:
We are inviting prospective researchers to apply for a PhD position led by Dr. Mahsa Shabani. This position offers a unique opportunity to work on an interdisciplinary project at the intersection of law, ethics, and technology. The candidate will have the opportunity to shape their own research plan within the broader VIDI project.

Join our team!
Artificial intelligence and genomics technologies are transforming healthcare, offering powerful tools for diagnosis and treatment. Yet, these innovations often fail to serve diverse populations fairly, which can reinforce existing inequalities. Current regulatory frameworks lack a comprehensive approach to fairness, often focusing narrowly on anti-discrimination measures while overlooking broader socio-ethical considerations. This PhD project would focus on building a multidimensional conception of fairness in medical AI and genetics, integrating technical, clinical, ethical, and legal perspectives. The project will employ a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical studies (including focus group studies and Delphi studies) to assess the real-world implications of fairness in data-driven healthcare. The PhD project is within the NWO-VIDI project Fairness in Data-Driven Medical Technologies: Solidifying Regulatory Oversight Based on a Multidimensional Conception of Fairness.

What are you going to do
  • Design the scope of the individual PhD research project, and fine-tune the research questions and methodology together with the whole project team;
  • Engage autonomously in - as well as collaborate on - the collection, coding and analysis of data, through doctrinal/literature research, conceptual analysis, focus groups and Delphi study;
  • Present intermediate research results in internal discussions and at workshops and conferences;
  • Contribute to project activities, such as organizing stakeholder meetings, academic events and outreach; and communication of research results to relevant communities of academics, practitioners and policy makers; and
  • Optionally, and in mutual agreement with the project leader and in line with the teaching needs of the Health Law group, have teaching responsibilities.

What do you have to offer
You have:
  • (or are about to obtain) a master’s degree in law (with a focus on health law or technology law) or bioethics /philosophy. A background in both philosophy / bioethics and law is an advantage.
  • interest (and ideally experience) in conducting multi-method empirical and legal research;
  • interdisciplinary interest in issues on the intersection of law, ethics, and technology (bridging technical, ethical, and legal domains);
  • experience with conducting academic research and academic writing in English;
  • demonstrable team working skills;
  • excellent command of English, both orally and written;
  • interest in broader dissemination of your research findings in the public debate.
  • familiarity with EU regulations (AI Act, MDR, GDPR & EHDS) is an asset;
  • experience with stakeholder engagement (e.g. interviews, focus groups, Delphi studies) is an asset.

What do we offer you
We offer you the opportunity to work in an intellectually stimulating and teamwork-oriented environment. We aim to provide tailor-made and careful supervision with the main goal of helping you grow and flourish academically and professionally. You have the opportunity and obligation to participate in the Amsterdam Law School’s PhD training program.

We offer a position for 1.0 FTE (38 hours/week) as a PhD student. The initial appointment is for 1 year with a trial period of 2 months. After a positive evaluation, your appointment will be extended for another 3 years. The start date will be determined by mutual agreement; it is currently scheduled around 1 January 2027.

Your salary ranges from €3,204 (in year 1) to €4,051 (in year 4) based on a 38-hour working week. This amount excludes 8% holiday allowance and 8.3% end-of-year bonus. The CAO Nederlandse Universiteiten (CAO NU) applies.

This is where you are going to work
You will become a team member of the Law Centre for Health and Life based at the University of Amsterdam’s Law Faculty. Within the Law Centre for Health and Life, you will join the Digital Health & Genomics research group, an interdisciplinary research group consisting of researchers from different academic backgrounds. There are multiple PhD candidates working at the Centre on various projects. You will be invited and expected to actively contribute to the academic life of the Centre, Faculty and University.

If you have any questions about the position, please contact by email: Dr. Mahsa Shabani, m.shabani@uva.nl

If you feel the profile fits you, and you are interested in the job, we look forward to receiving your application consisting of the documents listed below. Please apply online via the apply button. We will accept applications until 30 November 2026. We hope the candidates will start their position per 1 January 2027.

Please note that it is only possible to upload two documents, therefore please combine the required files in two (PDF) documents.

File 1
  • Motivation letter (maximum one page);
  • a CV of no more than three pages;
  • An initial research plan including a research question related to one of the topics, justification on why it warrants investigation, and propose a methodology to answer the question, and a potential reference list (in no more than 800 words, excluding references)
  • writing sample of a recently written, single authored manuscript (e.g., your master’s thesis or other work written during your degree) in English of no more than 30 pages.
  • Contact information of two academic referees

File 2
  • Copies of the LL.B. and LL.M. degrees or equivalent, providing information about the program's length, content, passed courses and grades.
  • If you choose to upload your documents differently, you run the risk that the files are rejected for being too big or that we miss part of your application.

jobs.title: PhD position in organisational science and cybersecurity
jobs.description_html:
For our NWO-funded project “From ‘what went wrong’ to ‘what works well?’ Using Safety 2 principles to develop new cybersecurity solutions”, we are looking for a PhD candidate interested in building positive cybersecurity solutions for organisations. In this five-year project, we aim to develop cybersecurity solutions that organisations can implement in their ways of working based on what we learn from organisations where cybersecurity is managed successfully. The main research question the team will answer is: “What do successful organisations do differently on the individual, team, and organisational level to prevent the occurrence of cyber incidents or reduce their impact?” This position focuses on the organisational level of the main research question.

What you will do
The successful applicant will work with researchers from the cybersecurity governance and the governance of crisis research group to help answering this question. Knowledge of (organisational) cybersecurity at the start of the project is not a requirement. However, we do expect the successful applicants to quickly familiarise themselves with the field through self-study or by taking in-house courses. The successful applicant will conduct empirical research on what successful organisations do differently on the organisational level. Is it the structure, power dynamics or perhaps the communication between departments that warrants success? Or can other factors be found that explain what organisations could do differently to improve their cybersecurity?

Where you will work
ISGA is a scientific institute specializing in security, safety, and global challenges. These include challenges in the fields of cybersecurity, crises, intelligence, terrorism, war, violence, and diplomacy. ISGA is characterized by high-quality, interdisciplinary education and the development of scientific knowledge with a high potential for societal impact. ISGA is part of the Faculty of Governance and Global Affairs (FGGA) and is based in the city of The Hague, the international city of peace and justice. FGGA is one of the seven faculties of Leiden University. This young, entrepreneurial, innovative organization has three scientific institutes, two centers, over 3,700 students, and 425 staff members. For more information about the faculty, click here.

The interdisciplinary Cybersecurity Governance research group works on the non-technical side of cybersecurity at all levels of society. This includes the cybersecurity of end-users in organisations, regulation on the national and international level, but also international relations and diplomacy. The group consists of scientists with a range of different background including psychology, criminology, public administration, philosophy, political science, sociology and law. These different backgrounds are used to create collaborations to understand how we can improve cybersecurity on both the national and international level.

What you bring
In this team, we are looking for someone who can work independently. Every job is different, so in the beginning we will devote attention to your onboarding. If some of the work activities are new to you, we will look together at what you need, and draw up a development plan. This position is a good fit for you if you recognise yourself in the following:
  • A Master’s degree in organisational science, psychology, communication science, behavioural sciences, political science, sociology, or a related field.
  • An interest in cybersecurity and the willingness to learn about this field if it is new to you.
  • Demonstrated experience in quantitative research. Experience in qualitative research is considered an asset.
  • A collaborative mindset, the ability to work in a team.
  • Strong communication skills for interaction with stakeholders and communicating scientific findings.
  • A proficiency in Dutch is considered an asset.

If you immediately recognise yourself in this profile, or if do you not quite meet all the requirements, but you believe that this is the right job for you, we look forward to your application!

What we offer
Our goal is to work together to create a transparent and inclusive work environment in which everyone feels welcome and appreciated. Our organisation is always evolving and we need your ideas for improvement and innovation to take us further. We want to devote attention to your personal development.

You can count on an enjoyable job within the socially relevant world of education and research. The University's challenging and international work environment is located in the bustling city centre of The Hague. We also want to work with you to devote attention to your health and vitality, for example with the fun activities we organise through Healthy University.

We also offer:
  • An employment contract for 38 hours a week (1.0 fte) as a PhD candidate, initially for a period of 1 year, with the possibility of extension for 3 years after a positive evaluation. This contract falls under the CLA of Dutch Universities;
  • A salary of a minimum of € 3.204,- and a maximum of € 4.051,- gross per month, based on a full-time appointment (38 hours) (scale [P0-P3]);

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Harnessing Nature’s CO2 Catalyst to Accelerate Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal
jobs.description_html:
Could biology help us engineer a new way of removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?

Achieving carbon dioxide removal (CDR) at enormous scale is likely to be an important part of tackling climate change. The ocean naturally exchanges CO2 with the air, but because the alkalinity of that seawater buffers CO2, the amount of carbon dissolved in the ocean is vastly greater than in the atmosphere. For context, if you took all the CO2 that humanity has every emitted and stirred it into the ocean, the seawater carbon concentration would only increase by about 2%.

An extremely promising technique, known as Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement, aims to increase the buffering of CO2 by seawater. This would allow seawater to take up even more atmospheric CO2, helping us to balance the emissions from activities - such as flying and farming - that we don’t know how to decarbonise, and potentially even begin to reverse climate change.

But there is a fundamental problem.

Transferring atmospheric CO₂ into that seawater is slow. This means that CO2 uptake happens over tens to hundreds of kilometres downstream of where a carbon removal facility may be, with implications around marine ecosystem impacts, scalability, verification and cost. If this exchange could be dramatically accelerated, it could open the door to a different approach to marine carbon dioxide removal.

This PhD, part of the  CASE4CDR project which is aligned with ARIA’s Resilient Climate and Ecosystems Opportunity Space,  will explore whether  harnessing biology can allow us to overcome this problem.

Carbonic anhydrases catalyse the conversion between carbon dioxide and bicarbonate, speeding up the reaction by up to 10 million times. These enzymes are found in almost all living organisms, and we will work with you to isolate and stabilise them, utilising the same chemistry that operates in your body and in marine organisms to overcome the reaction bottleneck and rapidly convert carbon dioxide and water into ocean bicarbonate. The project will give you the opportunity to learn advanced skills in enzymology, structural work, and protein chemistry to develop these enzymes to meet the environmental challenge. It will also involve small lab-scale tests to quantify the efficacy of atmospheric CO2 absorption by alkalinity-enhanced seawater using immobilised enzymes.

You will work closely with a parallel PhD researcher working on larger-scale CO₂ exchange and measurement.

From laboratory experiments to the sea

A particularly exciting feature of this PhD is that, with the right safeguards in place, the work is intended to move beyond laboratory proof-of-concept.

Upon meeting key acceptance criteria, you will help translate fundamental measurements and engineering designs into trials using real seawater at the SeaCURE pilot facility situated on the coast near Weymouth.

This will create a unique opportunity to follow an emerging climate technology through multiple stages of development: from calculations and controlled laboratory experiments, through engineering and instrumentation, to operation in a real marine environment.

Carbon dioxide removal cannot succeed on engineering performance alone.

You will join a wider interdisciplinary project examining what would actually be required to deploy a new marine carbon removal technology responsibly. Alongside your core research, you will have opportunities to contribute to work around environmental permitting, regulation, environmental impacts, public and stakeholder engagement, and trials at the Weymouth plant.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B17 Finding the most explosive volcanoes on earth
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
While advances in volcanology have revealed much about eruption processes, research has largely concentrated on a small set of well-monitored volcanoes, geographically skewed towards continental and northern hemisphere regions. This focus has left significant gaps in our understanding of many volcanoes, especially in resource-poor regions including island arcs in Southeast Asia. These areas coincide with the world’s highest volcanic activity, yet eruption histories, geological maps, and monitoring data are incomplete or absent. Volcanoes capable of very large magnitude eruptions (M ≥ 6), with the potential to cause severe regional or global impacts, remain missing from current risk assessments.

This PhD project will address this critical knowledge gap by identifying which volcanoes are most likely to produce highly explosive, large-magnitude eruptions. The student will combine global datasets with targeted field investigations to test the attributes hypothesised to favour such eruptions. Using a training dataset of well-studied volcanoes with known large eruptions, the project will employ statistical and machine learning (ML) methods to identify the strongest predictors of eruption magnitude. These predictive models will then be applied to poorly characterised volcanoes, producing a prioritised list for further research and monitoring.

Fieldwork in Southeast Asia, in collaboration with Indonesian partners, will test and refine these predictions. The student will also help organise a joint field course (with the Global Volcano Risk Alliance charity), to train local and international students in volcanic mapping, tephra sampling, dating techniques, and the analysis of volcanic ash for health impacts. This component will strengthen scientific capacity, foster community engagement, and produce valuable new data for the project.

By integrating advanced data science with traditional field volcanology and community-based training, the project will identify hidden high-risk volcanoes and contribute directly to monitoring priorities and the next generation of volcano scientists. The outcomes will be relevant to global disaster risk reduction efforts and will support targeted investment in monitoring infrastructure where it is most urgently needed.

Applicants should be comfortable working with quantitative analytical methods (specific machine learning skills can be developed during the PhD). Willingness for fieldwork in challenging environments is essential.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B18 Modelling function in the jaws of sharks throughout their evolutionary history
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Sharks are a diverse, ecologically important, and vulnerable group of fishes with an ancient history. Although the word shark tends to conjure the image of a primeval apex predator, living elasmobranchs live in open ocean, nearshore, and freshwater habitats worldwide, with ecological roles as diverse as bottom-dwelling suction feeders, open ocean filter feeders, and flat-bodied shell-crunchers. Moreover, far from being primitive this rich biodiversity is rooted in a unique feeding system. Highly mobile jaws made from a specialised calcified cartilage and lined with ever-replacing tooth tows are linked to the skull via ligaments and a rod-like hyoid cartilage which allows them to swing outwards during feeding (Wroe et al. 2008). There is great variation in the shape of shark jaws and presumably their function.

The fossil record of isolated teeth shows that this feeding system extends back least 400 million years, and it has rich potential for understanding the relationship between ecology and evolution (López-Romero et al. 2023). However, understanding it is hindered in living sharks by the difficulty of studying anything but small, shallow-water species, and in extinct sharks by the sparse record of fossilised cartilages. Most functional studies have either focussed on specific taxa with specialised feeding mechanics (e.g. Wroe et al. 2008) or looked at the shape of individual parts of the feeding apparatus across the group (e.g. López-Romero et al. 2023, Griffin et al. 2025). Our understanding of how different jaw arrangements in both living and extinct shark relates to their function is very limited.

Recently surging use of tomographic methods has seen a huge increase in datasets on the skeletal anatomy of sharks both living and extinct (e.g. Dearden et al. 2025). This presents the opportunity to carry out quantitative, comparative functional morphological studies across the sweep of fossil and living sharks to understand their feeding apparatus as a multipart system. Using computed tomographic data on fossil and living elasmobranchs and multibody dynamics approaches (Lautenschlager 2020, Dearden et al. 2023) this project will investigate how different forms of the living shark feeding system affect its function throughout their long evolutionary history.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Engineering the Ocean-atmosphere Interface: Accelerating Atmospheric CO2 Removal into Seawater
jobs.description_html:
How do you engineer seawater to pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere and help to mitigate climate change?

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere at enormous scale is likely to be an important part of tackling climate change. The ocean naturally exchanges CO2 with the air, but because the alkalinity of that seawater buffers CO2, the amount of carbon dissolved in the ocean is vastly greater than in the atmosphere. For context, if you took all the CO2 that humanity has every emitted and stirred it into the ocean, the seawater carbon concentration would only increase by about 2%.

An extremely promising technique, known as Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement, aims to increase the buffering of CO2 by seawater. This would allow seawater to take up even more atmospheric CO2, helping us to balance the emissions from activities - such as flying and farming - that we don’t know how to decarbonise, and potentially even begin to reverse climate change.

But there is a fundamental problem.

If we increase the capacity of seawater to store carbon, atmospheric CO₂ does not instantaneously move into the water. The rate at which CO₂ crosses the air-water interface is the major bottleneck, with implications around marine ecosystem impacts, scalability, verification and cost. Overcoming that bottleneck could transform the way marine carbon dioxide removal is designed and deployed. This PhD, part of the CASE4CDR project - aligned with ARIA’s Resilient Climate and Ecosystems Opportunity Space - will investigate how to make that happen.

You will work at the interface of environmental engineering, marine chemistry, enzymology, fluid mechanics, and climate science to understand, quantify and ultimately engineer the transfer of CO2 from air into seawater.

A major focus will be the development and optimisation of systems designed to maximise gas exchange while minimising the energy, material and environmental costs of carbon removal.

You will design experiments to quantify CO2 exchange between air and seawater and investigate how performance changes with a wide range of factors. You will establish rigorous carbon budgets to quantify carbon removal. Working closely with a second PhD researcher and the project supervisors, you will explore a potentially transformative way of accelerating this process.

From laboratory experiments to the sea

A particularly exciting feature of this PhD is that, with the right safeguards in place, the work is intended to move beyond laboratory proof-of-concept.

Upon meeting key acceptance criteria, you will help translate fundamental measurements and engineering designs into trials using real seawater at the SeaCURE pilot facility situated on the coast in Weymouth.

This will create a unique opportunity to follow an emerging climate technology through multiple stages of development: from calculations and controlled laboratory experiments, through engineering and instrumentation, to operation in a real marine environment.

Carbon dioxide removal cannot succeed on engineering performance alone.

You will join a wider interdisciplinary project examining what would actually be required to deploy a new marine carbon removal technology responsibly. Alongside your core research, you will have opportunities to contribute to work around environmental permitting, regulation, environmental impacts, public and stakeholder engagement, and trials at the Weymouth plant.

That wider perspective is important. The central question is not just can we build it, but can we develop a carbon-removal system that is measurable, environmentally responsible, socially acceptable and capable of eventually operating at meaningful scale.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B19 Resolving the affinities of the earliest actinopterygian ‘macrodont’ radiation
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Main description:

Ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) are the most diverse group of vertebrates, accounting for over half of the >60,000 living vertebrate species. Although the group originated in the Devonian, most taxa from this period are morphologically conservative in overall size and shape, with very few exceptions. Ray-finned fishes exploded in taxonomic and morphological diversity in the Carboniferous, after the End-Devonian Mass Extinction, including the proliferation of diverse feeding strategies. This increase in morphological diversity and taxonomic richness has been interpreted as an adaptive radiation. Notable among these new forms are predatory, large-bodied, large-toothed ‘macrodont’ forms, an ecological category that is very rare in the Devonian. Despite an abundance of three-dimensional fossils, the anatomy and relationships of these macrodonts is poorly understood, presenting a barrier to understanding the evolutionary history of this specialised ecological role. A confused picture of relationships between lineages before and after the End-Devonian Mass Extinction also obscures patterns of survivorship and radiation. CT scanning will be used to target key taxa in order to resolve questions of phylogenetic affinity, clarifying whether the macrodont morphotype arose multiple times during the Palaeozoic diversification of actinopterygians and the innovations leading to their radiation. Although united by a common morphotype, different macrodont taxa show different specialisations of the teeth, jaws and internal cranial skeleton, hinting at varied ecological roles. Compilation of important geographic and environmental data will be used to investigate macroevolutionary patterns of dispersal and ecological expansion, including the contribution of macrodont actinopterygians to global trophic networks. In addition to resolving the long-standing puzzle of macrodont relationships, this project will have implications for understanding the radiation of actinopterygians in the aftermath of the End-Devonian Mass Extinction, building on the emerging picture of a more complicated pattern of extinction and recovery than previously thought.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Storylines of Risk Assessment for Wind and Flood Impacts in a Post-Net Zero Climate in the UK
jobs.description_html:
Explore the future of extreme weather in a post-net zero climate.

The UK is committed to achieving net zero greenhouse gas emissions, but important questions remain about how extreme weather risks may evolve after global temperatures stabilise. This project will investigate how the characteristics and impacts of extratropical cyclones, including damaging winds and associated flooding, may change in a post-net zero climate, and how these changes can be incorporated into climate-risk assessment frameworks.

Using simulations from the Zero Emissions Commitment Model Intercomparison Project (ZECMIP) and related climate-model datasets, the PhD student will analyse changes in storm tracks, frequency, intensity, and their associated compound wind-flood hazards affecting the UK. A key aim will be to translate climate-model outputs into risk metrics through the development of storyline-based approaches that capture plausible future hazard pathways. The project will explore how risk assessments can better represent uncertainty, high-impact low-likelihood events, and compound hazards.

The student will have significant scope to shape the direction of the research. Potential areas include investigating physical mechanisms driving storm changes, developing novel risk assessment methodologies, linking storylines to impact models, or improving the communication of future climate risks to decision-makers.

The student will receive interdisciplinary training in climate dynamics, extreme-event attribution and analysis, climate modelling, environmental risk assessment, and advanced statistical and data-science techniques. Training will include developing and evaluating risk metrics, working with large climate datasets, and translating scientific evidence into actionable resilience information for stakeholders.

The project is led by Professor Jennifer Catto and Dr Matthew Priestley at the University of Exeter, in collaboration with Professor Peter Watson at the University of Bristol. Through a CASE partnership with JBA Risk Management, the student will gain experience in industry-standard catastrophe modelling, flood and climate-risk analysis, and decision-support applications, including opportunities for placement-based training.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B20 Cooking with magma constraining the carbon emissions from large igneous provinces
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Past rapid climate change events like the end-Permian mass extinction, the end-Triassic mass extinction, the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, and many of the Mesozoic Oceanic Anoxic Events constitute some of the best analogues we have for anthropogenic climate change. These events feature some combination of rising atmospheric CO2, global warming, ocean acidification, and a negative carbon isotope excursion – all the hallmark signs of massive rapid emissions of carbon-based greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. The suspected trigger for these events is the coincident emplacement of large igneous provinces (LIPs); the intrusion of LIP magma into sedimentary rock is thought to be capable of generating massive quantities of greenhouse gases like thermogenic methane. However, when magma intrudes into sedimentary rock of various compositions it is still uncertain exactly which greenhouse gases are produced (e.g., methane vs. CO2) and in what quantities. Furthermore, the carbon isotopic composition of these gases is very poorly constrained. Carbon isotopes records (e.g. Fig. 1) show the net behaviour of the global carbon cycle across these past carbon cycle perturbation events. Knowing the mass and isotopic composition of LIP carbon emissions are critical to constraining Earth’s carbon cycle response – e.g., the short-term release of additional carbon as a response to the warming climate (positive feedbacks) and the longer-term subsequent carbon burial, cooling and restoring the climate (negative feedbacks).

In this project, you will conduct laboratory experiments subjecting a range of sedimentary host rocks to artificial thermal maturation to recreate the temperature and pressure conditions caused by magmatic intrusion. Your samples will include real exemplars of the host rocks into which the aforementioned LIPs were actually intruded. You will collect the thermogenic gases that result from this experimental maturation and measure the yields of the various gas types as well as their carbon isotopic compositions. Lastly, using numerical modelling, you will use your experimental results to make some predictions of the carbon emissions from several past LIPs, thereby constraining the Earth system carbon cycle response. Depending on the interests of the appointed candidate, the project could lean more heavily towards hands-on laboratory work or applying numerical modelling techniques.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - From Catchment to Tap Tracing Contaminants of Emerging Contaminants through South West Drinking-water Sources
jobs.description_html:
(a) Chemicals of emerging concern (CECs), notably PFAS, are increasingly detected in freshwaters abstracted for UK drinking water, as standards tighten (DWI, EU Watch List). Yet we cannot say which CECs reach source waters, where they come from, or which pass through treatment. This project asks: Which CECs occur across South West catchments and reservoirs, and from which sources? How do they partition, persist and transform between water, sediment and reservoir? Which escape removal by treatment such as granular activated carbon (GAC)? Answers underpin evidence-based catchment management and regulation.

(b) The Doctoral Researcher (DR) will design seasonal sampling from catchment to tap, including raw, in-process and treated waters at operational sites not publicly accessible. Suspect and non-target screening by GC- and LC-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), with targeted PFAS quantification, will characterise occurrence and sources. In vitro bioassays (effect-based monitoring) will link chemical profiles to biological activity, while laboratory columns and full-scale works data quantify GAC removal and breakthrough.

(c) Supervisors will provide hands-on training in fieldwork design, HRMS data acquisition and processing, compound identification, cheminformatics (Python), bioassay interpretation and sorption experiments, with weekly supervision and regular writing feedback. A CASE internship at South West Water will provide training in water-treatment operations, compliance monitoring and regulatory practice, building careers across environmental, regulatory and utility sectors.

(d) CASE partner South West Water will provide access to reservoirs, treatment works and operational data, samples beyond publicly accessible locations, a named co-supervisor and a minimum three-month internship, ensuring findings address real sector priorities. Exeter's CREWW brings non-target screening capability and Bristol (Dr Charlotte Lloyd) catchment contaminant expertise, with extended time in both groups. The DR will choose which catchments, contaminant classes and strand (sources, effect-based monitoring or treatment) to prioritise, supported by joint supervisory meetings with all partners.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Predicting Flood Impacts in Dynamic Rivers
jobs.description_html:
Flooding has the greatest socio-economic impact of all natural hazards and is expected to worsen due to anthropogenic climate change and population growth in flood-prone areas. In dynamic geomorphic environments (often in the global south), rivers migrate rapidly, reshaping floodplain topography, and driving changes in flood conveyance capacity. However, existing flood risk projections in such environments use flood models that treat rivers and floodplains as static landscape features. We invite PhD applications to investigate how dynamic rivers build evolving floodplain landscapes, generate changing risk scenarios, and impact floodplain populations.

Methods and Training: Project supervisors (Rolf Aalto, Andrew Nicholas, Jeff Neal) will provide a stimulating research environment for investigating dynamic river flood risk within which a student can develop an individual project supported by training in field and remote sensing data analysis, numerical modelling, and machine learning. The project combines Exeter’s strength in modelling and monitoring river evolution (e.g., Brückner et al., 2026, Science Advances; Brückner et al., 2025, Geology) with Bristol’s expertise in flood modelling, remote sensing and hazard exposure (e.g., Neal et al., 2026, Water Resources Research). The supervisors have collaborated for c. 5 years, including ongoing projects (NE/S015612/1, UKRI4333). The student will work alongside a team of researchers in river dynamics and population vulnerability to connect fundamental river science with assessments of floodplain habitability and river management.

Researcher influence: The researcher will determine: study locations (globally); morphodynamic focus (mechanisms/styles of river evolution); methodological focus (e.g., modelling, remote sensing, machine learning); optional inclusion of field work within project. For example, PhD research could combine several approaches to investigate how dynamic rivers respond to changing climate, sediment supply, and human intervention. Ultimately, the PhD will be developed jointly with the student, utilizing data and methods available through the team’s research on global river systems.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Learning the kinetic rules of DNA amplification through high-throughput EXPAR and machine learning
jobs.description_html:
EXPAR is an extremely rapid isothermal DNA amplification reaction, but its behaviour changes substantially with DNA sequence and reaction conditions. An assay that works well for one sequence can become slow, unreliable or dominated by spontaneous amplification when only a few bases are changed. This makes new EXPAR assays difficult to design and still requires substantial empirical optimisation.

This PhD will develop a high-throughput experimental approach to determine the rules that govern EXPAR. The student will measure complete amplification curves across many DNA sequences while systematically varying polymerase and nicking enzyme concentration, buffer, temperature, template design and starting target concentration. Statistical design of experiments, Bayesian optimisation and machine learning will then be used to identify the important factors and efficiently explore this large parameter space.

Our central hypothesis is that these data contain transferable sequence-kinetic relationships that can be used to predict how previously unseen DNA targets will amplify. This will be tested prospectively using new sequences. Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) will provide a particularly demanding test because the assay must discriminate DNA sequences that differ by only one base. This provides a stringent way to determine whether the models capture sequence-dependent EXPAR behaviour rather than simply fitting individual targets.

The outcome will be quantitative design rules for EXPAR rather than an optimised recipe for one target. This will make rapid nucleic-acid amplification more predictable, reproducible and transferable between biological sequences.

The project will be supervised by Dr Robert E Simpson. For more information, see: https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/cross_fac/mibtp/phd/supervisors/RSimpson/

Funding notes:

The MIBTP provides fully funded four-year PhD studentships, covering tuition fees, a tax-free annual stipend of £21,805 (2026/27 rate), approximately £4,500 per year for research consumables, and additional funding for travel and conferences.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Kinetic co-design of DNA amplification and ultrasensitive photonic sensing
jobs.description_html:
Our central hypothesis is that more reliable and earlier DNA mutation discrimination can be achieved by co-optimising DNA amplification and photonic sensing.

The PhD candidate will study how the DNA amplification reactions can be codesigned with a novel DNA sensing system. They will consider the system-level probelm rather than optimising each component in isolation. Statistical, kinetic and Bayesian models will be used to optimise this coupled biochemical-photonic system. Detecting Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) will provide a demanding test because the system must distinguish DNA sequences that differ by only one base. The PhD thesis will test whether whether co-designing the whole system can improve sequence discrimination when target and reference strands are otherwise almost identical.

Funding notes:
The MIBTP provides fully funded four-year PhD studentships, covering tuition fees, a tax-free annual stipend of £21,805 (2026/27 rate), approximately £4,500 per year for research consumables, and additional funding for travel and conferences.

References:

https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/cross_fac/mibtp/phd/supervisors/RSimpson/#photonic_sensing

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Polar Turbulence: Improving Boundary-layer Performance in Weather and Climate Simulations
jobs.description_html:
(a) Key science questions and their importance

The stratified atmospheric boundary layer is a key component in high-impact weather and climate predictions. Forecast applications include polar surface temperatures, the timing of thunderstorms and night-time low temperatures. There is a need to improve the way the stratified boundary layer is represented (parametrized) in these simulations and interrogate the models with high-quality observations. This project asks whether extending the parametrization from first to second order can improve simulations. It also asks whether observations can better constrain simulations of the stratified boundary layer.

(b) Methods

The project will develop and test a second-order boundary-layer parametrization in single column and Large Eddy Simulation settings, evaluating it against state-of-the-art British Antarctic Survey (BAS) observations under stably stratified conditions. Computational modelling will use Python and FORTRAN, with AI tools explored to analyse modelled turbulence patterns.

(c) Training opportunities for the Doctoral Researcher

The student will be trained in weather/climate model structure and in computational modelling using Python and FORTRAN, alongside a range of project-relevant Masters modules at the University of Exeter. The supervisory team and partners will also provide other hands-on training: interrogating models against BAS observations (see BAS visits below), developing data-analysis and scientific-writing skills. The student will take increasing ownership of the project in its duration, eventually writing their own code, initiating scientific writing and presenting their work to the scientific community. This training will equip them for a career in atmospheric science.

(d) Collaboration with project partners

The project is co-supervised by the British Antarctic Survey (Dr Alex Weiss) and SAMS (Dr Phil Anderson, formerly BAS), collaborations giving the student access to specialist polar observations and expertise. There will be at least one visit a year to BAS for the student, and Dr Weiss will visit Exeter at least once a year.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Nanoconfined Water From Molecular Physics to Mechanical Energy Absorption
jobs.description_html:
How does water behave when confined within spaces comparable to the size of individual molecules? Can we exploit this unusual behaviour to create materials with mechanical properties beyond those of conventional solids and liquids?

This PhD project will investigate water confined within nanoporous materials, particularly metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), which won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2025. Under mechanical pressure, water can be forced into hydrophobic nanopores, creating new solid–liquid interfaces and enabling efficient, reversible mechanical energy absorption. These molecular-scale processes can produce remarkable macroscopic responses, offering opportunities for impact protection, vibration damping and other technologies.

The research will explore how molecular interactions, pore structures, water transport and dynamic loading collectively determine material behaviour across multiple length and time scales, from molecular motion to engineering-scale mechanical responses.

Depending on the successful candidate's interests and expertise, the project may involve technique development, materials synthesis and characterisation, advanced mechanical and high-pressure testing, synchrotron/neutron/laser techniques, computational modelling, application prototyping, or combinations of these approaches. The specific scope will be developed collaboratively to build on the candidate's strengths while encouraging interdisciplinary exploration.

Who We Are Looking For

This is a highly interdisciplinary project, and we warmly welcome applicants from diverse scientific and engineering backgrounds, including but not limited to:

Chemistry: Nanoporous materials, crystallography, spectroscopy, physical chemistry, materials chemistry.
Physics: Molecular physics, multiscale modelling, thermodynamics, nanofluidics, shock physics.
Materials Science: Nanomaterials, soft matter, polymers, hydrogels.
Mechanics and Engineering: Solid and fluid mechanics, impact dynamics, acoustics, mechanical design.

Applicants are not expected to have experience across all these areas. We particularly value scientific curiosity, creativity, motivation and an interest in learning across disciplinary boundaries. Applicants should have a good degree (equivalent to a UK First or at least a 2:1) in one of the disciplines above.

Research Environment and Opportunities

The successful candidate will join an interdisciplinary research team at the University of Birmingham, working within a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship programme that bridges chemistry, physics, materials science and engineering. See: www.ysunlab.com

The project offers opportunities to work with advanced experimental techniques, access major research facilities including synchrotron, neutron, and laser sources, and collaborate with leading international researchers.

We are committed to providing a supportive, inclusive and collaborative research environment, with dedicated time, support, funding, and training opportunities for professional development, scientific communication, networking and career progression.

To apply, please contact Dr Yueting Sun (y.sun.9@bham.ac.uk) with a CV and a brief description of their research interests and background. Informal enquiries from applicants across different disciplines are very welcome.

References:

1. Sun et al, High-rate nanofluidic energy absorption in porous zeolitic frameworks. Nature Materials, 20(7), (2021).
2. Sun and Jiang, Mechanical energy absorption of metal–organic frameworks. In: Tan J-C (ed.), Mechanical Behaviour of Metal–Organic Framework Materials, Royal Society of Chemistry (2023).
3. Lai et al, Liquids with high compressibility. Advanced Materials, 35(44), 2306521 (2023).

Additional Funding Information

The successful applicant will receive 3.5 years of funding, covering tuition fees at the UK rate and a tax-free stipend at the UKRI minimum (£21,805 per year for 2026/27). A Travel and Training grant will support research and professional development throughout the PhD. International applicants are welcome to apply if they can cover the fee difference. Home fee status may apply to UK and Irish nationals and EU citizens with settled status, subject to relevant residency and eligibility requirements.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Improved Extreme Climate Indices for Food Security Risk Analysis
jobs.description_html:
Extreme weather is increasingly threatening UK food production, as shown vividly by 2026's wet winter followed by a record summer drought. Existing climate indices and process-based crop models poorly capture how such compound, rapidly-alternating extremes translate into yield and supply-chain shocks, weakening the evidence base for resilience and adaptation planning. This project asks: which climate indices and modelling approaches best explain observed UK crop losses from recent extremes, and how can these be improved to anticipate future risk?

The student will first benchmark existing extreme-event indices and process-based models (e.g. JULES-crop) against observed UK yield and production data, using 2026 as a key case study alongside other recent shock years. They will then develop improved indices, drawing on extreme value statistics to characterise compound and antecedent-conditions effects, and apply these across representative UK arable systems. Finally, they will combine these indices with climate projections to assess future risk and support adaptation planning, feeding findings back into climate model and observation development.

Training spans climate and crop-model data handling, extreme value and machine-learning methods, and scientific communication, via DLTP courses, Exeter's data science training, and close supervisory mentoring. The student will help shape the balance of observational, statistical and modelling work as findings emerge, with regular discussion of research direction and support to pursue their own ideas within the project's scope.

The project is co-developed with the Met Office (CASE partner: Falloon), whose Hadley Centre climate data, crop modelling expertise and food security service provide "on-the-job" training unavailable in academia; the student will spend substantial time working there. Co-supervision by Bebber (Biosciences) and Youngman (Mathematics and Statistics) at Exeter, alongside Falloon (Met Office and Bristol), brings together ecological, statistical and operational climate-service expertise. The student will benefit from interactions with Exeter's lively interdisciplinary research networks, including the Centre for Environmental Intelligence.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Closing the Aquatic Observational Gap: Low-Cost Environmental Sensing from Recreational Watercraft
jobs.department: Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Aquatic environments face increasing pressures, including extreme events and climate-driven ecosystem change. Yet existing observations often fail to capture fine-scale spatial and temporal variability of nearshore environments where people live and recreate. This study will investigate whether recreational watercraft can become distributed observing platforms, providing observations at scales poorly captured by conventional monitoring. It will address: (1) What spatial and temporal variability in nearshore environments is revealed by distributed observations from recreational watercraft?
