(2) Can low-cost sensing resolve biologically important variability, including phytoplankton dynamics and indicators of eutrophication? (3) Which combination of sensing technologies provides useful observations for understanding and managing aquatic environmental change?

You will develop, calibrate and evaluate a modular sensing package for surfboards, kayaks and stand-up paddleboards. Initial work will explore optical measurements, using low-cost technologies or solutions that can be efficiently scaled. Laboratory experiments, field deployments and data analysis will quantify sensor performance and uncertainty. Training will include low-cost sensor development, environmental and bio-optical measurements, field techniques, experimental design, programming, data science, statistics, machine learning and scientific communication, alongside GW4+ training. You can explore interests including signal processing using artificial intelligence, sensor miniaturisation, citizen science / public engagement, bio-optical modelling or uncertainty propagation.

The study is enabled by complementary expertise. Drs Brewin and Bresnahan contribute expertise in low-cost sensing and ocean observation, building on their work using recreational water users as observers. Professor Simis (Plymouth Marine Laboratory) provides expertise in phytoplankton ecology, bio-optics, in situ sensing and Earth observation, while Dr Panici (Exeter CREWW) contributes sensing and data-driven expertise and Dr Frensley on citizen science. The study will link to the PEDAL (Prediction and Early Detection of Algal Blooms in lakes and reservoirs) project, connecting sensing with Exeter–PML research on algal-bloom detection and prediction. Together, the partnership will translate sensing technologies into observations and solutions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Bee Behaviour and Pollination Services across Structurally Diverse Floral Habitats
jobs.description_html:
The diversity of bee populations is essential for sustaining the richness of plant communities. Yet little is known about how species-specific differences in behaviour influence pollination networks and ecosystem services. A key unresolved question is how bees move in structurally complex landscapes containing vertical barriers such as hedgerows which increase travel costs. Understanding how bees balance these costs, and how this shapes resource partitioning among pollinators, is crucial for predicting pollination services and ecosystem resilience. The rural landscapes of Devon provide an ideal setting for this research.

Devon hedges are biodiverse microhabitats but change the distribution of floral resources available to pollinators. By integrating behavioural observations, environmental data, and quantitative models, the project will identify how bees navigate and forage in heterogeneous landscapes, providing evidence-based guidance for conserving hedgerows and pollination services, and supporting rewilding and sustainable land-management strategies.

The project offers exciting opportunities to test how movement strategies result in species-specific trade-offs between navigation efficiency and pollination outcomes. Specific hypotheses will be developed collaboratively, goals set out together, whilst also considering how research directions and skills development align with the candidate’s background, interests and career ambitions. Training in field, experimental and modelling techniques is enhanced by state-of-the-art use of remote-sensing and spectral image analysis for habitat measurements, as well as newly developed tracking methods to record movement trajectories of forager bees. The team of GW4+ supervisors has previously developed and successfully collaborated, also jointly supervised research students, building on their complementary expertise in behaviour, ecology, remote sensing, computational and modelling work.

Their ongoing research collaborations with current project partners in Sheffield and Sussex offer the student access to unique development opportunities. This project equips the student with highly transferable quantitative, analytical, and field-based skills that are sought after in both academic research and the environmental, conservation, and land-management sectors.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Investigating the Viability of a Mainland Re-introduction of the Glanville Fritillary Butterfly: A Genomic and Habitat Viability Assessment
jobs.description_html:
(a) The questions. Britain's Glanville fritillary (Melitaea cinxia) is restricted to a single metapopulation on the Isle of Wight, repeatedly bottlenecked and probably among Europe's most genetically depauperate butterfly populations. Has inbreeding depression reached a level that limits viability? Which source populations would restore genetic variation without eroding local adaptation? And can genetically informed founders establish a self-sustaining population at a new site? Conservation translocation is expanding across England, yet source populations are still chosen with little genetic evidence.

(b) Methods. The researcher will sequence butterfly genomes from the Isle of Wight and from populations in the Channel Islands, Normandy and Åland to estimate population genetic diversity, inbreeding and genetic load. Experimental crosses among individuals between populations will test whether admixed offspring show improved performance. Larval survival depends on the availability of fine-scale warm microclimates; drone surveys will assess the suitability of potential reintroduction sites on the mainland against the thermal requirements identified by Curtis on the Isle of Wight. These complementary datasets will determine whether genetic rescue of the Glanville fritillary is feasible and inform the development of a protocol for reintroducing a rescued population on the mainland, where the species historically occurred.

(c) Training. Bilde and Orozco-terWengel train the researcher in population genetics, bioinformatics and conservation. Alford supervises in thermal ecology and physiology, and Curtis in field methods and drone imaging. Writing is staged from the first-year review to lead-authored papers.

(d) Collaboration. The supervisors have complementary expertise: conservation genomics and population recovery (Bilde and Orozco-terWengel), field ecology (Curtis), and thermal physiology (Alford). Through integrative collaboration, the researcher will learn to generate and analyse whole-genome data, design and run breeding experiments, and survey habitats in the field, following a single question from genome to habitat and covering the breadth of disciplines that conservation genomics now requires.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Dynamic Turbulence Modelling for Convective Storms
jobs.description_html:
Convective storms remain notoriously difficult to predict because of their highly localised nature and dependence on interactions across a wide range of scales, from turbulent motions to the synoptic environment. Operational forecasting is therefore moving towards increasingly high-resolution models to better capture high-impact weather events. However, refining model resolution does not necessarily lead to an improvement in forecast skill, particularly at sub-kilometre resolutions where turbulent motions are only partially resolved.

This project will investigate how the representation of unresolved turbulence affects convective-scale simulations and develop an adaptive turbulence parametrisation that can improve convective weather forecasting. At these so-called grey-zone resolutions, the assumptions underlying conventional parametrisations break down, requiring a fundamental rethinking of how turbulent processes are represented.

The researcher will develop and test a novel approach originating from computational fluid dynamics, in which turbulence closure parameters are dynamically diagnosed from the evolving flow rather than prescribed beforehand. The scheme will be implemented in Met Office modelling systems and tested using high-resolution simulations simulations of reference shallow and deep convection case studies and observational data.

They will be encouraged to take increasing ownership of the project and its scientific direction. Depending on their interests, they may explore physical interpretation, develop new diagnostics, or investigate data-driven approaches to turbulence closure. This can lead to new research questions, supporting progression towards independent research.

Training will include atmospheric science, fluid dynamics and numerical modelling, alongside substantial practical experience in High Performance Computing, scientific programming, model development, data analysis, visualisation and scientific writing.

The project forms part of an established partnership with the Met Office to develop turbulence parametrisations for the next-generation forecasting systems. The researcher will spend time at the Met Office, working directly with model developers, participate in joint project meetings and have opportunities to shape future developments in weather prediction systems.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Automated AI-based Monitoring of Interaction Networks for Biodiversity Conservation
jobs.description_html:
Loss of biodiversity is threatening essential ecosystem functions such as pollination. To provide an early warning of ecosystem degradation and assess ecosystem health using plant-pollinator interactions as a model system, we propose to research and develop innovative approaches that can capture community- and function-level responses to disturbance in near real time to overcome long-standing challenges in network ecology and provide actionable insights into ecosystem health.

Objective: This PhD project aims is to research, develop and operationalise a fully automated, AI-based system for detecting, tracking, and analysing plant-pollinator interactions, generating high-resolution plant-pollinator network data at scale. The project contains four components characterised by specific methodologies supported by training expertise within the team:

  • Computer vision optimisation to record plant-pollinator interactions (Partner: UKCEH’s Tom August, Chair of Insect AI, a COST action network on computer vision for insects);
  • Deep-learning models for species identification and tracking (Supervisor: Thomas O’Shea-Wheller, UoExeter);
  • Quantify and validating AI vs. human-derived interaction networks (Supervisors: Chris Kaiser-Bunbury (PI) and Dirk Sanders, UoExeter); and
  • Operationalise AI-pipeline (Supervisor: David Baker, UoExeter; Partner: Matt Heard, National Trust’s chief scientist) to deliver evidence-based network tools to monitor and enhance ecosystem recovery to land managers and policymakers.

The supervisory team includes experts in each research component, providing the student with in-depth training and supervision, e.g. in network analysis, community ecology, insect and plant identification, app development). In addition to the mandatory training, the student will receive access to National Trust habitats and will gain experience on the research-policy-interface through a placement at the project partner. UKCEH will provide specific training in automated pollinator monitoring (incl. AI-based computer vision) and data processing through extended research stays at UKCEH.

We are actively encouraging students to increase depth and complexity of these research components based on their specific interests and desired skill sets.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Harnessing the Appetite of Sea Cucumbers as Detritivores to Clean up Aquaculture Practices
jobs.description_html:
Existing aquaculture practices in open and semi-open pens generate large amounts of excess organic waste (uneaten feed and faeces), which when it accumulates can significantly degrade coastal sediments having a major impact on ecosystem processes. This contrasts with intensive closed aquaculture systems where advanced filtration systems are used to prevent waste entering surrounding environments. Detritivorous sea cucumbers could provide a viable natural solution to process excess organic material.

In this PhD project, the role of sea cucumbers will be assessed for their efficacy to consume excess organic matter from open and semi-open sea pens. The project will involve working closely with collaborative project partners at the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre (SMSRC) in the United Arab Emirates and Jaffna in northern Sri Lanka to establish nature-based solutions to support sustainable aquaculture practices. Controlled and field trials will quantify Holothuria scabra's waste-processing thresholds, guiding transferable, sediment-safe aquaculture across tropical coasts.

The Doctoral Researcher will be supported by an interdisciplinary supervisory team to co-design a project that explores invertebrate physiology, feeding practices, and sediment biogeochemistry.  The student will be trained in a wide range of interdisciplinary skills via supervisory support at Exeter and Bristol including experimental design, data analysis and scientific writing, with partners at SMSRC contributing expertise in analytical approaches.

The Doctoral Researcher will have flexibility to develop physiological, biogeochemical, ecological and molecular approaches, exploring sea cucumbers' capacity to restore sediment function and their wider ecosystem contribution. Embedded within local teams at SMSRC and Jaffna, the student will have opportunities to provide new insights into the ecological role of sea cucumbers and integrate these directly into aquaculture practice. Outcomes will advance our understanding of the functional role of detritivores and support in the development of solutions to tackle the growing impacts of open pen aquaculture on coastal environments.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Costly Signalling and Mate Search in wild Fiddler Crabs
jobs.description_html:
Sexual selection is a potent evolutionary force, responsible for astonishing diversity in morphology and behaviour. To understand how such striking displays have evolved, we need to know (1) how individuals adjust their display behaviour depending on the social environment and their own physiological state; and (2) how individuals choose among potential mates whose displays change rapidly over time.

This PhD project will tackle these questions using a combination of evolutionary modelling and cutting-edge behavioural experiments in a wild population of West African fiddler crabs (Afruca tangeri). The theoretical component will involve building models (using dynamic programming, or evolutionary computer simulations, or both) to predict adaptive strategies for courtship and mate search. The empirical component will involve field trips (May-July) to our study site in southern Portugal, where thousands of fiddler crabs can be studied at close quarters in their natural environment. In this species, male crabs develop an enlarged major claw (around 30% of their body weight) that they use in waving and drumming displays to attract females. We have recently developed techniques to measure the energetic costs of male courtship in real time using flow-through respirometry, and to simulate competition from rival males using biomimetic robots.

We can also follow the detailed mate-search behaviour of female crabs using miniature Bluetooth devices and automated video tracking. Our supervisory team is an interdisciplinary collaboration across the DLTP partnership and will provide bespoke training in behavioural fieldwork (Darden—Exeter), ecophysiology and sensory ecology (How—Bristol), game theory and evolutionary simulations (Fawcett—Exeter), as well as more general skills including data analysis and scientific writing. There are many exciting directions the work could take and we are especially keen to hear from students who want to play an active role in designing the project.

Further reading:
Wilde et al. (2025) doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2025.1570
Hollon et al. (2023) doi.org/10.1007/s00265-023-03296-9

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: How do Peatland Restoration Activities Influence Drought Resilience and the Reliability of Water Supplies Under Future Climate Pressures?
jobs.description_html:
Peatland restoration is widely promoted as a nature-based solution for enhancing climate resilience, yet its effects on drought resilience and water resource provision remain poorly quantified. With ~70% of UK drinking water sourced from upland catchments and droughts projected to become more frequent and severe, there is an urgent need to understand whether peatland restoration can enhance water security and support evidence-based investment in restoration.

This project will address three key questions:

  1. How do peatland restoration activities influence water storage and hydrological response during drought?
  2. Which peat properties and ecohydrological processes control drought resilience? and
  3. How might restoration alter peatland hydrology and water resource provision under current and future climates?

The project will combine field monitoring of water table depth, soil moisture, rainfall and evapotranspiration with laboratory characterisation of peat hydraulic and physical properties. These observations will be integrated with existing environmental datasets to parameterise and evaluate site-scale process-based models and catchment-scale probabilistic models, quantifying the influence of peatland restoration on drought resilience and water-resource provision under current and future climate scenarios.

The supervisory team will provide training in field hydrology, environmental monitoring, laboratory techniques, data science, hydrological modelling, uncertainty analysis and scientific writing. The Doctoral Researcher will also benefit from training opportunities across the University of Exeter and CREWW, where they will be embedded within a multidisciplinary research environment.

South West Peatland Partnership (part of South West Water) will act as CASE partner, providing access to restoration sites, long-term datasets, practitioner expertise and an industry placement. Collaboration with the Environment Agency will provide policy and regulatory perspectives. Through training, supervision and partnership working, the Doctoral Researcher will shape the project direction, including methods, modelling approaches and management scenarios, ensuring outputs are scientifically robust and directly relevant to water-resource management and peatland restoration practice.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Seagrass as a Natural Defence: Microbiomes, Pathogens and Coastal Water Quality in the Face of Environmental Change
jobs.description_html:
Seagrass meadows provide vital ecosystem services, but their potential to reduce harmful waterborne bacteria remains largely unexplored. We ask whether Zostera marina reduces the abundance or persistence of bacterial pathogens in coastal waters, whether its associated microbiome contributes to this effect, and how these interactions respond to environmental change and episodic pollution. Resolving these questions could reveal an overlooked contribution of seagrass and its restoration to coastal water quality and further understand how this vital coastal habitat responds to multiple stressors.

The project will uniquely link field observations with mechanistic experiments under controlled conditions. Building on preliminary cultivation trials and expertise across the partnership, the researcher will optimise Z. marina cultivation in bespoke recirculating mesocosms within Exeter’s Containment Level 2 Global Meteorological Simulator (GMS). The GMS will provide a highly controlled environment for manipulating environmentally relevant bacterial pathogens alongside key aquatic conditions identified through field studies. Experiments will examine pathogen persistence with and without seagrass and test responses to gradual environmental change and acute water-quality perturbations. Quantitative microbiology and profiling of leaf, root and rhizosphere microbiomes will investigate underlying mechanisms. Field studies across contrasting seagrass environments will test laboratory-derived relationships under natural conditions and generate new hypotheses for controlled experiments.

The researcher will gain interdisciplinary training in seagrass cultivation and field ecology, pathogen microbiology, microbial community analysis, mesocosm experimentation, experimental design, data analysis and scientific writing. Findings will shape subsequent field and laboratory studies, enabling the researcher to develop their own questions and experimental directions with supervisory support.

The team combines complementary expertise in pathogen ecology and controlled-environment experimentation (Exeter-Streatham), seagrass field ecology and water quality (Exeter-Penryn), seagrass conservation, cultivation and restoration (Ocean Conservation Trust), and marine pollution and biogeochemistry (PML). These closely connected capabilities, alongside established regional water-sector partnerships, provide a distinctive field-to-laboratory framework for addressing this unresolved problem.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Understanding and Managing Solutions for Emerging UK Fisheries Challenges: Expansion of Bluefin Tuna into the North Sea
jobs.description_html:
RESEARCH QUESTION: Decades of work on protected areas, rewilding and careful management have produced several conservation gains. The return of Atlantic bluefin tuna to the North Sea after a 60-year absence is one such story, but it also poses an environmental solutions question that this PhD will tackle: how do we manage the re-emergence of an apex predator into ecosystems now naïve to it, and coastal communities that wish to exploit it? And how does this feed forward into rewilding and other conservation projects? This PhD will improve our understanding of the consequences of rapid re-expansion of the species, ecosystem function and stock management, and build the interdisciplinary, systems-thinking skillset for the researcher that NERC's environmental solutions agenda calls for.

METHODS: This project takes a science for environmental solutions approach, tackling demographic recovery (using fisheries surveys), genetic health (using molecular ecology), ecosystem function (with modelling) and fisheries governance (using stakeholder surveying) through a unique and diverse supervisory partnership across science and policy.

TRAINING: The researcher will be trained in marine field skills (tagging tuna and carrying out fisheries surveys) at Exeter and with NEIFCA, including time at sea on their research vessel. They will also be trained in programming and ecosystem modelling at Exeter and PML, in molecular ecology at Exeter, in policy at Natural England, and stakeholder engagement at collaborator The Angling Trust. They will present their work at international training courses and conferences, building personal reputation and understanding they can use to direct the research as it evolves. This multi-disciplinary approach to brand new challenges in fisheries will position the researcher at the front of the field.

PROJECT PARTNER COLLABORATION: The supervisors have built this meaningful and strong partnership over many years, working from diverse angles, and bringing together our shared needs and interests to this important project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - From Catchment to Coast: eDNA Surveillance of Eukaryotic Parasites in Aquatic Environments
jobs.description_html:
Environmental DNA (eDNA) is transforming biodiversity monitoring, but its potential to reveal the hidden distribution of eukaryotic parasites remains largely untapped. This project will develop and validate eDNA as a new, scalable surveillance tool for parasites affecting human, animal and ecosystem health. It will address three fundamental questions: which parasites can be reliably detected and quantified from environmental samples; which sampling and molecular approaches maximise sensitivity and repeatability; and which environmental processes drive parasite distributions across catchment-to-coast systems?

Using Cornwall as a natural laboratory for developing transferable monitoring approaches, the student will develop and optimise qPCR/ddPCR and next-generation sequencing approaches, experimentally compare conventional water filtration with integrative MetaProbe sampling, and undertake replicated spatial and seasonal freshwater, estuarine and marine surveillance. Environmental modelling will identify drivers including temperature, rainfall, land use and wastewater influence, and establish when eDNA abundance permits quantitative inference.

The student will actively co-design the project, selecting focal parasites from key eukaryotic parasites including Cryptosporidium, Giardia, Toxoplasma, Anisakis and Pseudoterranova, and selective among sampling locations, methodological comparisons and One Health questions to pursue. Results will determine subsequent sampling and experiments, supported by regular supervision, research planning and one-to-one coaching in scientific reasoning, writing and publication.

Training will span molecular biology, eDNA assay development, sequencing, bioinformatics and fieldwork in the Hayward laboratory; advanced quantitative modelling with Professor Mario Recker; and marine-eDNA training during a research visit with world-leading eDNA expert Professor Stefano Mariani. Annual placements with CASE partner Trace Biomonitoring will provide an industrial dimension, with hands-on experience in commercial eDNA workflows, QA/QC, scalable sampling, reporting and translation into operational environmental monitoring, ensuring methods are developed from the outset for scientific robustness, scalability and real-world adoption. Collectively, these complementary environments will train the student across molecular innovation and ecological discovery to quantitative analysis and development of real-world environmental solutions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Exploring the Influence of Magma-mush Processes on Volcanic Unrest
jobs.description_html:
Volcanic eruptions threaten 10% of the world’s population. To enable eruption forecasting, carry out hazard assessment, and mitigate risk, a thorough understanding of volcanic unrest is essential, but currently lacking. Surface deformation is one of the main indicators of volcanic unrest and has begun to be interpreted using models based on magma migrating and accumulating in a magma-mush reservoir, but they have limitations.

For example, how does heterogeneity in the system effect predictions? How important is the vertical connectivity of the system? How well do they relate to other indicators of unrest, such as seismicity and gravity? This PhD project will drive innovation in modelling magma-mush processes and the generated surface deformation and seismicity during volcanic unrest episodes. The student will incorporate the fast-evolving understanding of magma-mush systems into new numerical models (e.g., using the finite element method) simulating surface deformation from porous fluid (magma) flow, and test how predicted subsurface stress and strain may relate to patterns of volcanic earthquakes. Models will be applied to case-study volcanoes co-selected with the PhD student and collaborators at local volcano observatories.

Possible examples include volcanoes in Japan, the eastern Caribbean, Ecuador, and Costa Rica. The student will benefit from expert project co-supervisors from the University of Bristol and British Geological Survey, exploiting volcanology and geophysics research ties across the three institutions, and exposing the student to a greater variety of complementary research directions and applications. The student will also receive training in numerical modelling, data processing and analysis, and communication of science to diverse audiences, with options for overseas fieldwork for collaborative data retrieval. Project results will improve how surface deformation and seismicity are interpreted during volcanic unrest, with tangible impact for institutions dealing with volcanic crises.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Tracing Environmental Change Through Antarctic Food Webs: Stable-Isotope Ecology of Antarctic Seals
jobs.description_html:
Antarctic marine ecosystems are undergoing rapid environmental change, yet we do not know how changes in ocean productivity and food web structure propagate to top predators. This project will ask: (1) how do environmental variability and changing food web structure influence the diet, trophic position and foraging strategies of Antarctic seals? (2) Do individuals, populations and species respond differently through time and space? and (3) can stable isotope analyses (SIA) reveal ecological responses to environmental change and inform understanding of ecosystem resilience?

The Doctoral Researcher will combine bulk-tissue SIA and compound-specific SIA (amino acids) of seal tissues with environmental and prey data, enabling complementary investigation of trophic ecology and food web baseline variation. Analyses will include isotope mixing and niche approaches, Bayesian modelling, multivariate statistics and reproducible data science workflows. The student will have flexibility to refine hypotheses, develop their own research questions and pursue emerging opportunities as results develop, supported by the supervisory team.

The project will provide training in animal biological sampling, sample preparation, laboratory protocols, Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometry (Elementar Analyser and Gas Chromatography), analytical quality control, isotope interpretation, statistical and Bayesian modelling, coding, data visualisation, scientific writing and field techniques. Collaborators from different Antarctic international research programmes have already committed samples, providing samples across Antarctica, with opportunities for the student to contribute to biological sampling during field activities where feasible. The student will also benefit from the GW4+ DLTP training programme.

Collaboration between University of Exeter, British Antarctic Survey and University of Bath will integrate expertise in marine predator and stable isotope ecology, Antarctic spatial and environmental ecology, and molecular, evolutionary and quantitative ecology. Co-supervision and opportunities to work across partner institutions will provide interdisciplinary training, expand the student’s scientific network and develop their ability to connect biochemical, ecological and environmental approaches to Antarctic ecosystem change.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Quantifying the Risk of Persistent Extreme Weather Events in a Changing Climate
jobs.description_html:
Persistent extreme weather events such as heatwaves, cold snaps, or particularly rainy and/or stormy seasons have huge socio-economic impact; estimating the probabilities of their occurrence which can inform assessments of health or flood risks is therefore an important task. These probabilities are likely to change in a nonlinear way under climate change.

This project will develop and explore novel data-driven techniques for quantifying the likelihood of persistent weather extremes. The approach is based on large-deviation theory, originally introduced in statistical physics to quantify probabilities of rare trajectories in dynamical systems. In particular, the methodology allows for extrapolation to events of so far unprecedented duration and severity. We will apply the methodology to data sets from the large-scale CMIP climate model simulations and the convection-permitting UK Climate Projections (UKCP18) as well as observational data sets such as the Central England Temperature time series and ERA5 reanalysis.

The project offers scope for the student to shape its direction, whether by focusing on a particular type of extreme, investigating multivariate approaches designed for compound events, or linking persistent extremes with large-scale atmospheric circulation regimes.

The student will receive sector-leading training encompassing technical research skills broadly in the areas of statistics, data science, machine learning and computing with applications in weather and climate science as well as generic skills such as science writing, presentation and networking.

The research will be carried out in close collaboration with two project partners, the Met Office and the company JBA Risk Management, with interests in UK heatwaves as well as high cumulative precipitation events and their implications for flood risk. The collaborative partners will provide non-commercial and commercial, non-academic research environments; these will enhance the student's training and research experience through co-supervision directing the project towards relevant risk applications, provision of data sets, and opportunities for work placements.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Understanding the Ecological and Evolutionary Drivers of Virus and Bacteria Host Shifts in UK Moths
jobs.description_html:
Emerging infectious diseases often arise when pathogens jump into new host species, yet the factors determining which hosts share viral and bacterial pathogens remain poorly understood. Using an unparalleled dataset comprising meta-genomic data from >7000 individual moths representing >330 UK moth-species as part of an ongoing NERC PtF grant, this project will address:

  1. How frequently microbes (viruses and bacteria) shift between host species
  2. How host species relatedness, ecology and abundance, together with environmental conditions, shape patterns of infection

The project will provide fundamental insights into the processes underlying pathogen emergence while generating knowledge relevant to conservation, biocontrol and applied virology.

The Doctoral Researcher will combine sequencing, phylogenetic comparative analyses, ecological datasets and statistical modelling to characterise moth-virus associations and identify predictors of virus sharing. Analyses will integrate information on host distributions, abundance, environmental conditions, life-history traits and recent range expansions. The student will have significant flexibility to refine hypotheses, develop analytical approaches and pursue emerging research directions, enabling ownership of the project.

Training will be delivered through a combination of “on-the-job” supervision, formal training and collaborative research. The supervisory team have extensive experience, with former team members going into roles in academia and government-agencies. They will provide one-to-one training in genomics/bioinformatics/phylogenetics, statistical modelling and reproducible research. Additional training in data science, project management, research integrity and communication will be enabled through training programmes, workshops and conferences. By progressively leading analyses, publications and presentations, the Doctoral Researcher will develop the skills needed for an independent research career.

The project brings together complementary expertise in virology/microbiology, genomics, evolutionary biology and ecology across GW4+ partners (Bath) and existing collaborators (Edinburgh, Butterfly Conservation). Access to unique long-term moth monitoring datasets, collaborative visits and co-supervision will provide exposure to diverse perspectives, methods and professional networks, creating an outstanding interdisciplinary training and research environment.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - How Does Saline-mine Water Influence the Fate of Metals in Mining Impacted Catchments?
jobs.description_html:
Increased mining activity is the uncomfortable paradox the world faces to meet energy-transition targets. Metal-bearing mine water is a global environmental issue, with unmanaged discharges capable of causing acute toxic shock to ecosystems and long-lived reductions in water quality, weakening ecosystem services. While most research to date has focused on understanding acidic saline mine water, very little is known about circumneutral saline mine water, the focus of this PhD, despite its widespread occurrence.

The Red River (Cornwall, UK) is a globally relevant natural laboratory for catchments impacted by circumneutral saline mine water, located in a region experiencing a resurgence in critical minerals mining activity. Applying hydro(bio)geochemical approaches, this project aims to answer the overarching question: 'How does saline-mine water influence the fate of metals in mining-impacted catchments?’, and societally-relevant questions such as: 'How can we ensure sustainable water-management solutions in mining areas protect the environment for people and nature?'.

This project will utilise multi-decadal monitoring data, alongside detailed sampling and analysis of waters and sediments within the Red River catchment, to develop hydrogeochemical models for the fate of metals essential to informing catchment-scale management solutions. Training will be provided in field sampling, analytical (bio-)geochemistry, and data analysis including hydrogeochemical modelling.

This project is supported by a diverse supervisory team with strengths in mine water and environmental management (Environment Agency), hydrogeochemistry (British Geological Survey), and (bio-)geochemistry of mineral systems (University of Exeter), enabling the researcher to investigate solutions that fit interest and experience. The researcher will benefit from access to facilities, data and institutional knowledge of these organisations. The researcher will be embedded within the NERC-funded Critical Minerals Challenge Centre, enabling exceptional networking opportunities with industry, NGOs, and policymakers. Researcher will have opportunity to present their work at national and international conferences.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Exploiting InSAR Loop Closure for Monitoring Soil Moisture and Vegetation Dynamics
jobs.description_html:
Changes in soil moisture and vegetation structure alter microwave scattering from the land surface, generating phase inconsistencies in Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) observations.

These inconsistencies appear as non-zero phase around closed interferometric loops. Recent studies, including our ESA-funded research on InSAR phase bias, have demonstrated systematic relationships between loop closure and vegetation and land-surface conditions. However, the physical controls on these signals and their potential for quantitative environmental monitoring remain poorly understood.

This PhD will investigate: (1) how soil moisture, vegetation water content and structural change influence InSAR loop closure; (2) whether their contributions can be separated; and (3) how sensitivity changes with radar wavelength and polarisation. Multi-temporal Sentinel-1 C-band observations will be combined with newly available NISAR L-band data to investigate these processes across contrasting vegetation and soil conditions. Forward modelling will be used to simulate how changes in soil and vegetation properties generate closure-phase signals, while inverse modelling will investigate whether these properties can be retrieved from the observations. Closure-phase time series will be analysed alongside backscatter and coherence and validated using independent soil-moisture, vegetation and meteorological observations.

The Doctoral Researcher will have substantial flexibility to shape the project, including selecting study environments and developing physical, statistical or data-driven approaches for separating environmental contributions to closure phase. The supervisory team will provide hands-on training in InSAR processing, radar scattering, environmental Earth observation, scientific programming, geospatial data analysis, reproducible research and scientific communication.
CASE partner SatSense Ltd will provide industrial co-supervision, access to operational InSAR expertise and datasets, and a three-month placement where the researcher will gain experience in large-scale processing, product development and validation. This academic-industry partnership will enable the researcher to test whether fundamental understanding of environmentally driven phase closure can ultimately be translated into scalable Earth observation products.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Evolution and Spread of a Bacterial Gene for Organic Nitrogen Acquisition in Marine Phytoplankton and its Biogeochemical Impact
jobs.description_html:
Questions: Ocean nitrogen budgets rest almost entirely on nitrate, ammonium and urea. We have recently found that marine phytoplankton also grow on a small nitrogen compound that many bacteria expel as a toxin, using an enzyme acquired from bacteria by horizontal gene transfer. If this capability is widespread, a nitrogen pool missing from current ecosystem models supports primary production in coastal seas, changing how nutrient budgets and eutrophication risk are assessed. The Doctoral Researcher will ask how this capability spread across plankton lineages and ocean regions, how the compound's concentration varies seasonally in coastal water, and how much including it changes modelled nitrogen cycling.

Methods: combining global metagenome and metatranscriptome archives (Tara Oceans, Bio-GO-SHIP) with phylogenomics to map where the trait is used, ocean by ocean; LC-MS/MS quantification of the compound in coastal time-series samples; isotope-labelled growth experiments on wild-type and CRISPR knockout diatoms to derive uptake and yield parameters; and implementation in the trait-based ecosystem models developed, then validation experiments.

Training: At Exeter the Researcher will learn phylogenomics, axenic culturing and molecular genetics with Dr Monier, and metabolite quantification and stable-isotope methods with Professor Smirnoff, a plant and algal biochemist. An extended placement in Bristol adds modelling, high-performance computing and parameter estimation with Professor Monteiro. Sequencing and mass spectrometry are funded by the supervision team's NERC grant on phytoplankton interactions with nitrogen-fixing bacteria. A patent application on the enzyme as a selection marker for synthetic biology also shows the Researcher how discovery becomes technology.

Collaboration: All co-supervisors already work on that grant. Bristol's modelling turns Exeter's measurements into nitrogen budgets, and the Researcher will spend an extended period in Bristol. After a supervised first-year survey, they will choose which strand to lead, in analytical chemistry, comparative genomics or global modelling, and which taxa and ocean regions to focus on.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Digital Twinning for Post-Mining Environmental Transitions
jobs.description_html:
Post-mining transitions that support economic diversification and regional growth depend on geology and placement in/under the landscape, socio-environmental context and the opportunistic actions of motivated entrepreneurs. This project investigates how to manage mining transitions holistically, at a time when many old mine landscapes need repair and global demand for mined raw materials continues to escalate.

The key questions are:

  1. How is socio-environmental resilience built on the foundations of former extractive sites?
  2. How can modern digital technologies support technical design decisions that incorporate environmental sustainability?
  3. How can valuation of former sites be achieved for alternative future end-of-life of mine scenario?

The student will desk-survey the ways in which (and how well) old mine/quarry/tip sites are internationally remined for: resources, environmental restoration, tourism or cultural heritage projects, alternative and innovative manufacturing and research industries. They will use remote sensing, laser scanning field-survey, build lab-based digital twins of UK post-extractive underground and overground landscapes and then use gaming technologies to visualize alternative and sustainable future working environments that make space for nature. The student will then consider how the digital-twinning methodology can transform local and regional understanding and decision-making for management of industrial extraction and post-extractive resilience, in variably geodiverse and biodiverse landscapes. UK-based case studies will be selected from a shortlist in Isle of Portland, S Wales, SW England, and the Peak District.

No one candidate can have all competencies required for this project. Training in mining-oriented solutions, laser scanning and digital twinning is provided in the Camborne School of Mines (CSM) and Deep Digital Cornwall facility at the University of Exeter. Training for gaming technologies will be at Bristol Digital Game Lab facilities. Collaborators on the project are Island Community Action and the Mine Remediation Authority (at case studies) and SLR consulting (consultation/placement).

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Assessing Microplastics as Drivers of AMR Selection and Spread
jobs.description_html:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global health threat and environmental issue attracting significant research, industry and policy attention. Microplastics, persistent and ubiquitous environmental contaminants, can support the growth of bacterial communities and AMR. Wastewater environments are particularly important as they contain microplastics, resistant pathogens and antibiotics that may select for AMR. However, the role of microplastics in the persistence, selection and transmission of AMR is poorly understood.

We encourage the researcher to shape the research as it progresses, but preliminary research questions include:

  • Do antibiotics sorb to and accumulate on microplastics, increasing AMR selective pressures?
  • Do microplastic polymers differ in their ability to support growth of resistant pathogens?
  • Can microplastics ‘shelter’ resistant pathogens, facilitating their survival and transmission through wastewater systems, and beyond?
  • Can this knowledge be used to inform wastewater treatment processes, and risk management?

The Doctoral Researcher will receive interdisciplinary training across microbiology (culture-based and molecular, e.g., next-generation sequencing, bioinformatics), evolutionary biology, chemistry (e.g., LC-MS), and microplastic characterisation (e.g., FTIR spectroscopy). They will be supervised by internationally recognised researchers with strong policy and industry links, and a track record of collaboration. We are committed to providing a welcoming, inclusive environment that supports collaboration and development of independent researchers.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Sentinels of the Sea: What can Marine Mammals tell us about Biodiversity Change in UK Waters?
jobs.description_html:
Marine biodiversity is changing rapidly, yet the processes driving these changes and their wider consequences are often poorly understood. Marine mammals are increasingly recognised as ecosystem sentinels due to their sensitivity to variation in ocean conditions and human pressures. This project will investigate what shifts in occurrence patterns and habitat use across multiple species can reveal about biodiversity change in UK waters. The project is designed to provide flexibility for the student to develop their own research direction but potential questions include: How have marine mammal distributions changed through time, and to what extent can the processes driving those changes be identified and attributed? Can marine mammals provide early indicators of wider ecosystem reorganisation? Can we forecast future ecological responses and their implications for conservation and management? Addressing these questions will generate evidence to support biodiversity monitoring, adaptive conservation and environmental decision-making.

This project will adopt a multidisciplinary approach integrating historical and contemporary ecological and social information to investigate ecological change through time. Potential sources include archived records and biological samples, strandings and sightings data, environmental datasets and stakeholder perspectives. Analytical approaches may include historical ecology, spatial analysis, ecological modelling and forecasting and social science. The specific methods will depend on the research focus developed collaboratively with the student.

The project brings together complementary specialist expertise from the University of Exeter's Centre for Ecology and Conservation, the British Antarctic Survey, and the Cetacean Strandings Investigation Programme at the Zoological Society of London/ Institute of Zoology, providing access to unique datasets, archived samples and research and policy networks. Through close collaboration with the supervisory team and project partners, the student will receive extensive on-the-job training in marine ecology, historical ecology, quantitative and qualitative analysis, scientific communication and stakeholder engagement, gaining experience across research, conservation practice and public outreach.

Funding

For eligible students the studentship will cover home tuition fees plus an annual tax-free stipend.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Pests, pathogens and forest carbon: building a prognostic disturbance module for the JULES land surface model
jobs.description_html:
Forests currently absorb roughly a third of human carbon emissions, but this service is not guaranteed. Pest and pathogen outbreaks - already devastating forests from North American bark beetles to European ash dieback - are expected to intensify under climate change, yet we have almost no capacity to predict impacts on future carbon storage. This project asks: how will pest and pathogen outbreaks reshape forest carbon dynamics as the climate changes, and can we build a predictive capability for this risk within a global climate model?

The student will develop and test a new capability for simulating pest/pathogen outbreaks within a leading UK land surface model (JULES), linking outbreak dynamics - informed by observational and satellite records of tree mortality and defoliation - to how forests grow, compete and recover. Methods include process-based model development, sensitivity and attribution experiments, and evaluation against satellite disturbance and biomass records across European and North American forests.

The student will have significant freedom to choose which pest/pathogen systems, regions and processes to prioritise, shaping their own research direction as understanding develops; supervisors provide a strong technical foundation while actively supporting that independence from year one.

Training includes climate/land-surface model development and computational skills (Exeter) and regular visits to the Met Office with our Collaborative partner (Arthur Argles), a leading developer of next-generation vegetation models (JULES-RED), providing hands-on training in ecosystem modelling and operational practice, alongside remote-sensing and data science skills. The close, pre-existing collaboration between Exeter's climate modelling group and the Met Office underpins this partnership, embedding the student in both academic and operational research.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Ecosystem Engineers: Can Beaver Wetlands Provide Resilience to the Hydrological Extremes of Flooding and Drought
jobs.description_html:
Beavers are well known for their ecosystem engineering activities. Via the creation of structures such as dams, ponds and canals beavers can create extensive and complex wetlands. These wetlands have been shown to have a significant impact on hydrology, increasing water storage within the landscape and attenuating downstream flow regimes. This in turn has led to significant interest in whether beavers can act as a Nature-based Solution increasing resilience to the hydrological extremes of drought and flood.

There remains a lack of detailed understanding into the hydrological behaviour of beaver wetlands particular in terms of low flow conditions, water storage and groundwater dynamics. There also remains a need to improve representation of beaver wetland dynamics in modelling and geospatial upscaling approaches. There is a direct need for this information from policy makers seeking to incorporate beaver wetlands into management and policy.
 
Using a suite of approaches including hydrological monitoring, geospatial analysis and hydraulic models this PhD will seek to gain novel understanding of the mechanisms by which beaver engineering could increase the hydrological resilience of our landscapes. This PhD will address the following questions.

1) Quantify the hydrological performance of beaver wetlands in terms of high flow, low flow, surface water storage and groundwater dynamics.
2) Can modelling and geospatial frameworks be used to upscale our understanding of beaver hydrological impacts. I.e. under future beaver population and climate scenarios can beaver wetlands have a significant impact addressing the hydrological extremes of drought and flood.
 
This PhD will be supported by a research group that has pioneered beaver reintroduction and Nature-based Solutions research within Great Britain and undertaken in partnership with the Environment Agency, contributing directly to the ambitions of the 25 year environment plan. This partnership will offer extensive training opportunities, industry application and direct pathways to impact.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Future-proofing ecosystem restoration in the tropics through understanding if manipulating seed sources can increase climate resilience
jobs.description_html:
Most ecosystem restoration programmes target the tropics, where biodiversity and carbon gains are highest. Brazil plays a key role in this, with a target to restore 12 million ha of degraded land by 2030, requiring 15,000 tonnes of native seeds. However, climate change is increasingly driving restoration failure. Using seeds that will be more resistant to future climates can increase restoration success. However, it remains uncertain if seeds collected from different climate conditions have different functions which can be exploited to increase climate resilience and restoration success.

The PhD student will explore the role climate-related variation in plant function can have in promoting restoration success in the Brazilian savanna, a global biodiversity hotspot, hosting more plant species than the Amazon rainforest. The student will have the opportunity to undertake fieldwork in Brazil, measuring plant physiological variables that determine drought resistance. These can be measured at seed collection sites that exist across a rainfall gradient, or at a common garden–rainfall exclusion experiment in Brasilia, one of the first of its kind in the tropics.

The student will co-develop this project with the supervisory team and support from a NERC-funded project with its long-established international partners, who can train the student in restoration science and practice, experimental design and data-analysis, as well as facilitate international fieldwork. The student can also be trained in plant physiological measurements by a University of Cardiff co-supervisor, an expert in developing plant sensor technology, and with whom we have a decade-long collaboration and an excellent publication track record. In addition, the student will work closely with our partner NGO’s WWF Brazil and ISA (The Brazilian socio-environmental Institute), who are leading seed collection and restoration efforts in Brazil, bridging the gap between science and practice. This offers excellent opportunities for training in knowledge transfer and public engagement.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Self-Sabotage or Secret Advantage? The Biology of Fish Thiaminase
jobs.description_html:
All animals require thiamine (vitamin B1) as an essential nutrient, yet many fish species paradoxically produce thiaminase enzymes that destroy it. Thiaminase activity has been linked to disease, reproductive failure, and population declines in fish-eating wildlife, but its biological function, regulation, and evolutionary origins remain poorly understood. This interdisciplinary PhD will explore the biological and environmental drivers of thiaminase production in fish, including the tissues and cell types involved, variation in thiaminase enzymes among species, and the influence of environmental conditions on thiaminase activity. Improved understanding of thiaminase biology will strengthen our ability to predict and manage thiamine deficiency events that threaten aquatic ecosystems.

The project combines genomics, molecular biology, biochemistry, and experimental biology. The student will have the opportunity to employ a variety of techniques including single-cell transcriptomics to identify thiaminase-producing cells and tissues; comparative sequence and structural analyses to investigate enzyme evolution and function; development of improved approaches for measuring thiaminase activity; and experimental studies examining environmental regulation and physiological consequences of thiaminase expression. The student will have significant scope to direct the research programme, including selecting study species, identifying environmental variables, designing experiments, and pursuing emerging research questions.

A major strength of the project is its interdisciplinary supervisory team: Dr Sarah Salisbury (fish genomics and single-cell RNA sequencing), Dr Ioanna Katsiadaki (fish physiology, ecotoxicology and welfare), Professor Nicholas Harmer (enzyme biochemistry and structural biology), and Dr Irene Cano Cejas (molecular biology and environmental genomics). Leveraging a strong and established Exeter-Cefas collaboration, the student will have access to complementary expertise, facilities, and mentoring across academic and government research environments while receiving hands-on training in bioinformatics, molecular laboratory techniques, protein modelling, experimental design, statistical analysis, scientific writing, and project management. This unique training environment will equip the student with highly transferable skills for careers across academia, industry and government.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: When does ecosystem engineering create ecological opportunity? How landscape context shapes biodiversity and ecological networks following beaver restoration
jobs.description_html:
Ecosystem engineers such as beavers create new habitats and ecological opportunities, yet biodiversity responses to restoration remain highly variable. This project will investigate how local habitat modification interacts with landscape composition and connectivity to shape biodiversity responses. Specifically, it will test whether beaver-driven habitat heterogeneity increases species diversity and ecological interactions, and how the surrounding landscape determines whether these ecological opportunities are realised. Understanding these relationships is essential for predicting biodiversity responses and informing evidence-based nature recovery.

The Doctoral Researcher will survey plant and pollinator communities across beaver restoration sites spanning gradients of occupation history, habitat complexity and landscape context. Combining ecological field surveys, plant–pollinator network analysis and Earth observation, the project will quantify local habitat heterogeneity, landscape composition and connectivity. Satellite image classification and time-series analysis will characterise habitat structure and environmental change, while statistical and spatial modelling will examine how local and landscape-scale processes interact to shape biodiversity and ecological network structure. Supported by the supervisory team, the Doctoral Researcher will develop independent research questions within this framework, with opportunities to explore functional diversity, ecosystem services or restoration scenarios.

The project provides hands-on training in ecological field methods, community and network ecology, quantitative modelling and scientific writing at Exeter (Dirk Sanders). Through research visits to Cardiff, Lu Zhuo will provide specialist training in Earth observation, GIS, satellite image classification and spatial analysis. The Doctoral Researcher will work with environmental data science researchers, accessing specialist computing facilities and high-resolution satellite imagery. Cornwall Wildlife Trust has confirmed its support as a CASE partner, offering a three-month research placement, practical conservation training and co-supervision. The partnership will enable the Doctoral Researcher to work alongside conservation practitioners and translate ecological findings into restoration planning and management.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Solving the puzzle of contrasting Arctic and Antarctic sea ice changes
jobs.description_html:
The global climate is unequivocally warming, but sea ice at both poles continues to surprise. Arctic sea-ice cover has remained relatively steady for the past ~20 years, following three decades of rapid decline. In the Antarctic, sea-ice cover remained stable for decades, but has declined dramatically since 2016. To explain the recent Arctic slowdown and Antarctic surge, and to avoid being taken by surprise again in the future, we need a deeper understanding of decadal sea-ice variability, its mechanisms and their representation in climate models.

This is important because changes in sea ice affect global climate and ecosystems, and credible sea ice predictions are needed for decision-making on climate change, biodiversity loss, and (inter)national security. You will be supported to co-design a project to address this research gap, that suits your interests and vision. You will apply innovative statistical methods (e.g., low-frequency component analysis, pattern recognition, emergent constraints) to observations and state-of-the-art climate models, to establish the processes that cause decadal sea-ice variability, the ability of climate models to represent these, and how they will respond to long-term climate change. You will gain skills in the following areas: weather and climate physics, oceanography, data analysis, numerical modelling, remote sensing, statistics, AI, and science communication.

You will benefit from the extensive training offered by the DLTP, Exeter, British Antarctic Survey, and Met Office; and on-the-job training provided by the supervisors, a designated post-doc ‘buddy’, and vibrant peer-to-peer support networks. You will join a small, well-established and productive team of leading UK and US scientists working on this topic (through an allied NERC-NSF funded project), which will provide a stimulating and supportive research environment, with opportunities for wider collaboration, including with stakeholders (e.g., UK government). You will also have opportunities to attend international conferences and training courses, some possibly in the Arctic.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Machine Learning the Building Blocks of the Weather Forecast
jobs.description_html:
Weather forecasts are essential for informing decisions made by the public, industry and the government. Recent technological advances have led to a proliferation of machine learning (ML) weather models that are outperforming traditional models by some measures, although challenges remain. As ML models are not designed based on physical principles they are not explainable and do not perform reliably outside of regimes seen in their training data. This project aims to address these challenges by breaking the weather forecast into its fundamental building blocks and applying different ML architectures to each.

Key questions are:

  1. In matching the structure of the ML architecture to the underlying mathematical structure of the model component, can we improve the representation of physical processes?
  2. To what extent does this approach result in a model that is more efficient, stable and robust outside of its training data, for example, under a warming climate?

This approach aims to improve understanding of how ML models represent different building blocks of the weather forecast, progressing towards a model that is human-understandable rather than a black box. This is crucial to increase trust in ML methods as they move towards operational use.

The Researcher will receive training through taught and self-study modules, directed reading, supervisory discussions, hands-on coding, and regular hackathons. They will acquire specialist skills in geophysical fluid dynamics and ML techniques, as well as sought-after transferrable skills in software development, reproducibility, data management and scientific communication. As the project progresses, the Researcher will be encouraged and supported to take the lead in steering the direction of the project. Through the CASE partnership and a decade-long supervisor-Met-Office collaboration, they will gain experience in working closely with Met Office scientists, relating their research directly to weather forecasts with the potential to shape future Met Office forecast system development.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: From crisis to opportunity: SARGASSO (Sargassum As Raw material for Green, Affordable, and Sustainable Shelter Opportunities)
jobs.description_html:
Climate-driven Sargassum inundations generate ecological, health and waste-management pressures, particularly in low-GDP coastal regions,exacerbated by climate changes. This project will investigate whether this problematic biomass can become a locally available feedstock for affordable, ultra-low-carbon building materials. It will ask: how do three Sargassum varieties, and simple treatments (e.g., washing, chopping or drying) affect compatibility with lime-based binders; which reaction products and interfacial bonds control strength, durability and hygrothermal performance; and can supply chains deliver materials with credible biogenic-carbon storage and mineral carbonation?

The ECR will co-design the research pathway, selecting processing routes and performance targets with the supervisory team and partners. Three Sargassum varieties will be sampled from the Caribbean, West Africa and Europe to capture geographical and compositional variability. Methods will combine field-informed sampling, locally feasible processing, chemical and mineralogical characterisation, lime–pozzolan mix design, mechanical and physical characterisation, SEM/EDS, XRD and FTIR analysis, and micro-to-macro modelling. Techno-economic and life-cycle assessment will compare the proposed materials with conventional alternatives.

Training will span marine environmental science, algal-biomass characterisation, low-carbon binder chemistry, microstructural analysis, data science, modelling, life-cycle assessment, circular economics and sustainable building design. On-the-job training will include laboratory testing, experimental design, data analysis, scientific writing, stakeholder engagement and responsible innovation. The Researcher will lead method refinement, supported through regular supervisory reviews, publication opportunities and specialist DLTP courses.

Dr Raffaele Vinai contributes expertise in bio-aggregate/lime materials, while Prof Mike Allen contributes expertise in Sargassum ecology, composition, containment and environmental risk. Cefas as DLTP-approved Collaborative Partners will support providing data, lab results, and specialistic training. CASE partner SeaGen will advise on detection, collection, logistics and carbon-removal constraints. These partnerships connect marine science, materials engineering and environmental application across the GW4+ network. The project aligns with Science for Environmental Solutions and NERC priorities in environmental change, carbon cycling and sustainable resource transformation.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Detecting Ecological Change in Intertidal Habitats Using Repeat Photography and Machine Learning
jobs.description_html:
Intertidal habitats provide important ecosystem functions and services, supporting biodiversity, fisheries productivity, coastal resilience and cultural values. However, these dynamic environments are increasingly exposed to acute and chronic climate-driven pressures. Conventional ecological monitoring is constrained by cost, spatial coverage and sampling frequency and scalable approaches that can reliably detect ecological change are urgently needed.

This project will investigate whether repeat photography, combined with citizen science and machine learning, can provide robust monitoring of ecological change in intertidal habitats. Smartphone imagery can generate large-scale observations, but variation in viewpoint, lighting, tidal state, season and image quality presents a major challenge.

The project will address two questions:

  1. How should repeat-photography surveys be designed to reliably detect ecological change in intertidal habitats?
  2. Can machine-learning approaches account for environmental and observational variability, whilst robustly detecting and quantifying ecological change from repeat photographs?

The Doctoral Researcher will combine field data collection, statistical analysis and image-based AI methods, testing methodology across locations, seasons, and environmental conditions. Methods will be validated against the MarClim 25-year time series, comprising annual surveys of rocky intertidal species across 100 UK sites. The project offers flexibility to shape its direction, with scope to place greater emphasis on environmental monitoring, image analysis, or machine learning as the project develops and the Doctoral Researcher's interests evolve.

The project brings together expertise from four leading marine research and higher education institutions in the South West, providing access to complementary expertise, facilities and networks. The Doctoral Researcher will gain training in fieldwork, experimental design, image analysis, machine learning and ecological monitoring, alongside statistics, scientific writing and communication. They will also benefit from stakeholder engagement, established monitoring programmes, and GW4+ and University of Exeter researcher-development opportunities. The project will integrate marine ecology, statistics and AI to develop innovative tools for addressing real-world ecological challenges.

jobs.title: CHE PhD Studentship Opportunity 2027/28
jobs.description_html:
We are looking for exceptional students to apply for a funded PhD opportunity at the Centre for Health Economics (CHE). Future PhD's are able to choose from the following six topics, with one studentship offered overall. 

CHE will fund a studentship from the following 6 topic areas:

Topic 1 - Economic burden of poor mental health on working-age adults
Supervisors - Vijay Gc and Laura Bojke

Topic 2 - The economics of AI in healthcare
Supervisors - Nils Gutacker and Joe Spearing

Topic 3 - Valuing Child Oral Health: Addressing Complexity and Inequity in UK Dental Care
Supervisors -  Sebastian Hinde, Laura Bojke, Greig Taylor (University of Newcastle)

Topic 4 -  Marginal productivity
Supervisors - Francesco Longo and James Lomas

Topic 5 - Heat, work and adaptation: the economics of a warming South Asia
Supervisors - Sumit Mazumdar and Vijay Gc

Topic 6 - Health Systems Modelling - Incorporating Capacity Considerations in HTA
Supervisors - Praveen Thokala, Dina Jankovic and Simon Walker

Proposals relating to other areas of research in health economics will be considered. However, the best opportunity to get a funded studentship is to take note of the prioritised topics listed above.

Further details are available on our webpage including full description of each topic, eligibility criteria, process for application and requirements for onsite attendance. We are unable to offer the studentship on a part time basis or via Distance Learning.

Supervision and research environment

The successful candidate will be supervised in CHE and will be registered through the Department of Economics and Related Studies at the University of York. This is an opportunity to work with researchers in one of the most successful health economics research groups in the UK. CHE has a leading international reputation, and is one of the world’s largest health economics research centres. Its mission is to undertake “high quality research that is capable of influencing health policy decisions”. The Centre attracts some of the best and brightest people in the field in the form of PhD students and visitors from overseas, creating a vibrant research environment. The University of York is widely recognised as one of the leading research universities in the UK and is also at the top of the teaching quality rankings.

CHE has an Athena SWAN Silver award which recognises our commitment to good practice in recruiting, retaining and supporting the careers of women. We strive to provide a supportive culture and family friendly work environment and to offer equal opportunities to all staff members. We seek to ensure the policies and procedures in the department are fair and support good work practices for everyone.

The award

The award will cover academic fees for the 27/28 entry, at UK or international rates as appropriate, plus a maintenance stipend for 3 years at UKRI rates (£21,805 for 26/27).

Applications should be received no later than 15th January 2026 before 16:00 (UTC).

Interviews

Shortlisted candidates will be interviewed in person or via zoom. Interview date to be confirmed.

At the interview, candidates will be expected to give a short presentation (5 minutes) on their proposed project including relevant literature, potential data sources and applicable methods by Powerpoint or Google slides. It should also focus on their plans for the studentship and the skills they would bring to their doctoral research.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Tiny Multimodal Learning Under Resource Constraints
jobs.description_html:
Modern artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on combining multiple sources of information, such as sound, motion, images, and sensor data, to achieve robust and intelligent behaviour. However, most existing multimodal AI systems depend on large, computationally intensive models that are difficult to deploy in settings with limited resources. This PhD project explores a different question: how can multimodal intelligence be achieved using minimal, efficient representations under resource constraints?

The project will investigate Tiny Multimodal Learning, a research direction focused on understanding what is essential for multimodal learning when computation, memory, or energy are limited. Rather than scaling up models, the research aims to identify principled, lightweight methods for representing and combining multimodal information over time. Grounded in machine learning, representation learning, and efficient algorithms, the work addresses real-world challenges in sustainable and accessible AI.

As a PhD researcher, you will gain experience in multimodal machine learning, experimental benchmarking, and algorithmic design, with opportunities to explore connections to dynamical systems and efficient model architectures. You will work in a supportive, inclusive doctoral environment, with access to strong research facilities, interdisciplinary collaboration, training in research and professional skills, and opportunities to publish at leading international venues.

Objectives

The aim of this project is to develop principled and efficient methods for multimodal learning under resource constraints. The research seeks to understand how different types of data—such as audio, motion, images and sensor signals—can be combined using minimal representations without relying on large, computationally intensive models.

Key objectives include:

  • Reviewing and benchmarking existing multimodal learning approaches under limited computational resources
  • Investigating lightweight representations and fusion strategies for multimodal data
  • Studying how temporal structure and missing data affect multimodal learning
  • Identifying fundamental trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and robustness.

Funding

This studentship is open to home and international applicants. Home and international tuition fees will be covered for the duration of the 3-year award.

The student will receive a standard stipend payment for the duration of the award. The stipend rate is determined by the UKRI, currently £21,805 for the academic year 2026/27.

Candidate requirements

Essential:

  • A first-class or upper second-class (2:1) Bachelor’s degree or a Master’s degree (or equivalent), in Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, or a closely related discipline.
  • A strong foundation in programming (e.g. Python) and core concepts in machine learning/data analysis.
  • Ability to engage with research literature and develop analytical, problem-solving, and algorithmic thinking skills.
  • Good written and verbal communication skills; ability to work both independently and collaboratively.

Desirable:

  • Experience with deep learning (frameworks like PyTorch or TensorFlow), multimodal data analysis.

How to apply

Please contact Professor Liangxiu Han with any questions.

To apply, please complete the online application form for a full-time PhD in Computing & Digital Technology. Please note, you are not required to submit a research proposal.

Please complete the Doctoral Project Applicant Form; include your CV and a covering letter to demonstrate how your skills and experience map to the aims/objectives of the project, the area of research and why you see this area as being of importance/interest.

Please upload these documents in the supporting documents section of the University’s Admissions Portal or email the requested documents to pgradmissions@mmu.ac.uk.

Expected start date: October 2027.
