Quote the reference: SciEng-LH-2027-28-Tiny Multimodal Learning

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: How do Anthropogenic Contaminants Alter Zooplankton-mediated Biogeochemistry in a Changing Ocean
jobs.description_html:
Zooplankton are central to marine food webs and play a critical role in ocean biogeochemistry through nutrient recycling, carbon export and trophic transfer. However, marine ecosystems are increasingly exposed to complex mixtures of anthropogenic contaminants, including plastics, plastic alternatives and metals, alongside global change stressors such as ocean warming, altered salinity and nutrient enrichment. Understanding how these interacting pressures affect zooplankton and the ecosystem functions they support is a major challenge for predicting and managing ocean change.

This PhD will investigate how environmentally relevant contaminant mixtures influence the physiology, behaviour and ecological functioning of key zooplankton species, and how these responses scale up to affect marine biogeochemical cycling. The Doctoral Researcher will combine field observations from the Western English Channel with laboratory experiments exposing copepods and other planktonic organisms to contaminants individually and in combination with changing environmental conditions. Measurements may include survival, growth, reproduction, respiration, feeding behaviour, oxidative stress biomarkers and transcriptomic responses.

Key research questions include:

  1. How do contaminant mixtures and climate-related stressors interact to affect zooplankton health and performance?
  2. Do contaminants alter grazing, nutrient regeneration and carbon export processes mediated by zooplankton?
  3. How do zooplankton influence the transport, transformation and trophic transfer of contaminants through marine ecosystems?
  4. Which contaminant-stressor combinations pose the greatest risk to ecosystem functioning and biogeochemical resilience?

The questions are intentionally broad to support student-led development of novel research directions. Fieldwork will be conducted at PML's long-term monitoring site L4 aboard RV Plymouth Quest, complemented by experiments in PML's ultraclean facilities and University of Exeter laboratories. Through collaboration between PML and University of Exeter, the student will undertake research visits, access specialist FlowCam and plankton culture facilities, and receive interdisciplinary training spanning marine ecology, ecotoxicology and biogeochemistry.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: From Plankton to People: Marine Bioaerosols and Human Respiratory Health
jobs.description_html:
People living and working near the coast are exposed to sea spray aerosols containing biologically active compounds derived from marine planktonic microorganism. Climate change is altering plankton communities through ocean warming, marine heatwaves and ecosystem shifts, potentially changing the composition of these aerosols and their effects on human health.

This project will investigate:

  1. how sea spray aerosol composition varies with plankton communities;
  2. which bioactive compounds are transferred from marine ecosystems to the atmosphere;
  3. how human lung cells respond to environmentally relevant aerosol exposures; and
  4. how climate-driven ecosystem change may alter coastal air quality and respiratory health.

These questions address a major knowledge gap at the interface of ocean science, atmospheric chemistry and human health.

The Doctoral Researcher (DR) will combine field observations, laboratory analyses and experimental approaches. They will collect aerosol samples at the Penlee Point Atmospheric Observatory (PPAO), characterise their chemical composition and identify candidate bioactive compounds. In parallel, plankton observations from the Western Channel Observatory (WCO) time series station will be analysed to determine links between ecosystem structure and aerosol chemistry. Human lung-cell experiments will assess biological responses to aerosol exposure, while relationships between plankton communities and aerosol composition will be used to explore future climate-related risks.

The DR will receive interdisciplinary training in marine ecology, aerosol chemistry, analytical techniques, cell-culture methods, data science, statistical analysis, scientific writing, communication and stakeholder engagement. They will work across the University of Exeter and Plymouth Marine Laboratory (PML), benefiting from internationally recognised expertise, facilities and long-term observational datasets.

While the overarching themes are defined, specific research questions, experimental and analytical approaches, data analysis and publications/presentations will be directed by the DR, allowing them to shape the project direction and lead decisions according to their interests and develop as an independent researcher within a closely integrated GW4+ partnership.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: How do Invasive Non-native Species Transform Ecological Connectivity Across Landscapes and Ecosystems, and What are the Consequences for Biodiversity, Ecosystems, and Ecosystem Services?
jobs.description_html:
Invasive non-native species are a major and growing threat to biodiversity and ecosystem. However, biological invasions do not act in isolation but interact with other indirect and direct drivers of environmental change. To date, there has been little consideration given to the interactions between land-use change and biological invasions in shaping landscape connectivity, even though land degradation and fragmentation are known to exacerbate the spread of invasive non-native species.

The proposed research would address the following questions:

  • How do invasive non-native species alter landscape structure and habitat connectivity at varying spatial scales and in different contexts?
  • What are the implications of altered landscape structures for ecosystem functions, including pollination, pest control, carbon storage and recreation?

Using islands, specifically Isles of Scilly, as study systems, the Doctoral Researcher would use a combination of spatial modelling and field approaches to address questions on scale-dependent processes within invaded systems. The Doctoral Researcher would also gain experience in community engagement working with diverse stakeholder groups to understand not only the ecological implications but also social dimensions including perceptions and values that might inform management actions.

The Doctoral Researcher would be given training through both the Centre for Ecology and Conservation (University of Exeter in Cornwall) and the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology including in spatial modelling but also stakeholder engagement and science communication. The experienced supervisory team would provide the training needed for the field and modelling components.

The Doctoral Researcher will benefit from connections through the Memorandum of Understanding between the two lead organisations and established collaborations between some members of the proposed supervisory team but will also provide new connections for others within the team. Furthermore, the Doctoral Researcher would work close with communities on the Isles of Scilly and relevant NGOs.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Soil Carbon Dynamics Following Amazon Forest Wildfires
jobs.description_html:
Tropical forest soils are crucial to the global carbon cycle, yet increasing wildfire, land-use change, and climate warming may cause large carbon emissions.

This PhD will investigate:

  1. How soil respiration responds to post-wildfire conditions across Amazonia, and how soil properties mediate this response;
  2. How pyrogenic carbon (PyC, charcoal) additions affect soil respiration dynamics in southern Amazonian soils; and
  3. How the JULES land surface model can be improved using novel field and experimental data.

The doctoral researcher will shape the project, lead field experiments in southern Amazonia and advance modelling in collaboration with the UK Met Office. As part of the NERC-funded Amazon Pyrogenic Carbon Project, they will join workshops, access extensive datasets (soil respiration, stable and radiocarbon isotopes, pyrogenic carbon, microclimate) and develop a new soil microcosm experiment.

Training will include tropical field methods, environmental sensors, experimental design and geospatial analysis in R, alongside advanced modelling with JULES. Co-supervisors in Brazil will provide field and logistical expertise, while the Met Office will offer world-class training in modelling and climate impact assessment. This UK-Brazil partnership ensures cutting-edge, interdisciplinary research to improve understanding of climate change and wildfire impacts on the world’s largest tropical forest.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Fixing the North Atlantic Storm Track Bias: High-resolution Modelling for Improved UK Climate Projections
jobs.description_html:
The North Atlantic storm track drives changeable weather, ranging from rain-bringing depressions in autumn and winter to the blocking patterns that bring prolonged drought in spring and summer. In the last 12 months, the UK has experienced both: prolonged winter rainfall driving extreme flooding, and spring and summer drought. Despite this, almost every state-of-the-art climate model places the storm track too far equatorward and too zonal, a bias that has resisted decades of model development. Fixing this bias would significantly increase confidence in predictions of future UK climate, and the associated risks, as the latest Independent Assessment of UK Climate Risk (2026) highlights.

This project will quantify how much increased resolution over the storm track reduces this bias through enhanced air-sea coupling and latent heating (Schemm, JAMES, 2023). The researcher will use LFRic, the Met Office’s new state-of-the-art climate model, to embed local high-resolution grids over key parts of the North Atlantic, investigating how the strength of diabatic processes affects cyclone propagation and storm track biases. Complementary experiments with Isca, Exeter’s own simplified climate model, will isolate the role of diabatic heating more cleanly. The researcher will shape these experiments from the outset, leading directions of their own choosing, such as the storm track’s response to climate change or tropical SST changes.

Training will combine on-the-job supervision in model development, nested-grid configurations, large-dataset analysis and scientific writing with formal LFRic courses co-delivered by Sergeev (www.metoffice.gov.uk/blog/2026/learning-lfric-a-new-modelling-system-for-weather-prediction-and-climate-projections), and courses in mid-latitude dynamics and atmospheric fluid dynamics from Catto, Thomson and Seviour. The studentship coincides with a funded Isca development project, letting the researcher work alongside experienced Research Software Engineers, enhancing technical training. Visits to Sergeev’s group at Bristol and work with Morcrette’s group at the Met Office will link the researcher to operational model development and an extensive early-career network.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Using Next Generation Ocean Observations and Machine Learning to Transform mixed Layer Depth Predictions
jobs.description_html:
The Mixed Layer Depth (MLD) governs ocean-atmosphere exchanges, vertical mixing and ocean dynamics. Ocean models can simulate high-frequency MLD dynamics—such as realistic storm mixing—they often fail to resolve them temporally, which means they cannot be used directly to resolve or predict day-to-day changes. This project addresses a key science question: What physical processes and high-resolution inputs are required to temporally resolve hourly MLD dynamics?

Answering this is increasingly critical. Precise, temporally resolved MLD forecasts provide essential acoustic and operational advantages for maritime activities, including Navy operations and sustainable management of marine infrastructure deployment. Furthermore, offshore wind farms physically alter the local MLD through wake turbulence, impacting regional stratification and the ecosystem it supports.  

Methods: This project will address this using the MaLCOM machine learning framework. The researcher will develop neural networks to transition MLD prediction from a purely statistical baseline to a temporally resolved forecast, utilizing high-resolution, in-situ and Earth observational datasets for rigorous testing and validation.

Researcher Ownership: We emphasize project flexibility. The Doctoral Researcher will actively steer the research direction by selecting specific geographic test sites, defining target temporal scales, and choosing which oceanographic and meteorological variables to integrate into their ML architecture.

On-the-job Training: The supervisory team will provide comprehensive skill development. Exeter will mentor the student in advanced Python programming, AI development, and MLD modelling. PML will train the student in handling complex in-situ MLD observations, while the Met Office will provide instruction on operational forecast requirements and output evaluation.

Collaborative Strength: This partnership tightly integrates Exeter’s ML expertise, PML’s observational science, the Met Office’s forecasting capabilities, and autonomous vessel data collected by Oshen. This multi-institutional synergy ensures the researcher gains cross-disciplinary mentorship and access to unique datasets, significantly enhancing their PhD experience.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Leopard Seal Migration as an Early-warning Signal of Antarctic Ecosystem Change
jobs.description_html:
The project will address three key questions:

  1. how does variability and long-term change in sea ice affect leopard seal migration phenology and population dynamics;
  2. how do resulting changes in arrival timing influence predation pressure and prey communities at key Antarctic islands; and
  3. how changes in leopard seal migration provide an early-warning indicator of wider ecosystem responses to climate change.

Leopard seals occupy a highly dynamic apex position in the Southern Ocean, as the only species that regularly preys on other warm-blooded vertebrates while maintaining a unique ability to filter-feed on krill. Their seasonal movements are closely associated with the expansion and retreat of Antarctic pack ice, connecting coastal, pelagic and potentially deep-sea ecosystems across Antarctic and sub-Antarctic regions.

Using decades of individual-based leopard seal data from British Antarctic Survey's unique long-term monitoring programme, integrated with remotely sensed sea-ice and environmental data, the student will learn to apply population, phenological and movement models, alongside machine-learning approaches for conservation, to quantify environmental drivers of migration and associated changes in predator occurrence and predation pressure.

The student will receive direct training in population and movement ecology, statistical modelling, remote sensing and machine-learning applications for wildlife conservation, alongside opportunities to develop transferable skills in scientific communication, collaborative research and reproducible data analysis.

The collaboration between the British Antarctic Survey and the University of Exeter will give the student access to complementary expertise in long-term population studies, behavioural ecology, trophic ecology, quantitative methods and ecological modelling. The student will benefit from integration within research groups at both institutions, gaining exposure to different research environments, analytical approaches and professional networks. This builds on an established collaboration in pinniped ecology, providing both the long-term datasets and methodological expertise required to deliver the project successfully.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Autonomous Satellite-linked Acoustic Monitoring of Biodiversity and Threats in the Celtic Sea
jobs.description_html:
Science question:

This project addresses the GW4+ Science for Environmental Solutions priority: an autonomous, satellite-linked payload transforming biodiversity and physical ocean-state monitoring. The proposed use case: anthropogenic noise and ship strike assessment - leading causes of cetacean behavioural change and mortality. Current "risk" maps use historic averages, not real-time whale locations. Scientifically, this project tests whether concurrent acoustic and sea-state sensing can quantify, not just reduce, the uncertainty separating biological signal from noise, establishing a rigorous method underpinning whale vessel-strike mitigation and ocean-state science. Use cases are broad, hence providing agency to the student to direct further development, including ocean-atmosphere fluxes, marine surveillance and species tracking.

Methods:

The researcher will develop a payload, building on existing open-source technology, combining a proven Iridium-linked hydrophone system with in-situ wave and sea-state sensing, testing whether onboard sea-state inference reduces whale false detections and improves classification confidence. Machine learning spans acoustic classification (e.g. YOHO) with PML's David Moffat, and sea-state inference with Exeter's Ian Ashton (e.g. MaLCOM), both run at the edge, minimising data transfer. Engineered, bench-tested and deployed in the Celtic Sea to support Exeter’s soundscape research (Matthew Witt), will, generate real-time evidence for threat assessment and marine spatial planning.

Training:

The student will be trained in marine acoustics, machine learning and ocean technology, moving across workshop, computer-lab and sea. The candidate will develop hardware and shape acoustic and oceanographic analytical methods alongside the Environmental Intelligence group at PML, and Ashton's research groups, joining Witt's Celtic Sea fieldwork. The student is embedded in supportive, inclusive research environments spanning Exeter-PML.

Partner collaboration: The PML partnership is central: Moffat's acoustic machine-learning expertise, alongside PML's wider mission translating oceanographic and remote-sensing science into environmental solutions, covers ground unavailable at Exeter alone. This pairs Ashton's physical oceanography with Witt's marine ecology, keeping both strands are equally supported.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Can we Trust AI to Help Save Biodiversity?
jobs.description_html:
AI is transforming how we monitor biodiversity, but could errors in what machines detect lead us to the wrong conservation decisions? This project will establish when automated monitoring provides reliable ecological evidence and how to improve it. Combining large biodiversity datasets with simulation and statistical modelling, the student will investigate which species and environmental conditions challenge AI, quantify how detection errors affect estimates of occupancy, abundance and population trends, and test whether ecological context or complementary sensors improve reliability.

The student will examine how traits, taxonomy, habitat, season, environmental conditions and training-data availability shape AI performance, then track how false positives, false negatives and uncertainty influence ecological conclusions. They will also explore ways to make automated monitoring more trustworthy, for example by using ecological information such as location, habitat and season to improve uncertainty estimates, or by combining cameras, acoustics, eDNA and remote sensing. The project has a clear core structure, but the student will be strongly encouraged to develop their own ideas, choose focal taxa and datasets, and shape the final direction of the research.

Training will cover reproducible data science, AI and computer vision, hierarchical ecological modelling, uncertainty quantification, high-performance computing, scientific writing and communication. Benno Simmons (Exeter, Ecology), Sareh Rowlands (Exeter, Computer Science) and Chris Clements (Bristol, Ecology) will provide hands-on training through coding, joint analysis, research meetings and paper writing. The student will also gain experience communicating technical results to conservation organisations, local environmental partnerships and policy audiences, learning how to turn methodological advances into evidence that can be used in practice.

The Exeter–Bristol collaboration brings together complementary expertise in ecology and computer science. Joint supervision, regular interaction and research visits to Bristol will give the student access to both research communities, broaden their networks and support them in developing an independent research profile.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Predicting 'Unseen' Stratospheric Extremes: Integrating Operational Ensembles, AI, and Health Impact Modelling
jobs.description_html:
Key science questions and importance

Detailed observations of the stratosphere have existed only since the satellite era. What are the chances of unprecedented extremes, such as powerful sudden stratospheric warmings, not found in this record? How would these impact surface weather, and can predicting these events provide early warnings for public health? Understanding this is vital for climate resilience, as the stratosphere is a critical source of predictability on seasonal timescales.

Methods

The researcher will analyse a very large ensemble of operational seasonal prediction models from the EU’s Copernicus (C3S) database to estimate probabilities of unprecedented stratospheric extremes. They will run complementary ‘hindcast’ simulations using ACE2, a leading AI-based model used at Exeter and the Met Office. Finally, these outputs will be combined with epidemiological models to quantify public health impacts. The researcher will be encouraged to steer the project's direction by selecting specific geographic regions, targeted health impacts, or focusing more deeply on the AI simulation.

Training opportunities

The project will contribute towards a new initiative of the Stratospheric Network for the Assessment of Predictability (SNAP), within the World Climate Research Programme, providing international networking and communication experience. 'On-the-job' training will prioritise the computational skills needed to handle large-scale weather and climate data and AI models. The researcher can take taught modules in atmospheric fluid dynamics and will be encouraged to attend summer schools both climate modelling (e.g. NCAS Climate Modelling Summer School) and impacts (e.g. EEPE Environmental Epidemiology course).

Collaboration

The supervisory team bring complementary expertise in stratospheric dynamics (Exeter), seasonal prediction (Met Office), and impact modelling (Bristol). The researcher will be encouraged to spend extended periods visiting project partners at the relevant milestones. The team have an extensive record of collaboration, including in the co-supervision of PhD students and in several scientific publications.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Submesoscale Ocean Flows and Processes in the Southern Ocean
jobs.description_html:
The Southern Ocean is the primary sink for excess anthropogenic heat and carbon, placing this region at the forefront of the Earth's climate system. Understanding the Southern Ocean circulation is therefore crucial for improving climate projections and predicting future climate trajectories. Prominent features in the Southern Ocean are large-scale eddies (10 km—100 km & months—years). They transport warm waters from subtropical to subpolar regions, effecting a meridional heat transport of particular importance for the global ocean circulation, heat and carbon capture, and the regional sea-ice dynamics. However, eddy dynamics is complex and involves interactions with smaller-scale oceanic flows (

Recent studies have demonstrated that these cross-scale interactions channel an energy pathway from small to large scales, energising the large-scale eddy field and increasing its heat transport by twofold. This project focuses on the processes underpinning small-to-large-scale interactions and energy transfers in the Southern Ocean.

The student will:

  1. identify the dominant interaction processes using state-of-the-art numerical simulations (developed at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, USA, and the National Oceanography Centre, UK) and
  2. ground their findings against observations (using satellite altimetry and in situ observations collected by BAS, including moorings, gliders, and ship-based observations).

Depending on the student's interests, different dynamical regimes can be investigated, with contrasting levels of eddy activity and areas both influenced and unaffected by sea-ice, with the possibility to use artificial intelligence techniques to optimise the observations coverage and resolution. The project offers training in ocean modelling and sea-going experience (NOC), sensor piloting, and possibly the opportunity to contribute to fieldwork in Antarctica (BAS). Visits to Scripps Institution of Oceanography (US) may also be supported through DTP funding, providing access to one of the world's leading oceanographic research centres.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Development of Heated Garments for Patients with Raynaud’s Phenomenon
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000 / annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Development of Smart Knitted/ 3D printed Heated Gloves for Raynaud's Phenomenon

Raynaud's phenomenon (RP) is a condition characterised by episodic reductions in blood flow to the fingers triggered by exposure to cold temperatures or emotional stress, resulting in pain, numbness, colour changes and impaired hand function. RP affects approximately 5% of the population and may occur as a primary condition or as an early manifestation of systemic sclerosis (SSc), a rare autoimmune disease associated with severe vascular complications including painful digital ulcers.

The research will investigate the use of advanced textile materials, conductive yarns, knitted sensor structures and integrated heating technologies to create gloves capable of monitoring finger skin temperature and providing responsive thermal regulation. The project will involve the development of novel knitted/ 3D printed constructions, integration of temperature sensing and heating elements & technologies, prototype manufacture, and laboratory evaluation of thermal and functional performance.

For further details see here.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Sensing Circular Cities: Testing Low-Carbon Construction Materials through Urban Living Labs
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Cities need construction materials that reduce embodied carbon and make better use of waste, yet adoption is constrained by uncertainty about long-term performance and by a lack of evidence about where these innovations should be deployed. This PhD will develop a multiscale “material-to-map” framework that connects laboratory characterisation and structural sensing with AI-enabled spatial planning. It will establish not only whether low-carbon materials work, but also where their deployment could deliver the greatest carbon, infrastructure and social value.

Under the supervision of our interdisciplinary team, the student will first develop/identify cementitious systems incorporating recycled construction materials or industrial by-products and capable of lowering emissions or storing carbon (i.e. the supervision team will propose feasible options). Laboratory research will quantify reaction mechanisms, microstructure, mechanical performance, carbon uptake and resistance to relevant deterioration processes.

Instrumented specimens and demonstrator components will combine embedded or surface-mounted sensors with non-destructive evaluation to monitor strain, temperature, moisture, cracking and changes in material condition under mechanical loading and representative environmental exposure.

For further details see here.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Sensing BRCA2 Loss: Synthetic Antibodies for Precision Prostate Cancer Treatment
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

Prostate cancer is the second most diagnosed cancer in men worldwide and remains a major cause of cancer mortality. Loss of BRCA2, a protein essential for DNA repair, is associated with an aggressive disease and can confer sensitivity to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors. Althougth genomic testing can identify BRCA2 alterations, there is currently no reliable antibody-based method for detecting functional BRCA2 protein loss in tumor tissue. This limits spatial analysis of BRCAS expression and does not enable selecting patients for precision treatment.

This project will develop molecularly imprinted polymer nano particles (nanoMIPs) as stable, reproducible synthetic alternatives to antibodies for sensing BRCA2 loss in prostate cancer tissue.

The objectives are to: (1) generate high-affinity nanoMIPs against defined BRCA2 regions; (2) develop labelled nanoMIP systems for detecting BRCA2 in protein and cell-based assays; and (3) establish and validate a tissue-based assay that distinguishes BRCA2-mutant from wild-type prostate cancers.

The project directly advances the Sensing the World theme by connecting biological recognition and physical sensing with quantitative interpretation and clinical decision-making. It establishes a new way of working across faculties to address a complex global health challenge while training a doctoral researcher to translate discoveries between engineering and clinical practice.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B14 Atmospheric Chemistry of Hydrofluoroolefins: Spectroscopic and Computational Studies of Fluorinated Criegee Intermediates
jobs.description_html:
Hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs) are a new generation of refrigerants designed as environmentally friendly replacements for older halocarbons. They have very low global warming potential and zero ozone depletion potential, leading to their rapid adoption in commercial and domestic systems, such as automotive air conditioning and heat pumps. Global emissions of HFOs are projected to exceed one million tonnes annually by 2050, primarily in densely populated regions. Despite their growing use, the atmospheric breakdown of HFOs is poorly understood. Once released, they are oxidised to form potentially hazardous products such as carbonyls, secondary organic aerosols (SOA), and trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), a persistent “forever” chemical with implications for air quality, health, and climate.

A particularly important but underexplored process is the ozonolysis of HFOs, especially at night when photochemical oxidants like OH are absent. Ozonolysis of alkenes generates highly reactive Criegee intermediates (CIs), which are now known to be key drivers of radical and particle formation in the atmosphere. However, the chemistry of fluorinated Criegee intermediates (HFO-CIs) has scarcely been studied. Their potential to form toxic oxidation products, drive SOA growth, and influence tropospheric oxidative capacity represents a major knowledge gap.

This studentship will focus on fundamental laboratory and computational studies of HFO-CIs, providing the first direct spectroscopic detection of their structures, reaction rates, and branching ratios with common atmospheric species. Experiments will be conducted using cutting-edge laser techniques uniquely capable of selective detection of trace reactive intermediates. In parallel, high-level quantum chemical calculations and master-equation modelling will characterise the reaction pathways and provide insights into conformer-specific reactivity.

The results will be incorporated into the Master Chemical Mechanism (MCM), the international benchmark for atmospheric modelling, and applied in urban air quality scenarios (e.g. Beijing, Delhi) to assess the wider impacts of HFO chemistry on oxidative budgets, ozone formation, and aerosol production. This interdisciplinary project bridges laboratory spectroscopy, computational chemistry, and atmospheric modelling, offering the student a unique opportunity to contribute to a pressing environmental challenge at the interface of physical chemistry, climate science, and public health.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B15 Embedding Biodiversity Protection into Battery Supply Chains
jobs.description_html:
The global transition to electrified transport is driving unprecedented demand for battery minerals such as lithium and cobalt, frequently extracted in ecologically sensitive biodiversity hotspots -notably, nickel-cobalt production in Indonesia and the Philippines and copper/lithium production in the high-Andes. However, biodiversity risks remain poorly mapped and weakly integrated into risk assessment, with existing approaches operating at mismatched spatial scales, from localised environmental impact assessments (EIAs) to global sustainability reporting. This creates a disconnect between local ecological impacts and strategic supply chain decisions.

This PhD addresses this gap by combining spatial ecological analysis, comparative tool evaluation and case study evidence to develop a spatially explicit, evidence-based approach to identifying and evaluating biodiversity risk across lithium supply chains, using case studies from the UK and South America, structured around four research questions.

First, what are the strengths, limitations and data gaps of existing biodiversity assessment approaches for supply-chain decision-making? The project critically compares analytical tools (life cycle assessment, EIAs, spatial mapping, emerging risk modelling) and frameworks (the mitigation hierarchy, ICMM principles) for their ability to inform CSRD, TNFD and SBTN implementation.

Second, where are the highest biodiversity risks located across lithium supply chains, and how do these vary by region and production stage? Building on UoB/BGS spatial mapping methods, the project overlays biodiversity hotspot data (IBAT, IUCN Red List, Key Biodiversity Areas, protected areas, species-richness layers), strengthened by eDNA and bioacoustic monitoring, with georeferenced supply chain data (Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Earth Observation (EO) and hydrological modelling) to distinguish direct impacts (habitat loss, fragmentation) from indirect impacts (land-use change, water stress, pollution).

Third, what risks identified through spatial analysis are omitted or underrepresented in existing reporting frameworks? Findings are compared against submitted EIAs to identify reporting gaps and inform EIA methodology.

Fourth, what mitigation strategies exist, and how can they best be deployed? The project evaluates siting, technology choice and pollution control mechanisms for their effectiveness and practical constraints.

In collaboration with industry, NGOs, regulators and sustainability practitioners, the student will synthesise their findings into a practical, coherent and transferable framework for integrating biodiversity risk into mineral governance and responsible sourcing.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B12 AI-Enabled Prediction of UK Pollen Season Magnitude for Next-Generation Forecasting
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Understanding and forecasting airborne pollen is essential for improving operational environmental prediction across the UK. While daily pollen forecasts have improved substantially in recent years, one of the greatest remaining challenges is predicting the overall magnitude of each pollen season. For example, total birch pollen concentrations can vary by a factor of eight between consecutive years, driven by complex interactions between previous-season pollen production, meteorological conditions during the preceding summer, and weather during the flowering season itself. These processes remain poorly understood and are not currently represented within operational forecasting systems.

This project will harness a unique UK-wide pollen reanalysis (2000–2025), developed by the UK Met Office under the stewardship of Co-I Lucy Neal, together with long-term pollen observations and meteorological datasets, to develop next-generation machine learning approaches for predicting seasonal pollen magnitude. The resulting models will improve understanding of the environmental drivers of interannual variability while providing practical tools to enhance the operational Met Office NAME pollen forecast.

With only 8 active regulatory-grade pollen monitoring sites across the UK, equivalent to approximately one site per eight million people, long-term pollen observations are extremely sparse. The pollen reanalysis provides an unprecedented spatially and temporally complete dataset for developing and validating artificial intelligence methods. The student will investigate how biological memory, antecedent weather conditions and environmental variables combine to determine pollen production, developing interpretable machine learning models capable of predicting seasonal severity months in advance.

This PhD will be embedded in a vibrant interdisciplinary research environment at the University of Birmingham, combining expertise in environmental science, artificial intelligence and applied mathematics. Joint supervision from Environmental Sciences, the School of Mathematics, and the UK Met Office will provide outstanding training in machine learning, environmental modelling and operational forecasting. The research will directly address a major limitation in current pollen forecasting systems, delivering new scientific understanding alongside AI tools with clear operational impact for the UK Met Office and wider environmental forecasting community.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Radicals and Reactive Intermediates in Heavy Main-Group Chemistry
jobs.description_html:
A fully funded PhD studentship is available for a highly motivated, outstanding chemist with a passion for inorganic synthesis and spectroscopy.

Heavy pnictogen compounds have received considerable attention in recent years as competent reagents for two-electron redox chemistry and the activation of small molecules. In comparison, the area of heavy main-group radical compounds remains relatively underdeveloped. Their electronic structures are typically affected by strong spin-orbit coupling effects, leading to fascinating spectroscopic features and reactivities. The capability of heavy main-group elements to stabilise open-shell fragments in their vicinity remains equally underexplored but holds great promise for the development of atom-transfer reactions with small molecules.

In this PhD project, we aim to access open-shell main-group species either by redox reactions (authentic main-group radicals) or via the formation of open-shell fragments (carbenes, nitrenes and higher homologues) in their direct vicinity. The electronic structures of the synthesised compounds will be elucidated by spectroscopy, and reactivity studies towards small molecules will be conducted. This will require the appointed student to undertake inorganic synthesis (Schlenk and glovebox techniques), followed by characterisation using a range of spectroscopic and analytical techniques (NMR, IR, UV/vis, EPR, SQUID, XAS and scXRD). The focus at the start of the project will be on bismuth chemistry, but extension towards other heavy elements, e.g., antimony, tin, lead, indium or thallium, will be targeted based on the results obtained.

In addition to training in the above techniques, the student will receive training in scientific writing, oral and poster presentations, lab management, lab safety and other transferable skills. The student will benefit from co-supervision by experts in inorganic synthesis and magnetism. The project offers opportunities for publication in leading international journals, presentation of results at national and international conferences, and collaboration with researchers across the UK and Europe.
This project is expected to start in late September / early October 2027.

Eligibility

Applicants should hold, or expect to obtain, a First Class or high Upper Second Class degree in Chemistry or a closely related discipline. Prior experience with synthetic chemistry under inert conditions is essential, while experience in spectroscopy of paramagnetic compounds is advantageous but not required.

To apply, please contact the main supervisor, Dr. Josh Abbenseth. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B06 Combatting Insecticide Pollution: An Evolution-Informed Molecular Docking Framework to Protect Pollinators and Beneficial Insects
jobs.description_html:
Insect populations are declining worldwide, and agrochemical pollution is a principal driver. Current insecticide safety assessments underestimate environmental harm because they rely mainly on short-term mortality tests on a few surrogate species, most often honeybees, and overlook sublethal and community-level effects. The central environmental problem this project will solve is evolutionary: broad-spectrum insecticides—pyrethroids, neonicotinoids, organophosphates, carbamates and diamides—act on molecular targets conserved across the arthropod phylogeny, so pests, pollinators, natural predators and parasitoids share vulnerability through ‘toxicity by descent’. This project will deliver a predictive, evolution-informed molecular docking framework that protects beneficial insects by quantifying how sequence and structural divergence in insecticide target proteins translates into differential susceptibility across species. Key research questions are: (1) How does target-site divergence across arthropod phylogenies predict insecticide binding and toxicity? (2) Can molecular docking of representative insecticides against structurally modelled target proteins recapitulate documented resistance and species-sensitivity data? (3) Can the resulting framework guide selection of chemistries that spare vulnerable nontarget species and reduce environmental pollution?

To answer these questions, the project will compile target-protein sequences for five major insecticide classes across a phylogenetically representative panel of pests and beneficial arthropods, generate and refine structural models using homology modelling and AlphaFold, and run validated molecular docking pipelines against a panel of environmentally relevant insecticides. Predictions will be benchmarked against empirical resistance and sensitivity data from the literature and validated experimentally in Drosophila melanogaster and cell-based assays.

The outcomes are oriented directly to solving an environmental problem: a species-risk prioritisation framework and a cheminformatics tool that enable regulators and industry to identify at-risk species, avoid harmful chemistries and design safer insecticides, informing evidence-based risk assessment under the precautionary principle and contributing to halting insect declines.

The project will run over 3.5 years: Year 1 will focus on phylogenomic data assembly and structural modelling; Year 2 on docking pipeline development and benchmarking; Year 3 on experimental validation and case-study application with the industrial partner; the final six months on integration, thesis writing and dissemination.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B07 Biodiversity Digital Twin: Leveraging Environmental DNA and Artificial Intelligence for Monitoring Biodiversity Loss
jobs.description_html:
Biodiversity is declining at an alarming rate, affecting the delivery of ecosystem services on which we all rely for our well-being and the economy. These services include climate regulation, food provisioning, clean water and recreation, to name a few. With the exit from the EU, the UK established the 25-year environment plan to improve environmental quality within a generation, and the Environment Act 2021 to maintain biodiversity net gain while enabling growth. These necessary regulations demand a rapid response from industry to assess the impact of production processes on biodiversity.

However, we lack the tools to predict the impact of industrial processes on natural biological diversity, thereby limiting our ability to conserve critical resources and the services they provide. One of the main challenges that conservationists face is predicting the severity of biodiversity loss and identifying the main drivers of this loss. Traditional methods focus on individual species, missing by design the species interactions and with the environment. Holistic, community-level approaches are still largely missing.

In this project, the DR will develop state-of-the-art AI algorithms to monitor and predict biodiversity loss under different climate and pollution scenarios. The DR will apply graph neural networks (GNNs), especially temporal graph networks (TGNs) and spatiotemporal graph neural networks (STGNNs), to model historical biodiversity data obtained from freshwater lake ecosystems across England. This will be done using sediment core environmental DNA. GNN is a cutting-edge AI model. It will integrate spatiotemporal eDNA and environmental data to create a digital twin to simulate the dynamics of freshwater lake biodiversity. This Biodiversity Digital Twin will offer multi-scale, holistic modelling that tracks changes across taxonomic groups over space and time and links them to environmental change, identifying the main drivers of loss.

To make the tool accessible to end-users, the DR will develop an intuitive analytical dashboard. This dashboard will allow the direct assessment of production processes, land use, and other human activities on biodiversity. By synergistically combining advanced computational and bioinformatics technologies with end-user insights, the team aims to accelerate the transition from traditional to science-driven, technologically enhanced solutions for biodiversity conservation.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Neuromorphic Systems for Low-latency and Efficient Multimodal Processing
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Modern AI systems achieve remarkable performance on tasks ranging from language modelling to computer vision. However, their large size, and significant data requirements, make them costly to train and deploy, with AI systems set to consume 3% of global energy supply by 2030. Neuromorphic systems aim to solve this challenge, by taking inspiration from the brain, to develop algorithms and computational substrates that can achieve intelligent processing on a similar power (approx. 20W).

However, while modern AI systems have benefited from access to large volumes of high-quality and labelled data, these resources do not exist in the neuromorphic domain, limiting overall progress. The proposed supervisory team are addressing this gap and are currently collecting the world’s first phonetically rich multi-modal neuromorphic dataset, containing audio and video recordings of spoken language (ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11043887). [ieeexplore.ieee.org] The unique contribution captures data using neuromorphic sensors allowing high temporal accuracy, while simultaneously introducing sparsityto increasing overall efficiency. 

However, while neuromorphic processors can exploit these data structures, specialised algorithms are required to perform tasks such as classification and reasoning, which are severely lacking in the community.

The project is structured into 3 equally weighted research streams to deliver new fundamental knowledge through harnessing the capabilities of neuromorphic sensors to better capture and process speech (Streams 1 & 2), and generate impact through applications of this technology in society (stream 3):

Stream 1: Algorithmic exploitation of neuromorphic audio-visual speech data, to address the major computational bottlenecks in speech recognition and speech production analysis, e.g. minimising data movement using neuromorphic algorithms and chips such as Intel’s Loihi2.

Stream 2: Developing language understanding through neuromorphic representations. Speech sounds are produced using coordinated movements of articulators to achieve specific acoustic targets (e.g. fast movements of the tongue and lips). These are challenging to process using conventional techniques, as individuals can produce the same sound in multiple ways, and the same articulatory movement in different individuals can lead to different sounds.

Stream 3: Impact through real-world applications of low-power speech processing, for tasks such as lip reading for the hearing impaired, and language understanding. The goal will be to develop technology suitable for deployment at the edge, such as in mobile devices and hearing aids, and with potential for embedding in augmented reality scenarios.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B03 Managing Contrasting Landscapes for Soil Carbon Sequestration, Soil Biodiversity and Tree Health
jobs.description_html:
The City of London Corporation manages a nationally significant portfolio of open spaces including Epping Forest, Burnham Beeches, Hampstead Heath, Queen's Park, West Ham Park, Copped Hall and Patmore's Field. Through its Carbon Removals Programme, the Corporation is investing in habitat restoration, meadow creation, soil improvement initiatives and woodland resilience measures to support climate mitigation, biodiversity recovery and ecosystem resilience.

Land management practices influence soil microbiology and chemistry, which in turn regulate carbon sequestration, nutrient cycling and tree resilience. By understanding these relationships, it is possible to design management interventions that simultaneously enhance carbon storage, biodiversity recovery and ecosystem resilience. However, there remains a significant evidence gap regarding which site-specific land management interventions most effectively improve soil condition, increase carbon sequestration and strengthen ecosystem resilience.

Research Aim 

To develop evidence-based land management recommendations that maximise soil carbon sequestration, enhance soil biodiversity, and improve tree resilience across a diverse network of restored meadows, urban parks, wood pasture and forest landscapes. We would like to answer following questions:

1. How do different interventions influence ecosystem resilience, tree and soil health? 

2, Which soil microbial communities and processes are most strongly associated with carbon accumulation, nutrient cycling and ecosystem recovery under various management strategies? 

3. How can monitoring evidence be translated into practical land management decisions?

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - UTIs and the Menopause
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Why does prevalence of UTIs increase so substantially during the menopause? How do the hormonal changes associated with menopause come to affect competition between bacterial species in the unique flow conditions of the bladder and urethra? We hypothesise that menopause-associated changes in hormone signalling alter the urinary tract environment, disrupting the balance of microbial communities and their interactions with the host.

We will use an interdisciplinary approach, combining mathematical modelling, microfluidic lab-on-a-chip experiments with cells, and bioinformatics and genomics to study how cell signalling affects gene expression. In particular, we want to capture how microbial competition is communicated -how cells sense and respond to biochemical and mechanical signals from the same and other microbial species and those from the host environment. A further goalis to understand our role as scientists and sensors: how should microfluidic devices best be designed and deployed as sensors and emulators of disease?

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - The Role of Adaptive Evolution in the Microbial Sensing of Anthropogenic Molecules

This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Introduction. There is now a realisation both in the public and scientific communities that discarded plastic materials present a growing hazard to the natural environment and human health across the globe. Here, a major concern is the release of molecular breakdown products that alter the biochemistry of the exposed organisms. Since microbial life is abundant in the natural environment, it is hypothesised that they will be the most significantly impacted by any such effects. However, it remains unclear as to how microbes sense the presence of such molecules, and whether they could be adapting their behaviour or evolving to enable the detection of these compounds.

Aims, Objectives and Methods. This project aims to investigate the biochemical and genetic changes that occur to these microbes upon exposure to various small molecule degradants of plastics. The technical objectives are thus the: (1) culturing of microbes in the presence of these compounds and the profiling of their growth behaviour; (2) transcriptomic analysis to identify which genes have been expressed; (3) proteomic DNA-binding analysis (e.g. reverse-ChIP) to identify the proteins that bind to the regulatory regions of differentially expressed genes (i.e. the transcription factors that are performing the molecular sensing of these compounds); and (4) validation of transcription factor function in a model microbe (E. coli).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B11 Learning the Changing Extremes of European Precipitation in a Warming Climate
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
One of the major challenges for the current and future climate diagnostics is the occurrence of very rare, but extreme intense precipitation events. Those record-shattering events lead to the Valencia-Flood in October 2024 in Spain or the Ahr-floods in July 2021 in Germany with billions of Euro of financial losses and unfortunately significant numbers of fatalities (cf. e.g., Leckebusch & McCarthy (2026) and references therein).

While the principal underlying physical mechanism of precipitation formation and the principal mechanisms of necessary precursor conditions are well understood, the exact amount of extreme precipitation and when and where those events may occur are less well understood. The same holds true for the principal rate of occurrence, which is difficult to estimate as those events may occur only once or twice per century in the current climate. Even more difficult is an assessment of those events for future climate conditions, altered by human activities. We can already diagnose that those events are more likely to occur under the influence of a warming climate, but the exact changes in those statistics of their occurrence remains a challenge. One of the reasons for this is the inability of current climate models to fully simulate those rare and extreme precipitation events in their full characteristics, from very local scale processes to the wider statistical occurrences for e.g., 30-years climatic time spans.

This project will develop and test a novel approach to estimate those rare events. It will investigate whether a combination of AI- and Extreme Value Theory (EVT)-approaches can produce reliable estimates for future climate states. Thus, can AI–EVT models trained on reanalyses and large hindcast ensembles estimate regional extreme-rainfall distributions that remain reliable when transferred between global warming levels and circulation regimes?

This project would best suit a student with a Computer Science background, or otherwise a numerical background for example Meteorology, Physics, or Maths, with experience coding in Python or similar (e.g. R, Matlab), and preferably with some experience in AI approaches.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B05 Novel Ways to Deal with the Complexities of Detecting Selection for Antimicrobial Resistance under Realistic Natural Conditions
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major public health threat. The environment plays an important role as resistant microorganisms are transmitted between people and animals through the environment; they also survive or thrive there and exchange genes.

One of the big debates is whether the low concentrations of antibiotics in the environment are selecting for resistance.

One approach to experimentally test this is to compete a ‘special pair’ of sensitive and resistant bacteria at a range of antibiotic concentrations in the lab, where their only difference is resistance so they share the same ecological niche. This is an accurate and sensitive method, but the conditions in the lab do not mimic the environment.

An alternative approach is to bring a complex sample from the environment into the lab and measure whether resistance genes are increasing at different antibiotic concentrations. This would seem to mimic the environment as a diverse community of bacteria is used, but the inevitable shifts in microbial community composition when incubating in rich media can result in increased resistance levels in the absence of selection.

We have a different idea, to use mathematical models based on results from simple lab experiments and then create the complexity in the model by including the effects of diversity, predation, low substrate concentrations etc, ultimately predicting at which concentration selection happens in the environment and also understanding the effects of the complications. This will be coupled with experiments under natural conditions to test and validate the model, in flume mesocosms that can mimic river conditions in the lab at UKCEH Wallingford and also in situ in rivers. For this, we will put the special pair in ‘cages’ (dialysis bags) so they cannot escape but are immersed in the environment and experience the same nutrient concentrations etc. as the other bacteria in the surrounding environment.

Such a validated mathematical model that can predict the risk of selection under environmental conditions is hugely important because it is impossible to expose thousands of different pathogenic and environmental bacteria with various (combinations) of resistances to many levels of hundreds of potentially selective antibiotics and other compounds under a variety of relevant environmental conditions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B13 Health Risks from Individual and Synergistic Heat and Air Pollution under Climate Change
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Extreme heat and air pollution are among the leading environmental threats to human health. They frequently occur together, yet their health impacts are still commonly assessed independently. This is important because simultaneous exposure may produce health effects greater than expected from either hazard alone. As climate change intensifies heat extremes and alters patterns of PM2.5 and ozone, understanding these interacting risks is increasingly important for climate adaptation, air-quality management and public-health protection.

Our recent analysis across England and Wales provides compelling evidence of this interaction. In London, when temperature and PM2.5 simultaneously exceeded their 97.5th percentiles, the relative risk of all-cause mortality reached 1.51, with a relative excess risk due to interaction of 0.33. Synergistic effects were particularly strong for respiratory mortality, while older adults and females showed greater susceptibility (Fig. 1). Importantly, applying London’s higher absolute PM2.5 thresholds to other regions revealed similar synergistic effects where sufficient co-exposure occurred, suggesting that interactions may become especially important once pollution exceeds critical concentrations.

These findings raise an urgent wider question: how important are synergistic heat–air-pollution health risks globally, and how will they change as the climate warms? Existing studies have examined historical interactions or projected future compound events, but a globally consistent framework linking observed synergistic mortality effects with future climate and air-pollution change is currently missing.

This studentship will address this gap through four linked objectives:

  • Establish how heat, PM2.5 and ozone have individually and synergistically affected mortality across different regions and vulnerable populations.
  • Determine how the frequency, intensity and geographical distribution of compound heat–air-pollution events will change under future climate and emission scenarios.
  • Quantify future mortality attributable specifically to synergistic exposure and determine where conventional single-hazard assessments underestimate health risks.
  • Evaluate the health benefits and economic implications of alternative climate and air-quality mitigation strategies.

By connecting observed health responses with emerging CMIP7 projections, the project will provide a global assessment of compound heat–air-pollution risks from the past through the twenty-first century. It will identify emerging hotspots and vulnerable populations and establish where integrated climate and air-quality interventions can deliver the greatest public-health benefits.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B02 Microbial Lipid Cycling in the Oceans: An Integrated ‘Omics’ Approach
jobs.description_html:
Lipids, containing carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur, are a major component of all living cells and are constantly released into the oceans due to programmed cell death, viral infections and zooplankton grazing. Current estimates suggest that lipids can account for 10% of total dissolved organic matter (DOC) in the oceans. However, our knowledge on microbial lipid transformation in the oceans is very limited. Neither the identities of the microbes involved, nor the mechanisms by which lipids are degraded, have been well understood.

A major hurdle in understanding the microbial lipid cycle lies in the difficulty in characterizing and quantifying numerous lipid classes in marine samples. Commonly observed lipids in marine ecosystems include phospholipids, glycolipids and amino acid-containing lipids. Recent advances in technologies such as liquid chromatography electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (LC-ESI-MS) has enabled high throughput identification and quantification of thousands of cellular lipid molecular species (Shevchenko, 2010), which now enables lipid characterization both qualitatively and quantitatively. Indeed, lipidomics is starting to complement the rapid progress made in genomics, metagenomics, transcriptomics and proteomics.

Here in this project, we will combine laboratory and filed based methodologies to fully uncover the lipid cycle in marine waters. The aim of this project is thus twofold:

Firstly, we aim to establish a high throughput workflow for simultaneous determination of common lipids species in marine surface waters using our in house HPLC MS platform. This will involve examining samples from the Western English Channel, collected via the Marine Biological Association research vessel, Sepia.

Secondly, we aim to determine the identity and activity of key microbial populations in the recycling of representative lipids in marine surface waters and coastal marine sediment using integrated omics approach, e.g. high throughput sequencing of 16S/18S rRNA, metagenomics, metagenomics and lipidomics.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B04 Microbial Degradation of Trace Gases in Post-wildfire Soils
jobs.description_html:
Background

Wildfires are increasing in frequency and severity in many regions as a consequence of climate change1. In addition to releasing large quantities of carbon dioxide, wildfires generate atmospheric trace gases including carbon monoxide (CO), methane (CH₄) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs)2,3. The fate of these gases after deposition to soils is poorly understood, despite the potential importance of microbial trace-gas oxidation for atmospheric chemistry, soil carbon cycling and ecosystem recovery.

Wildfire substantially alters soil physicochemical properties and microbial communities through the loss and transformation of organic matter, formation of pyrogenic carbon, changes in pH and nutrient availability, and alterations in soil moisture and structure. These changes may strongly influence the capacity of soil microbial communities to consume atmospheric trace gases. Early studies have shown that organic amendments can increase soil atmospheric methane uptake in agricultural soils4. However, we lack a mechanistic understanding of how wildfire severity and post-fire recovery affect microbial trace-gas oxidation.

This PhD will investigate how wildfire alters the capacity of soils to act as microbial sinks for atmospheric trace gases and whether this function can be enhanced during ecosystem recovery. It will examine interactions between fire severity, soil properties, pyrogenic carbon and trace-gas-oxidising microbial communities.

The research will employ a combination of gas measurements, soil mesocosm, and cutting-edge molecular techniques. DNA sequencing and metagenomic analyses will identify functional genes responsible for trace gas oxidation. Mesocosm experiments will test the effects of organic amendments on microbial activity and trace gas consumption, providing critical data on soil recovery and greenhouse gas mitigation.

Overall outputs:

The project will establish how wildfire affects soil trace-gas consumption and identify the microbial and environmental mechanisms underpinning this process. It will generate datasets linking fire severity, soil properties, microbial community composition and trace-gas oxidation, and provide a platform for future research on microbial ecosystem services and restoration of soil biogeochemical functions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B01 Can a Tree Remember a Drought? Understanding the Mechanisms of Tree Memory
jobs.description_html:
Trees are long living, sessile organisms that represent a fundamental component of most of earth ecosystems. Being immobile during their life, trees need to efficiently adapt to changes of environment and to stresses, in order to reach maturity and reproduction.

Recent advanced in genomics studies are always more convincingly showing that environmental information can be recorded at molecular level on DNA through epigenetic marks. Epigenetics studies molecular changes of DNA (mostly DNA methylation) in response to developmental or environmental stimuli, which does not involve a change of the DNA sequence itself. These changes can be inherited during cell division and are particular stable in plants, where they represent the base of an epigenetic “memory”, which remains encoded in biological tissues and can be transmitted to progenies.

In trees, wood is produced by plant cells that lignified and die to provide physical functions such as of mechanical support, storage and water conduction. However, part of their DNA is preserved unaltered, and retains the epigenetic information encoded in the cells in the moment they died. In temperate zones, most trees produce in their wood one growth-ring each year, so that the entire period of a tree’s life remain impressed in its wood material. As wood growth is affected by environmental conditions, trees have marks of past interactions with the environment recorded into their wood as they grow, at both physical and molecular level. However, while physical propriety of tree rings is well investigated, the possible epigenetic changes associated to the residual DNA in different rings re.

This project aims to understand how trees use environmental information to adapt to a changing condition. This will be done by extracting DNA from different parts of tree rings and compare their epigenetic profiles. The PhD researcher will compare the DNA methylation from different tree rings and associate epigenetic changes to historical and ecological record of drought. This will allow to connect tree molecular and physical responses to the environment in in tree rings, creating for the first time a direct connection among dendrochronology, ecology and epigenetic data in trees.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship Engineering - Chemical Probes to Sense Dynamic Molecular Neighbourhoods in Living Cells
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

How can we measure the fleeting molecular neighbourhoods that control signalling inside living cells?

Proximity-labelling methods provide a powerful way to address this problem by converting spatial proximity into a permanent chemical tag that can subsequently be detected by imaging or proteomics. However, current approaches face an important trade-off: the reactive chemistry needed to generate a measurable signal can perturb sensitive biological systems, while the spatial reach of labelling is difficult to control. This project will develop a new generation of chemically engineered proximity probes that act as tuneable molecular sensors of local cellular environments.

The student will design and synthesise new probe molecules whose chemical and physical properties are systematically varied to control their behaviour during proximity labelling. Combining synthetic chemistry with biochemical and cellular experiments, the project will establish how molecular structure determines key sensing properties including labelling efficiency, biological compatibility and spatial precision. Preliminary work from the supervisory team supports the feasibility of this concept while leaving substantial scope for fundamental discovery and technology development.

The project will progress through three linked stages. First, the student will create and characterise a focused library of new proximity-labelling probes and establish relationships between chemical structure and probe behaviour. Second, promising probes will be evaluated in living cells using biochemical assays, advanced fluorescence imaging and super-resolution microscopy to determine how accurately and efficiently they report local molecular neighbourhoods. Finally, selected probes will be applied to biologically challenging systems in which conventional proximity labelling can itself perturb the processesbeing studied. Proteomic analysis will be used selectively to identify the molecular networks revealed by the new sensing platform.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Mechanochromic Molecules for Cellular Forces Sensing
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Tensile forces influence a variety of important cellular processes including cell division, stem cell differentiation and gene expression.

  1. At the tissue level these forces play a crucial role in morphogenesis, wound healing, the immune response and in pathological processes such as cancer metastasis. However, our understanding of how force influences cell function is very limited due to a lack of techniques to measure force within live tissue. To date, genetically encoded tension sensors have been developed, but their use in whole tissues has so far been limited. One reason for this limited use is the low sensitivity of current in vivo tension sensors. At the molecular level, the unique ability of mechanical force to distort, bend and stretch chemical bonds has led to the development of mechanochromic molecules acting as spatially sensitive molecular probes or micro-crack sensors in synthetic materials.
  2. Chemical mechanosensors offer a potentially powerful solution to this problem but have yet to be translated into biological systems. Here we will take a multidisciplinary approach to bridge this gap and aim to develop and test novel chemical force sensors suitable for measuring tensile forces at cellular/tissue level.

The goals of this project are:

  • The creation of new mechanochromophores that can be used as force sensors in a biological context
  • Determine how physicochemical parameters influence mechanochromophore activation and fluorescence.
  • Demonstrate the performance of selected mechanochromophores using human cells as a biological model system.

The postgraduate researcher (PGR) will be trained by means of a training-through-research model by:

Prof. De Bo and senior members of the De Bo group on mechanochemistry and various aspects of organic and polymer chemistry.

Dr Amer and senior members of the Amer group on cell culture, confocal microscopy, and force microscopy.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Treatment Planning of FLASH Delivery of Cancer Therapy with Focussed Very High Energy Electron Beams
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. The global burden of cancer continues to increase, with more than 500,000 new cases predicted annually in the UK by 2040. Radiotherapy remains a cornerstone of cancer treatment, but irradiation of healthy tissue surrounding or traversed by the tumour remains a significant limitation. Very High Energy Electron (VHEE) radiotherapy offers substantial penetration and may complement existing photon and particle therapies. Combining VHEE with ultra-high dose-rate (UHDR) delivery, including FLASH dose rates, could further exploit physical and biological advantages.

This project will investigate treatment planning and focused VHEE delivery in the FLASH regime. Methods will include Monte Carlo modelling of beam transport and dose deposition, treatment-plan optimisation, analysis of dose distributions, and evaluation of parameters influencing healthy-tissue sparing and target coverage. Computational results will, where appropriate, be compared with experimental dosimetry and existing radiotherapy data. Outcomes will include improved understanding of VHEE dose deposition and assessment of focused FLASH-VHEE delivery for future clinical translation.

The student will receive interdisciplinary supervision from the Faculty of Science and Engineering and School of Medical Sciences, with training in Monte Carlo methods, radiation transport, treatment planning, optimisation, dosimetry, data analysis and scientific computing, supported by cross-faculty expertise and wider postgraduate research training.
