jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Phase-optimised PUFA Production in Oleaginous Yeast via Transcriptomics-Guided Enzyme-Constrained Metabolic Modelling
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

We hypothesise that defining empirical reaction-specific translational efficiency operators (TE = [E]/mRNA) within phase-specific ecGSMMs will enable resource-balanced cassette design and allow inference of enzyme abundances from RNA-seq data alone in subsequent iterations. Combined with genomic information and genome-scale modelling, this framework will predict production efficiency and identify phase-optimised targets.

The project will:

  • Estimate the mRNA expression levels required to achieve desired increases in reaction capacity.
  • Categorise transcriptionally versus translationally bottlenecked genes under nitrogen limitation.
  • Deliver predictive models of PUFA production efficiency across selected oleaginous yeasts.

Methodology (DBTL)

Design & Build

Round 1: Curate a library of native phase-responsive promoters from selected oleaginous yeasts (examples include Yarrowia lipolytica, Rhodotorula toruloides or Lipomyces starkeyi). Characterise promoter kinetics using RNA light-up aptamers. Subsequent rounds will design phase-specific expression cassettes informed by modelling outputs and assemble them using modular cloning toolkits appropriate to the chosen host(s).

Test

Perform controlled fermentations under exponential and nitrogen-limited conditions. Measure process kinetics, lipid titres (GC-MS), phase-resolved RNA-seq and LC-MS proteomics to calibrate TE operators. Later rounds will rely primarily on RNA-seq and process data. Genomic data (genome sequences, annotations and comparative analyses) will support model construction and strain selection.

Learn

Apply enzyme-constrained flux scanning based on enforced objective flux (ecFSEOF) and kinetic flux control coefficient analysis on protein-constrained GSMMs to identify systemic pathway demands and kinetic bottlenecks. Verify protein headroom for overexpression. In subsequent iterations, infer enzyme states from TE operators and new RNA-seq data, rank rate-limiting constraints via dual variables, and update models to guide further engineering. Genome-scale models will explicitly predict production efficiency (titre, yield and rate) under different genetic and process scenarios

Focussing on the international flower trade, where temperature and spatial control are essential to preserving flower quality across borders, we will assess how proposed future autonomous systems alter the social perception and material footprint of this complicated delivery process.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Terahertz Photons for Quantum Control and Topological Quantum Information
jobs.department: Physics and Astronomy, Mathematical and Physical Sciences (MAPS)
jobs.description_html:
Principal supervisor name: Arijeet Pal

Principal supervisor UCL profile website: https://profiles.ucl.ac.uk/66876-arijeet-pal 

Funding: Maintenance stipend at UELA enhanced rate - rises each year (For 2026/27, the total stipend is expected to be £26,022, i.e. £1,500 above the UKRI London-weighted rate of £24,522)

Project summary

Terahertz (THz) frequencies occupy a largely unexplored regime for quantum technologies, bridging conventional microwave quantum circuits and optical platforms. The energy of a THz photon naturally matches important excitations in quantum materials, including cyclotron transitions, collective modes and Landau-level excitations. This PhD project will investigate how quantum states of THz radiation can be used to manipulate matter at the single- and few-photon level and, ultimately, to engineer robust qubits based on topological quantum states.

A central direction will be the strong and ultrastrong coupling of confined THz photons to two-dimensional electron systems in high magnetic fields. In the quantum Hall regime, coupling cyclotron and collective electronic excitations to THz cavity modes produces hybrid light–matter states known as Landau polaritons. The project will develop theoretical models for controlling these states using shaped THz pulses, cavity engineering and nonlinear interactions. We will investigate whether individual polaritonic excitations can constitute effective two-level systems and determine how their coherence, interactions and readout could be optimised.

A more ambitious objective is to explore whether THz cavities can manipulate or mediate interactions between topological excitations in integer and fractional quantum Hall states. In particular, the project will investigate cavity induced interactions, photon-mediated coupling between spatially separated edge or bulk excitations, and protocols for creating and controlling entangled states. An important question will be whether coupling to THz photons can provide new routes towards protected quantum information processing, including manipulation of fractionalised excitations and candidate topological qubits.

The research will combine quantum optics, condensed-matter theory and numerical modelling of driven open quantum systems, with close connections to experimentally achievable THz cavities and quantum materials. It will establish the opportunities †and fundamental limits- of THz photons as a new resource for quantum control and topological quantum technologies.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Mineral–Fluid–Rock Interactions for Sustainable Subsurface Energy Technologies
jobs.description_html:
Subsurface geological formations play a vital role in supporting the energy transition, including geothermal energy extraction, geological CO₂ storage and underground energy storage. The performance and long-term integrity of these systems are strongly influenced by interactions between fluids, minerals and fractured rocks. Understanding these coupled processes is therefore essential for developing safe, efficient and sustainable subsurface energy technologies.

This interdisciplinary PhD project will investigate fundamental mineral–fluid–rock interactions, with particular emphasis on mineral crystallisation, interfacial processes and their relationships with the hydraulic and mechanical behaviour of fractured rocks. The research will integrate environmental geochemistry and mineral–water interface science with experimental rock mechanics and fracture characterisation. Depending on the expertise and background of the successful candidate, specific investigations may include mineral nucleation and crystal growth, mineral–surface interactions, geochemical reactions in confined environments, and the evolution of fracture properties under coupled chemical and physical processes.

The project is jointly supervised by researchers at The University of Manchester and Peking University, bringing together complementary expertise in environmental geochemistry, mineral crystallisation, rock mechanics and subsurface engineering. The successful candidate will receive interdisciplinary research training and gain access to complementary experimental and analytical capabilities at both institutions.

The PhD follows a 1+2+1 structure, with Years 1 and 4 based at The University of Manchester and Years 2-3 at Peking University. Applications are welcomed from candidates with backgrounds in environmental engineering, geoscience, geochemistry, chemical engineering, civil engineering or related disciplines.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Developing Density Functional Approximations for Accurate Modelling of Magnetic Organic Conjugated Systems
jobs.description_html:
Density functional theory (DFT) has become the most widely employed approach for electronic structure calculations, with broad applications spanning chemistry, physics, biology, materials science, and related fields. The accuracy of DFT predictions is however limited by the approximations inherent in existing density functional approximations (DFAs), that can lead to deviations from experimental observations or even erroneous interpretations. These limitations are particularly pronounced in the study of organic conjugated systems displaying magnetism. In this project, we aim to develop an advanced DFA with enhanced accuracy for such challenging systems. The newly developed DFA will be applied to investigate how spin can be used to control light emission or electric conductance.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Mapping the nanoscale architecture of T cell sensing
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Immune cells continuously patrol the body to maintain health. Central to this process is their ability to sense environmental cues and respond appropriately. When T cells engage antigen-presenting cells (APCs), they simultaneously encounter numerous stimulatory, co-stimulatory, inhibitory, and adhesive signals at specialised contact sites known as immune synapses. Growing evidence suggests that the nanoscale spatial organisation of these molecular cues plays a critical role in determining how T cells interpret and integrate information.

The nanoscale architecture of the immune synapse, including how receptors and their ligands cluster, segregate, and reorganise in space and time, varies substantially depending on the combination of signals present. Because signalling output appears to depend as much on this spatial organisation as on ligand identity itself, the same receptor may generate distinct downstream responses depending on the nanoscale context in which it is engaged. Understanding immune signalling therefore requires not only identifying the molecular components involved but also determining how these components are wired into functional signalling circuits.

This project will directly address this challenge by combining a synthetic antigen-presenting cell platform with state-of-the-art nanoscale molecular mapping technologies. Engineered APCs displaying bioorthogonal click-biology handles will be used to present precisely defined combinations of peptide-MHC complexes, co-stimulatory receptors, co-inhibitory receptors, and integrin ligands at controlled surface densities. These programmable cells will provide an unprecedented ability to manipulate the composition and organisation of immune synapses. Using a combination of super-resolution imaging and photocatalytic proximity-labelling approaches, the student will generate detailed molecular maps of synapse architecture and determine how distinct combinations of extracellular cues are translated into intracellular signalling outcomes.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

Applications are now open for four-year PhD studentships at the EPSRC and BBSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Engineering Solutions for Antimicrobial Resistance at University College London, starting in October 2027.

About the programme

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a complex challenge that must be tackled on multiple fronts. It requires people who can work across government, industry and research disciplines—from microbiology and antimicrobial chemistry to building engineering.

Our interdisciplinary programme trains the next generation of academic, industry and public-sector leaders to develop and coordinate engineering solutions to AMR

Alongside your PhD research, you will join a bespoke cohort training programme covering the AMR context, research translation, entrepreneurship, science communication, research integrity and more. Our external partners range from innovative SMEs to government agencies and global industry leaders. Explore our training programme and partner network.

  • Diagnostics and Surveillance
  • Novel Therapies

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Interdisciplinary Methods for Liquid Crystal-Based Biosensing
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Liquid crystals (LCs) are exceptionally versatile and functional mesophases that combine fluidity with the ordering of solids. LCs have tremendous potential as low-cost and non-invasive bio-sensors and have been used to sense glucose, proteins, enzymes, cells, micromolecules etc. In this project, we will use mathematical modelling, ex-vivo (laboratory) and in-silico experiments to quantify the fundamental interactions between LCs and prototype cells. This will address open questions on - (i) how interfacial LC- cell interactions induce reorientation and structural changes in LCs and (ii) how these changes can be used to produce quantifiable signals. These signals can be used for sensing different types of cells, for detecting infected cells and for targeted drug delivery. The project has four core objectives incorporated into work packages (WP) at the interface of mathematical modelling, mechanics, machine learning and laboratory experiments, as listed below.

[1] WP I: Develop novel mathematical models for LC interactions with soft flexible surfaces, representative of human tissue;

[2] WP II: perform benchmark experiments on how LCs interact with epithelial tissue and cells;

[3] WPIII: validate and refine models with experimental data and

[4] WPIII: develop neural networks/machine learning tools for translation of LC outputs to sensing applications, e.g. in digital diagnostics and healthcare.

These WPs will set up a paradigmatic framework for the design of LC biosensors with bespoke properties.

jobs.description_html:
Metal-ligand multiple bonding is a burgeoning area for making chemically novel structural motifs, probing chemical bonding, and being applied to catalysis, some of which defines the state-of-the-art in element bond forming reactions. Most metal-ligand multiple bonds involve transition metals, but in recent years we have advanced f-element, and in particular actinide, metal-ligand multiple bonding by realising unprecedented bonding combinations (e.g. Nat. Commun. 2025, 16, 7136; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 137, e202419987; Nat. Chem. 2024, 16, 780-790; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2024, 146, 4098-4111; Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 4657; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 21766-21784; Nat. Chem. 2022, 14, 342-349; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 9764-9774; Nat. Commun. 2021, 12, 5649; Nat. Commun. 2021, 12, 4832; Nat. Commun. 2020, 11, 337). Nevertheless, there are still many actinide-ligand multiple bonds whose synthesis and in-depth characterisation would represent major milestones.

Building on recent preliminary results confirming the utility of a new ligand class in f-element chemistry, this PhD will target the synthesis of unprecedented actinide-ligand multiple bonds and explore their characterisation through in-depth experimental (reactivity, spectroscopic, magnetic) and computational (single- and multi-reference methods) characterisation.

The successful applicant will be a highly motivated, outstanding chemist ready to undertake research in the field of actinide synthesis, structural, spectroscopic, magnetic, and computational characterisation.

In addition to the wide range of transferable skills developed during a PhD, the appointed researcher will learn and use: (i) Schlenk and glove box techniques; (ii) characterisation methods, e.g. crystallography, NMR, IR, Raman, UV/Vis/NIR, and EPR spectroscopies, magnetometry, XAS/XANES/RIXS, and quantum chemical calculations; (iii) reactivity studies supported by analytical characterisation and modelling methods.

You will benefit from a joint supervisory team that comprises Prof. Liddle (Manchester, synthesis), Dr Baker (Manchester, XAS/XANES/RIXS), Prof. Jiang (Peking, computational), and Prof. Huang (Peking, synthesis), and also experience the diverse cultures and opportunities that come from living in the two vibrant cities that are Manchester and Beijing.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Sensing Urban Heat: Integrating Bicycle-Based Measurements, Local Climate Modelling and Spatial Optimisation
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. Sound is fundamental to how people sense, interpret and respond to the world. Yet hearing needs vary between individuals because ear-canal geometry, hearing ability and the sounds that are most important for communication vary from person to person. This PhD will develop a new type of 3D-printed metal structure, i.e. the next generation of additively manufactured metallic acoustic metamaterials, that can shape and amplify specific sounds, particularly those important for human communication. The aim is not to build a complete hearing aid but to create a key functional component that could improve future hearing technologies.

The project will establish a human-informed inverse-design framework. Information about ear-canal geometry and speech-relevant sounds will be used as design inputs. Mathematical and computational models will then optimise metallic metamaterial architectures for targeted wave compression and pressure amplification. The resulting structures will be manufactured by additive manufacturing (AM) or 3D printing, enabling compact, geometrically complex metallic components that cannot be produced using conventional methods. Dimensional metrology, materials characterisation and acoustic testing will quantify manufacturing accuracy and functional performance. The measured data will be fed back into the models to understand how AM-induced deviations affect acoustic response and to improve subsequent designs. Artificial-ear models and acoustic sensors will be used to quantify performance and determine how manufacturing deviations affect acoustic responses.

The project brings together expertise from engineering, applied mathematics, acoustics and hearing science. The student will receive training in acoustic-wave modelling, numerical optimisation, metamaterial design, AM, process monitoring, metrology, materials characterisation, acoustic measurement, psychoacoustic experimental design, research ethics and data analysis. The project will operate through an iterative human-input, design, make, measure and perceive cycle, providing the student with an unusually broad and integrated research skill set.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Metal-Organic Framework Materials for Gas Adsorption and Catalysis
jobs.description_html:
There is increasing concern over global air quality, with high concentrations of smog posing significant health risks and environmental problems worldwide. SO2 and NOx are important components in smog causing significant respiratory disease. There is therefore an ever-increasing demand for sorbent materials that can capture SO2 and NOx in order to mitigate emissions. However, this is a very challenging target since SO2 and NO2 are highly corrosive and reactive and most materials are not sufficiently stable. Despite their widespread and successful use in separations of gases such as N2, CO2, CH4 and other small molecules, MOF materials that reversibly bind SO2 and NO2 are extremely rare. Recently, our project team has discovered a number of porous Cu-, Al- and Zn-based MOFs that exhibit unprecedented performance for SO2 and NO2 capture, demonstrating record high SO2 and NO2 selectivity, uptake capacity and storage density. Part of our research results have been recently published (Nature Materials, 2018, 17, 691-696; Nature Materials, 2019, 18, 1358-1366; Nature Chemistry, 2019, 11, 1085-1090; Nature Review Chemistry, 2019, 3, 108-118; Figure 1) and highlighted in CNN News as a breakthrough technology for a clean air. This represents a unique and very timely opportunity to study SO2 and NOx chemistry within MOF materials. The PhD project aims to support the systematic investigation of the adsorption, binding, phase behaviour, electronic structure, release, and separation of gases in a series of stable MOFs with robust framework structures and decorated pore environments. Our extensive experience in handling corrosive gases in MOFs will (i) enable their evaluation as emerging sorbents for adsorptive removal of air pollutants; (ii) afford key insights into the design of new MOFs with improved stability and gas binding properties. The project will provide an excellent training environment for the PhD student at National Facilities Worldwide. Of particular interest will be the capture of SO2 and NOx at low partial pressures using narrow pored, microporous materials, reflecting the relatively low concentration of these gases in flue emissions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (UoM-Peking) Advanced Energy Materials for Bright and Efficient Optoelectronic Devices
jobs.description_html:
How to apply: 

About 20% of the world’s electricity production is used for lighting and powering our displays, which account for 6% of the world’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Organic Light-Emitting Diodes (OLEDs) have a major role as energy-saving technology with applications in displays, solid-state lighting panels, wearable electronics, sensors, and virtual/mixed-reality displays. New advanced materials discoveries are highly required on multiple fronts to increase OLED devices' colour purity, device lifetime, and light output and reduce energy consumption.

The successful candidate will be supervised by Dr Alexander Romanov and Prof. Michael Turner at the University of Manchester (2 years) and Prof Zhiwei Liu at the College of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering Peking University (2 years). The project is part of a comprehensive programme exploring a new family of strongly photo-emissive coinage metal complexes based on carbene-metal-amide (or acetylides) and the doublet state-luminophores based on Ce(III) or Eu(II) complexes. These materials recently demonstrated excellent photoluminescent properties and are capable of producing OLEDs with high efficiency and operating stability (Advanced Materials, 2024, 36, 2306249; Advanced Materials, 2024, 36, 2404357; Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2408118; Adv. Func. Mat., 2025, e05661). The successful applicant will become a part of the established team at the University of Manchester and will work in collaboration with Peking University (Prof Zhiwei Liu). The post will involve substantial collaboration and would suit an ambitious, highly motivated and practical researcher with some experience in synthetic inorganic chemistry and/or organic materials chemistry. There will also be the opportunity to develop complementary skills in the photophysical characterisation and OLED device fabrications, therefore, an additional interest in materials science would be desirable. Applicants should hold a First degree (2:1 or above) in Chemistry.

Manchester entry is open to UK and international students. Chinese nationals from Mainland China, Taiwan, Macau and Hong Kong, including dual nationals, should apply through Peking.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Synthetic Polymers to Stabilise Sensing Proteins into Membrane Nanodiscs
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Membrane proteins are essential components of cells, allowing them to sense and communicate across their outermost barrier. Ion channels translate chemical an physical signals into cellular responses and are consequently major therapeutic targets and candidates for incorporation into synthetic cells. However, studying membrane proteins is challenging because their structure and function depend on the surrounding lipid membrane. Conventional detergent-based extraction can disrupt this native environment, resulting in loss of protein activity or structure.

Amphiphilic polymers can directly excise nanoscale sections of cell membranes to form soluble “nanodiscs”, retaining membrane proteins together with their surrounding lipids. Styrene-maleic acid (SMA) polymers are widely used for this purpose but have significant limitations, including pH and ion sensitivity, low protein extraction efficiency and limited tunability for different transmembrane proteins.

This interdisciplinary PhD project will develop a new generation of chemically defined polymers for extracting and studying membrane proteins in native-like nanodiscs. The central objective is to determine how polymer structure controls membrane insertion, lipid extraction and nanodisc formation, and use these relationships to create materials that outperform conventional SMA polymers. Particular emphasis will be placed on extracting ion channels to understand how cells sense signals across their membranes.

The student will synthesise libraries of amphiphilic polymers in the Gibson group, using automated polymer synthesis to vary composition, hydrophobicity, charge and molecular weight. Polymers will be characterised using NMR spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography and complementary analytical methods, then screened for membrane interaction, lipid extraction and stable nanodisc formation. Resulting structure–activity relationships will guide subsequent polymer design.

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

Before you apply: Please contact the main project supervisor, Dr Christos  Pliotas, to learn more about the project and discuss whether it may be suitable for you.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Sensing Soil Health: Linking Biological Indicators and Human Perceptions
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Healthy soils underpin food production, biodiversity, climate resilience and ecosystem restoration[1]. Yet the biological processes that maintain soil health occur largely out of sight, making them difficult to monitor, interpret and communicate. Soil organisms such as earthworms and microorganisms respond rapidly to environmental change and are widely used as indicators of soil condition[2]. At the same time, gardeners, land managers and communities make decisions based on their own observations and experiences of soil[3]. Emerging environmental sensing technologies offer further opportunities to detect belowground processes that are otherwise hidden. However, little is known about how these different systems of sensing align, what aspects of soil condition they capture, and how they influence environmental decision-making. This project addresses the Sensing the World theme by investigating how biological , technological and human systems sense, interpret and respond to soil condition across urban environments.

Aim. To understand how different biological, technological and human sensing systems detect and interpret soil condition, and how these perspectives can be integrated to improve soil management, stewardship and public engagement.

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship - Geospatial Foundation Modelling to Improve Agricultural Monitoring in Smallholder Farming Systems
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

Satellite remote sensing is revolutionising agricultural monitoring. However, smallholder farms - which produce a third of the world's food - remain challenging to monitor using Earth Observation (EO) because fields are small and irregular, cropping diverse and mixed, cloud cover persistent, and reference data scarce. Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) such as TESSERA and AlphaEarth present opportunities to overcome these challenges. These models reduce labelling requirements and improve transferability of EO-based sensing approaches. However, existing GeoFM benchmarks are skewed towards homogeneous, large-scale farming in Europe and North America, whereas we know little about whether GeoFMs improve mapping of smallholder farms.

Aim and questions

This project will assess if GeoFM embeddings outperform conventional remote sensing features and models for mapping smallholder agriculture. The project will answer four questions:

How robust is current evidence? How reliable are current evidence and benchmarking protocols for GeoFM applications for smallholder agricultural remote sensing?

When and where do GFMs help? Under what conditions do GeoFM embeddings outperform conventional features and models for mapping smallholder agriculture, and do gains vary for different modes of use (e.g. frozen vs fine-tuned embeddings; single- vs multi-modal; annual vs sub-seasonal)?

How effectively do GeoFMs transfer? Do GeoFMs improve EO model transferability across regions, years and farming systems while reducing reference data requirements?

What do GeoFMs embeddings capture? What agronomic information do GeoFM embeddings capture, and does this explain where they succeed or fail to map smallholder agriculture?

This project is expected to start in September 2027.

jobs.description_html:
Criminology sits within the School of Social Sciences, adding complementary interdisciplinarity in legal studies, the Wales Observatory on Human Rights of Children and Young People, the Centre for Social Change, and the collaborative Centre for Criminal Justice and Criminology (CCJC). The CCJC undertakes interdisciplinary empirical research on areas including youth justice policy, drug policies and criminality, policing, sports criminology, sex work, crimes of the powerful, the political economy of crime in the Global South, terrorism and cybercrime. Swansea University also hosts the Administrative Data Research Centre (Wales), which facilitates access to linked, de-identified administrative data in a secure environment. 

The School of Law is located within the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences providing a unique setting within which to conduct empirical or socio-legal research connecting with law the concerns and methods of social science. Swansea’s School of Law has an active and vibrant research culture including: CCJC; Cyber Threats Research Centre (CYTREC); Institute of International Shipping and Trade Law (IISTL); Observatory on Human Rights and Social Justice; and the Centre for Governance and Human Rights. Previously the School has supported studentships across a wide range of sub-disciplines, including: public and constitutional law; legal education; human rights; disability law; asylum law; tort law; environmental law; European Union law and governance; family law; perceptions of risk in third sector sporting clubs; banking and environmental risk; comparative Welsh/English housing law/policy; and constitutional perspectives on Welsh Devolution. 

Students will predominately be based at Swansea University, although will be invited to attend WGSSS events at other locations in Wales. Throughout the PhD, all WGSSS students come together for joint workshops, residential courses, and annual conferences. Seminars include those organised by the Welsh Centre for Crime and Social Justice Conference (held at Gregynog, Powys) each year, who also hold residential postgraduate training days. jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Process Industries: Net Zero CDT: Energy and Resource Recovery from Spent Filters
jobs.description_html:
Overview

This PhD project is part of the EPSRC Process Industries: Net Zero (PINZ) Centre for Doctoral Training and is supported by PPT Filtercycle Ltd. The project aims to develop circular approaches to maximise the energy and resource value of spent filters, reduce material disposal, and minimise the environmental footprint of filtration processes. Its approach is to develop methodologies which can be usefully and quickly converted from pilot scale to operational for SME sites who otherwise may utilise broad waste management streams. This approach will consider bespoke solutions maximising the opportunity for reuse and recycle.

The project will consider the fuel capacity of combustible spent filters as a source of energy to safely separate other filter components for reuse. This will involve characterising different waste filter materials, investigating their composition, thermal properties and energy potential. Combustion behaviour, process safety and operational risks will be investigated to establish whether different filter materials can be safely incinerated, considering emissions and residue formation.

This primary investigation will facilitate the opportunity to investigate and develop the reuse and repurposing of spent filters to extend their useful life and reduce reliance on landfill for un-separated filter composite plus residue. All methodologies will be considered including cleaning and regeneration approaches.

The project will also investigate the recovery and utilisation of valuable inorganic components, particularly calcium-rich compounds, from filtration residues. These residues will be explored as potential feedstocks for CO2 capture through mineral carbonation. This will involve investigating material composition, recovery, carbonation kinetics, CO2 uptake, and the application of resulting carbonated products.

By transforming spent filters into energy and valuable materials, this project could help make industrial filtration more sustainable. The project will appeal to applicants in chemistry, chemical engineering, or materials science who are passionate to address real-world sustainability challenges.

Start Date

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: High-Performance Lanthanide Single-Molecule Magnets with Monodentate Ligands
jobs.description_html:
Application deadline: 18/12/2026
Research theme: Synthetic molecular inorganic chemistry

This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded by the School of Natural Sciences; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is October 2027.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

A University of Manchester-sponsored PhD studentship is available for an outstanding and ambitious chemist to undertake research in the field of synthetic inorganic chemistry in a collaborative project at Manchester Chemistry.

In this project we target molecular lanthanide single-molecule magnets (Ln SMMs). Recently at Manchester we have developed synthetic methodologies to prepare near-linear dysprosium SMMs bound by either one or two monodentate ligands (e.g. Nature 2025, 643, 125. DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09138-0; Nature Commun. 2026, 17, 10212. DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-77104-z). These compounds show the highest effective energy barriers to magnetic reversal and magnetic hysteresis temperatures of any SMM reported to date, with magnetic memory effects shown up to 100 Kelvin. Here we propose to extend this work by targeting dysprosium compounds with geometries closer to linearity and shorter metal-ligand distances, which are expected to show improved SMM properties.

The successful candidate, based in the laboratory of Prof. David Mills and co-supervised by Dr Michael Baker, will synthesise and fully characterise a novel, exciting series of highly air- and moisture-sensitive Ln compounds, and will deposit them on surfaces using a spin-coater. These compounds will be studied by a wide variety of techniques including single crystal and powder XRD, SQUID magnetometry, X-ray magnetocircular dichroism, and infrared, UV-visible absorption/emission, nuclear magnetic resonance, electron paramagnetic resonance and X-ray absorption spectroscopy, benchmarked by density functional theory and ab initio calculations. We will determine the relaxation times of Ln SMMs in different matrices as the necessary first step towards their application in devices.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in a relevant science or engineering related discipline.

To apply, please contact the main supervisor, Prof. David Mills. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Soft Robotics and Embodied Intelligence
jobs.department: Biomedical Science and Biomedical Engineering, School of Biological Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Project title: Emergence of embodied intelligence through bioelectrical learning in soft brain-body

Supervisors: Dr Yoshikatsu Hayashi (principal supervisor)

Project Overview

How can intelligence emerge when a brain and body interact, rather than being designed separately?

A new Leverhulme Trust-funded project at the University of Reading, led by Dr Yoshikatsu Hayashi, will explore how intelligence could emerge from interactions between soft materials, a robotic body and its environment.

In living organisms, the brain and body develop together through continuous sensory feedback, a principle known as embodiment. Neural communication fundamentally relies on the movement of charged particles called ions. Interestingly, ions also flow through water-rich hydrogels, where polymer networks can guide their movement. Could this provide a primitive form of electrical communication without neurons?

Previous research demonstrated that electroactive gels could improve their performance in the computer game Pong through feedback, suggesting that materials can exhibit adaptive behaviour without living neurons (https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-02704-y). Building on this discovery, the project will connect hydrogel networks to a soft robotic body, investigating whether ionic communication, rhythmic movement and sensory feedback can collectively generate adaptive behaviour.

By exploring how brain-like control and bodily movement might emerge together from physical matter, the research aims to uncover fundamental principles of Physical AI and inspire future generations of intelligent soft robots.

Training and development

You will develop skills in hydrogel fabrication, bioelectrical measurements, soft robotics, AI and feedback control, experimental design and data analysis. Working across materials science and biomedical engineering, you will gain experience connecting physical experiments with AI (Artificial Neural Networks) platform. You will benefit from the University’s bioengineering and movement laboratory facilities and the Reading Researcher Development Programme for doctoral and transferable skills training. The project will also provide opportunities to exchange ideas with international collaborators and develop scientific communication skills through presentations and outreach. 

Eligibility

  • Applicants should hold, or expect to gain, at least a UK 2:1 honours degree (or equivalent) in physical chemistry, robotics, mechanical/electronic engineering, physics, or a closely related discipline.
  • Interest in soft matter and soft robotics, control systems and interdisciplinary research is essential. Programming, experimental design/methods and data analysis experience are desirable.
  • Due to the nature of the funding this studentship is open candidates who qualify for Home/UK/Republic of Ireland fees.

Funding Details

  • Three-year award which covers Home fees and includes a maintenance stipend of £22,905 per year.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: 3.5 Year PhD Studentship in Artificial Intelligence for Eliciting Patient Histories
jobs.description_html:
A 3.5 year PhD studentship in Artificial Intelligence for Eliciting Patient Histories, funded by the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) UCLH Biomedical Research Centre, is available within the Institute of Health Informatics. The studentship will commence from 1 February 2027 under the supervisor of Professor Paul Taylor.

The PhD Project

Project Title: AI for Eliciting Patient Histories

The aim of this project is to understand how AI tools can be integrated into patient consultations to improve the quality of interaction between clinicians and patients. The consultation is the defining event in almost all episodes of care and remains one of the most important encounters in medical practice.

In recent years, consultations have begun to be transformed by the adoption of two distinct forms of technology. The first, AI scribes, aims to make consultations more patient-centred by automating administrative tasks. These tools record consultation audio, transcribe conversations, and generate summaries for clinicians to review before adding information to the patient record. The second technology, conversational agents or chatbots, provides a low-cost alternative to aspects of clinical consultations by eliciting information directly from patients.

The successful candidate will identify insights and frameworks from the literature on conventional clinical encounters, history-taking, and shared decision-making that are most relevant to the design of conversational agents.

The project will also develop and test AI-based approaches for analysing and assessing transcribed consultations. This work will provide an additional source of evidence on the characteristics of consultations and will enable testing of insights from the literature and exploration of more refined hypotheses, including the impact of factors such as age and gender.

Why Apply?

This PhD offers a unique collaboration between an AI start-up delivering cutting-edge technology, experienced AI researchers working in healthcare, and practising clinicians responsible for teaching communication skills to future doctors.

Applicants will be expected to contribute to teaching within the Institute of Health Informatics. The commitment is equivalent to approximately six months of teaching across the duration of the PhD.

This studentship provides an excellent opportunity to undertake supervised research at a world-leading institute, contribute to the development of AI technologies that enhance patient-centred care, and become part of a vibrant research community.

This award includes a starting stipend of £28,212 per annum and covers tuition fees at the UK (Home) rate. 

Personal Specification

Applicants should hold, or expect to obtain, an upper second-class Bachelor’s degree and a Master’s degree (or equivalent work experience) in a relevant discipline or possess an overseas qualification of an equivalent standard.

Eligibility

jobs.title: FSE PhD President's Doctoral Scholarship: Sensing Below, Cooling Above: Harnessing Urban Aquifers for Climate-resilient Geothermal Cooling (Sub-cool)
jobs.department: Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
This 4-year PhD studentship is open to both Home (UK) and international applicants. The successful candidate will receive an annual stipend at the UKRI minimum rate (currently £21,805 per year) plus £1,000/annum enhancement, and a research training support grant of up to £20,000 for the full 4-year programme. This project is in competition for funding with other projects. Usually, the projects that receives the best applicants will be successful.

“Sub-cool” brings together expertise in hydrogeology, climate change, and social sciences to explore how aquifers beneath urban areas can become reliable and sustainable cooling resources. This work is timely as successive European heatwaves have pushed cooling to the frontline of climate adaptation and exposed growing heath consequences, with approximately 2,877 [gov.uk] heat-related deaths in the UK, reinforcing the need for low-carbon cooling to ensure resilient to future climate conditions.

Nevertheless, how aquifer thermal and hydrological conditions will evolve under intensified climate change is uncertain. In the UK, warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers may alter groundwater levels, flow and heat transport. This may lead to very different thermal footprints despite the same cooling demand, while also affecting groundwater and connected surface-water quality and supply. Past technology rollouts [nature.com] show the necessity to understand how the public weigh cooling benefits against perceived risks, costs and environmental trade-offs, making the integration of these perspectives with hydrogeological modelling essential for informing climate-resilient system deployment.

“Sub-cool” therefore asks, if changing aquifer conditions, cooling needs and public perceptions jointly shape where, and how climate-resilient urban aquifer cooling can be deployed, via the following research questions (RQ):

RQ1: How do aquifer cooling opportunities align with place-based cooling needs, and how do residents and professionals understand their benefits, risks and trade-offs? Walking interviews could provide a valuable approach to connect lived experiences of overheating and cooling access with perceptions of the subsurface resource in a selected European case alongside GM. These findings would inform the spatial priorities, scenarios and constraints examined in RQ2.

RQ2: How might climate change alter aquifer cooling capacity and capability? GM will provide the base case, supported by existing geological and borehole datasets, groundwater monitoring and UK climate projections. [metoffice.gov.uk] The comparative site selected through the work in RQ1 will be incorporated into geo-referenced GIS-based groundwater-flow and heat-transport modelling to examine how hydrogeology, climate and existing use shape spatial patterns of cooling capacity and thermal response. Modelled opportunities will then be assessed against the findings from RQ1 to shape the deployment is technically suitable, and socially and environmentally appropriate.

Before you apply: Please contact the main project supervisor, Prof Hollis, to learn more about the project and discuss whether it may be suitable for you.

To be considered for this project you must submit a formal application through our online application portal by following the instructions provided here. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B10 A Multi-Scale Quantitative Investigation of Micro- and Nanoplastic Disruptions in Algal Physiology, Trophic Dynamics, and Carbon Sequestration
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Plastic pollution has introduced vast quantities of micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) into aquatic ecosystems, raising urgent questions about their impacts on biodiversity and global biogeochemical cycles. Among the most critical but poorly understood aspects is how MNPs interact with plankton communities, which form the foundation of food webs and drive the oceans biological carbon pump-a key regulator of atmospheric CO₂.

Emerging studies show that MNPs can impair nutrient uptake, photosynthesis, and growth in algae, while also reshaping community composition by favouring opportunistic species. These changes cascade through ecosystems: plastics can alter carbon export by binding with algal cells into fast-sinking aggregates or, conversely, reducing sinking when attached to buoyant particles. Moreover, predators often ingest MNPs indirectly through contaminated prey, with transfer efficiencies up to an order of magnitude higher than direct uptake. Yet despite these findings, our understanding of how MNPs affect plankton-driven processes and carbon cycling remains fragmented, with few quantitative datasets under realistic ecological conditions.

This PhD project will bridge that gap by combining field surveys, laboratory experiments, and advanced analytical tools. Water and plankton samples from UK coastal waters will be analysed to quantify MNP types, sizes, and concentrations, correlated with plankton community metrics. Using innovative labelling and state-of-the-art techniques, the student will investigate species-specific uptake across representative algae, linking particle properties to cellular physiology and nutrient assimilation. Controlled feeding experiments will trace trophic transfer into zooplankton and higher consumers, generating quantitative coefficients for ecological risk models. Finally, the project will integrate these data into a predictive framework to assess how MNPs disrupt plankton community dynamics and the efficiency of the biological carbon pump.

The research will provide fundamental insights into the ecological and climate implications of plastic pollution, with outcomes directly relevant to environmental agencies, fisheries managers, and international policy. Training will be highly interdisciplinary, spanning environmental nanoscience, plankton ecology, analytical chemistry, and ecological modelling, equipping the student with cutting-edge skills and an outstanding platform for career development in environmental science.

For further information on this project and details of how to apply to it please visit https://centa.ac.uk/studentship/2027-b10-a-multi-scale-quantitative-investigation-of-micro-and-nanoplastic-disruptions-in-algal-physiology-trophic-dynamics-and-carbon-sequestration/

Further information on how to apply for a CENTA studentship can be found on the CENTA website: https://centa.ac.uk/apply/

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Light at the Atomic Scale: A PhD in Single-Molecule Nanophotonics
jobs.description_html:
We are looking for a PhD student to work in the area of nanophotonics and plasmonics. In this experimental project, metallic nanocavities, metasurfaces and/or 2D materials will be used to confine light and enhance light-matter coupling at the nanoscale, with the aim of detecting mid-infrared (MIR) signatures of single molecules [1-5]. The project is part of a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship.

Detecting MIR light, where molecular vibrations act as chemical fingerprints, normally requires cooled detectors to suppress thermal noise. We take a different route: molecular frequency upconversion. Molecules placed in a nanocavity that confines both MIR and visible light absorb MIR photons through their vibrations and emit visible photons, which can be detected with single-photon sensitivity at room temperature [1,4]. This allows both the detection and the spectroscopy of individual molecules, with wide applications in sensing, chemical analysis and biological imaging.

The applicant should have completed (or be close to completing) an undergraduate degree in Physics, Materials Science, Physical Chemistry or a related physical science, preferably with first-class honours or equivalent. Strong analytical and experimental skills are desired. Details of the project will be agreed with the successful candidate to tailor the research to their interests.

The student will work on understanding how MIR and visible light are simultaneously confined in nanometre-scale gaps, and how this dual confinement controls the efficiency of upconversion and detection. They will build and develop optical microscopy and spectroscopy setups to probe these nanocavities, spanning the visible to the mid-infrared, and will study how the response changes as a function of temperature. This will give insight into the role of molecular vibrations, thermal population and noise in the detection process. The work also involves fabricating and self-assembling plasmonic nanocavities, and exploring chiral and other tailored nanostructures [3].

The project will take place in the research group of Dr Rohit Chikkaraddy (https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/staff/profiles/physics/chikkaraddy-rohit.aspx), which is part of the Metamaterials and Nanophotonics Research Centre (https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/research/activity/physics/quantum/metamaterials/index.aspx) in the School of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, UK. The thesis is strongly multidisciplinary, and candidates from physics, materials science and chemistry are welcome. You will join an active, international research group and will be supported in developing a personal vision and an autonomous scientific profile, as well as industrial links and scientific collaborations.

The University actively supports equality, diversity and inclusion and encourages applicants from all sections of society. In line with the Department’s Athena SWAN programme, we particularly encourage female candidates to apply.

Funding: Funding is available for UK nationals. For details of the funding, advice on making your application or any other informal enquiries, please contact Dr Rohit Chikkaraddy at r.chikkaraddy@bham.ac.uk.

You can apply by clicking the 'Apply' button above, clearly stating the title of the project, the name of the supervisor (Dr Rohit Chikkaraddy) and the Metamaterials and Nanophotonics Research Centre.

References

[1] Chikkaraddy, et al. “Single-molecule mid-infrared spectroscopy and detection through vibrationally assisted luminescence”, Nature Photonics, 17, 865 (2023).
[2] Chikkaraddy. “Single molecule ready to couple”, Nature Physics, 20, 694 (2024).
[3] Hou et al. “Extreme optical chirality from plasmonic nanocrystals on a mirror”, Nano Letters, 25, 1158 (2025).
[4] Xomalis et al. “Detecting mid-infrared light by molecular frequency upconversion in dual-wavelength nanoantennas”, Science, 374, 1268 (2021).
[5] Chikkaraddy et al. “Single-molecule strong coupling at room temperature in plasmonic nanocavities”, Nature, 535, 127 (2016).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Non-equilibrium quantum many-body dynamics
jobs.description_html:
Macroscopic matter is composed of a huge number of quantum particles whose dynamics are typically dominated by interactions. In spite of this immense complexity, when a macroscopic object is in (or close to) an equilibrium state its gross properties are efficiently described by a rather simple set of macroscopic equations: the glorious laws of thermodynamics. One of the greatest challenges of theoretical physics is to devise a quantitative description of matter when, instead, it is far from any equilibrium state.

This project aims to study the out-of-equilibrium regime of quantum matter, which has become accessible experimentally only about twenty years ago, and is now used to realise the first noisy quantum computers. In particular, the main goals are to understand: (i) the non-equilibrium dynamics of interacting quantum matter; (ii) how thermodynamics emerges from it. The project will involve analytical and numerical approaches. The PhD work will involve techniques from quantum many-body physics, quantum information, quantum integrability, and quantum many-body chaos.

The project will be supervised by Dr Bruno Bertini.

Funding notes:

The project is directly funded by a research grant.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Predicting Attention and Action in the Developing Brain with Wearable Neuroimaging and Modelling
jobs.description_html:
Why can we respond quickly and accurately one moment, then hesitate or make an impulsive mistake the next? Attention and action fluctuate even when a task stays the same. These fluctuations matter for learning and everyday behaviour, yet response times alone cannot reveal whether their source lies in visual attention, readiness to act, or interactions between brain systems.

This project asks how the developing brain turns sensory information into reliable action. Which brain signals predict a response before it happens? Do visual attention and motor preparation make distinct or shared contributions? How does their balance change from childhood to adolescence?

You will combine wearable magnetoencephalography using optically pumped magnetometers (OPM-MEG) with visual frequency tagging. Children and adolescents aged 8-16 and adults aged 18-30 will complete a task requiring frequent button presses and occasional withholding of responses. Central and peripheral stimuli will flicker continuously at different frequencies, allowing pre-cue visual responses to be tracked alongside motor beta rhythms. Adult and child pilots will establish reliable measurements, supported by eye tracking and attention and movement localisers.

Using multilevel statistical models, you will test competing accounts of behavioural variability, quantify the unique and shared contributions of visual and motor signals to response times and errors, and ask how these change with age. Models will be tested on held-out data, including unseen participants. Working directly with children and adults, you will gain skills in neuroimaging, scientific programming and quantitative analysis. Few laboratories can record OPM-MEG in children.

Following validation, the framework could extend to neurodiverse populations, including people with ADHD, to investigate how variation in these brain mechanisms shapes attention and action.

The project will be supervised by Dr Kyungmin An and Dr Carmel Mevorach.

Before applying for the studentship, please email me (k.m.an@bham.ac.uk) with your CV, academic transcript, and a published research paper.

Funding notes:

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Mechanistic Modelling of Biofilm-Induced Host-Cell Damage
jobs.description_html:
Biofilm-associated infections can cause persistent damage to surrounding tissues, but the mechanisms linking biofilm development to host-cell injury remain poorly quantified. Biofilm growth, nutrient availability, bacterial toxins, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signalling evolve together and may contribute differently to DNA damage, repair failure, and cell death. Experiments can measure many of these responses, but they cannot easily determine which mechanisms are dominant or how they interact across space and time. This project will therefore develop a mechanistic mathematical framework that integrates experimental observations, identifies the processes driving host-cell damage, and quantifies the uncertainty in those conclusions.

The PhD will pursue four integrated aims:

1. Mechanistic modelling: develop a mathematical model linking biofilm growth and structure with nutrient transport, bacterial toxins, reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signalling, DNA damage, repair and host-cell viability.
2. Computational simulation: develop efficient numerical methods to simulate how these interacting processes evolve across space and time, including changing biofilm structure and local biochemical gradients.
3. Parameter inference and mechanism identification: use experimental data to estimate hidden biological parameters, quantify uncertainty, and determine which mechanisms are supported by the observations.
4. Prediction and experimental guidance: use the calibrated model to identify informative measurements and sampling conditions, distinguish competing damage pathways, and predict responses to selected therapeutic interventions. These predictions will be tested using independent experiments.

The project will deliver an experimentally validated framework for explaining how biofilms generate host-cell injury and for identifying which biological mechanisms should be targeted to reduce damage while maintaining effective bacterial control.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: : High-Fidelity Electromagnetic-Thermal Modelling of Litz Windings for Next-Generation Cryogenic Machines
jobs.description_html:
This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is flexible but we are looking for someone to start as soon as possible.

Transport electrification is central to energy security and net zero. Electrical machines lie at its heart, providing propulsion across road, rail and maritime transport. In mass- and volume-constrained applications such as aerospace, these machines must become substantially more power-dense and efficient, a leap that calls for innovative technologies rather than incremental refinement.

Cryogenically cooled machines offer one of the most promising routes. At extremely low temperatures (around 20 K), the electrical resistance of high-purity aluminium and copper falls by up to a hundredfold, allowing windings to carry far higher currents with drastically reduced DC losses. Built from readily available materials, these “hyperconducting” windings offer a practical path to step-change performance.

However, this benefit comes at a cost. The same reduction in resistance strongly amplifies induced eddy currents, making AC losses a major concern. Litz windings, with thousands of fine, 3D-transposed strands, can mitigate these losses, but at cryogenic temperatures the losses become highly sensitive to temperature. Conductor resistance can change several-fold over a few tens of kelvin, while low heat capacity means even small losses cause significant temperature rises. Losses and temperature are therefore tightly coupled, making accurate loss prediction and assessment of thermal stability both critical and highly challenging.

This PhD project will tackle this challenge by developing high-fidelity, computationally efficient electromagnetic–thermal models of Litz windings at cryogenic temperatures, and using them to derive design guidelines for next-generation power-dense cryogenic machines with ultra-high-efficiencies.

You will:

  • extend established in-house analytical electromagnetic models to practical Litz windings, using reduced-order and data-driven AI methods for rapid, accurate loss prediction, verified against finite element simulations;
  • integrate these models with an existing thermal solver into a two-way coupled electromagnetic–thermal framework;
  • validate the framework through simulation and experiments on Litz winding samples, using an existing cryogenic test facility;
  • use the validated framework to understand the coupled behaviour, identify key design factors and optimise winding designs.

You will join the Energy Conversion group in the Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, with weekly supervision from a team with complementary electromagnetic and thermal expertise. You will have access to established models, dedicated simulation software and cryogenic test facilities, so you will build on a solid foundation rather than starting from scratch. Training will cover electrical machine fundamentals, analytical and finite element modelling, data-driven methods, programming and cryogenic testing, alongside the University’s doctoral skills training.

This project suits a motivated candidate with a background in electrical, electronic or mechanical engineering, physics or a related discipline, who enjoys combining theory, simulation and experiments. Experience in electrical machine design, electromagnetic fields, finite element analysis, thermal management or programming (e.g. MATLAB, Python) is desirable but not essential.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in a relevant science or engineering related discipline.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Reductive Dearomatisation through New-to-Nature Biocatalysis
jobs.description_html:
Application deadline: 28/02/2027
Research theme: Biocatalysis and enzyme engineering

This 4-year PhD project is fully funded by the School of Natural Sciences; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is October 2027.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

The Buller group have co-pioneered the development of a new cofactor that substitutes the central iron atom on haem for cobalt, CoPPIX.1,2 Recently, we have reported that this new cofactor can perform enantioselective metal-hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) catalysis, a reaction of superb synthetic utility in organic synthesis.

We are working to expand the scope of transformations possible via MHAT. For this project, we will focus on a new mode of reductive dearomatization discovered originally on highly electron-deficient anisoles.3 The project will use directed evolution to increase activity on increasingly inert substrates, with the ambitious goal of achieving activity on mono-substituted benzenes and substituted heteroaromatic systems. Success will yield both a new suite of catalysts for MHAT transformations and access to chemical building blocks for use in materials and medicinal chemistry research. Engineered enzymes themselves serve as tools to study how mutations can tune CoPPIX reactivity. This project may use AI tools to model sequence-activity relationships and offers comprehensive training in laboratory enzyme engineering research.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in a relevant science or engineering related discipline.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B09 Greener MOF Nanogels for Water Remediation and Critical Mineral Recovery
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Persistent organic pollutants, toxic metals and dyes threaten water quality, while discarded products and industrial residues contain valuable critical minerals. Sorbents can lose performance or release their own components as water chemistry changes. This project will develop greener metal–organic framework (MOF) nanogels and determine how their transformations govern remediation, resource recovery and environmental safety.

MOFs are porous solids with tunable binding sites. We will test whether confinement within hydrated biopolymer networks limits framework release while preserving accessible binding sites. You will prepare a small set of formulations using aqueous or reduced-solvent routes, then examine capture under different pH, dissolved organic matter and competing-ion conditions. Screening will cover persistent PFAS, represented by PFOA/PFOS, heavy metals and dyes. Detailed studies will focus on the most promising combinations. A separate pathway will test recovery of rare-earth elements, including neodymium and dysprosium, from secondary aqueous resources.

Building on our MOF remediation and transformation research, the project will connect structural and chemical changes to performance throughout synthesis, gelation, capture, regeneration and end-of-life ageing. Metal and linker release measurements, combined with pollutant mass balances, will identify potential secondary contamination. Mineral recovery will be assessed through desorption yield and product purity.

Safe and sustainable by design (SSbD) will guide material selection. You will compare treatment performance, aquatic effects, chemical and energy inputs, waste generation and reuse against relevant commercial sorbents. The outcome will be experimentally supported design rules for water treatment and resource recovery, identifying conditions that preserve useful performance while limiting environmental harm.

For further information on this project and details of how to apply to it please visit centa.ac.uk/studentship/2027-b09-greener-mof-nanogels-for-water-remediation-and-critical-mineral-recovery

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Studying the Langlands Program via Formalisation and AI
jobs.department: School of Engineering, Mathematics and Physics
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr Christopher Birkbeck

This fully funded PhD project, based at our Norwich campus, offers an opportunity to work at the intersection of number theory, artificial intelligence and formal mathematics. You will investigate how AI can help us formalise and deepen our understanding of the Langlands program, with the aim of producing new mathematical insights, proving new results and strengthening existing ones. 

A concrete starting point will be the local Langlands correspondence for GL2(F) where F is a non-Archimedean local field. This correspondence provides a deep bridge between harmonic analysis and number theory, relating irreducible admissible representations of GL2(F) to two-dimensional Weil–Deligne representations. Using AI tools alongside the Lean 4 proof assistant, you will work towards formalising this correspondence, developing computer-verified definitions and theorems on both sides and progressing towards its construction and proof. 

You will have access to leading AI tools to support both formalisation and mathematical exploration. You will investigate how these tools can help you understand difficult arguments, work through examples, formulate conjectures, explore proof strategies and develop formally verified proofs. A central theme will be the interaction between mathematical understanding and formalisation: using the process of making definitions and arguments precise to clarify existing mathematics and motivate new research questions. 

The project is not limited to verifying known results. Alongside the formalisation effort, you will use AI to explore questions within the wider Langlands programme, seeking opportunities to establish new theorems and insights, extend or sharpen existing results, and find simpler or more conceptual proofs. These investigations will develop together with the formal work, with insights from each helping to guide the other. 

The ambition is to produce both reusable, computer-verified mathematics and original contributions to number theory, while developing effective ways to combine AI-assisted exploration with rigorous mathematical proof.

Entry requirements: The minimum entry requirement is 2:1 in Mathematics.

Mode of study: Full-Time

Start date: 1 October 2027

Additional funding information

This four-year funded studentship, starting in October 2027, comprises tuition fees at Home fee rate, an annual tax-free stipend at the UEA rate (£20,409 in 2026/27, subject to any agreed inflationary uplift for 2027/28), and a Research Training Support Grant of £3,000 per annum. It is open to applicants eligible for Home fee status.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: CENTA 2027-B08 Less Emission, more Aerosol How Elevated CO2 Changes Organic Gas Emissions from Forests and their Capacity to Form Particles
jobs.department: School of Geography, Earth and Environmental Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Forests emit large amounts of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). In the atmosphere these are oxidised to form large, oxygenated gases which then form secondary organic aerosol (SOA): tiny particles that scatter sunlight and form cloud droplets. The effect of aerosol on clouds is the largest single source of uncertainty in how much humans have changed the climate. Forest emissions therefore feed back on climate, but we do not know how this feedback will change as atmospheric CO2 rises.

Trees respond to high CO2 by changing both how much they emit and what they emit. Isoprene is the most abundant VOC emitted by plants, and its emission from many species, including oak, falls under elevated CO₂, while monoterpene and sesquiterpene responses are more variable. These compounds differ enormously in how well they make particles. Isoprene makes little SOA itself, and it actively suppresses particle formation from monoterpenes by interfering with the chemistry that builds oxygenated gases. A forest that emits less isoprene but similar or more monoterpene could therefore make more aerosol, even though its total emissions have fallen (Figure 1).

This project will test that idea in a real forest. The Birmingham Institute of Forest Research (BIFoR) FACE facility has exposed a mature oak woodland to CO2 150 ppm above ambient since 2017, alongside control plots at current CO2. It is one of very few places in the world where the emissions of a future forest can be measured directly.

The doctoral researcher (DR) will measure the VOC mixtures emitted under current and elevated CO₂, recreate those mixtures in the laboratory to measure how much aerosol they form, and use a chemical box model to work out which compounds cause any difference. Part of the laboratory work will take place at the University of Eastern Finland (UEF) with Dr Angela Buchholz, within the ACE-Forest Centre of Excellence, a leading group in aerosol formation from real plant emissions.

The outcome will be the first direct, mechanistic estimate of how CO2 fertilisation changes the aerosol-forming potential of a mature temperate forest, something climate models currently have to assume.

For further information on this project and details of how to apply to it please visit centa.ac.uk/studentship/2027-b08-less-emission-more-aerosol-how-elevated-co2-changes-organic-gas-emissions-from-forests-and-their-capacity-to-form-particles

jobs.title: PhD Studentship (MRC NW-DMS) - Antibiotic Use in Hidradenitis Suppurativa
jobs.department: Division of Musculoskeletal and Dermatological Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Hidradenitis suppurativa, one of dermatology’s most painful conditions, affects around one in 130 UK residents, causing recurrent boils, abscesses and scarring in the armpits, groin and under the breasts. Oral antibiotics are a mainstay of treatment, often taken for months or years, but their impact on future antibiotic effectiveness is unknown.

This PhD will answer that question using electronic health records. You will work with the Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum, linked to hospital admission and mortality data. You will: map how antibiotics are prescribed for hidradenitis suppurativa across the UK and how this has changed; use machine learning to uncover distinct patterns of treatment over time and test whether they predict disease flares; and estimate whether prolonged antibiotic exposure is followed by antibiotic treatment failure when patients are later treated for chest or urine infections.

You will be trained in epidemiological study design, causal inference, survival analysis, machine learning and statistical programming, and in the governance of large health datasets. Supervision spans dermatology, pharmacoepidemiology and health informatics. You will join the Dermatology and Pharmaco-epidemiology Research Group in Manchester, within a dermatology centre that is a standalone theme of the NIHR Manchester Biomedical Research Centre. You will be supported to work with patients in shaping research.

Antimicrobial resistance is a national priority, yet dermatology evidence is scarce. Findings aim to inform clinical guidelines and stewardship policy, with all analysis code shared openly.

Entry Requirements

Competition for studentships is expected to be very high.

Applicants are expected to hold (or be about to obtain) a minimum upper second-class undergraduate honours degree (or equivalent) in medicine, pharmacy, epidemiology, public health, statistics, data science, health informatics or a related quantitative discipline. A relevant Masters degree is desirable. Research experience in health data analysis, and familiarity with a statistical programming language (R, Stata or Python), are desirable.

Successful applicants may also have:

  • A master's qualification.
  • Relevant research experience.
  • Experience demonstrating suitability for doctoral research.

Applicants who are offered a place must meet the University's English language requirements before commencing studies. Further information can accessed here: English language requirements | International | The University of Manchester

Application Guidance

Candidates must contact the primary supervisor before applying to discuss their interest and assess suitability.

Apply directly here: MRC North West Doctoral Programme in Medical Sciences | Biology, Medicine and Health | The University of Manchester or on the online application portal, select MRC NW-DMS PhD Programme as the programme of study.

You can apply for up to two projects within this scheme and you must submit a separate application for each, including a supporting statement tailored to the specific project.

Please ensure that your application includes:

  • Curriculum Vitae (CV)
  • Supporting Statement
  • Academic Certificates and Transcripts

Applicants must provide two references. References can be submitted shortly after the application deadline, but please provide them as soon as possible to avoid delays.

Incomplete or late applications will not be considered.
