jobs.title: 2 PhD Positions in Business Administration, Entrepreneurship
jobs.description_html:
Lund University was founded in 1666 and is repeatedly ranked among the world's top 100 universities. The University has around 46 000 students and 8 500 staff based in Lund, Helsingborg and Malmö. We are united in our efforts to understand, explain and improve our world and the human condition. 

Lund University School of Economics and Management is one of eight faculties within Lund University. More than 4 000 students and 450 researchers, teachers and other staff are engaged here in training and research in business administration, economic history, business law, informatics, economics, statistics and research policy. 

The doctoral thesis projects will be conducted under the auspices of the Sten K. Johnson Centre for Entrepreneurship. The Centre (SKJCE) is an active, internationally recognized arena for high-impact entrepreneurship education and research. SKJCE conducts research in areas such as entrepreneurial learning and education, academic entrepreneurship, entrepreneurial ownership and finance, social entrepreneurship and immigrant entrepreneurship. 

We announce two four-year, full-time PhD candidate positions in entrepreneurship at the Department of Business Administration, Lund University School of Economics and Management, Lund. The PhD students will receive a scholarship for the first year and be employed at the department the remaining three years. 

The PhD students will start in spring 2027, date to be agreed. 

Subject area 

We are looking for two PhD students in Entrepreneurship. Both positions are anchored in entrepreneurship research, and each is connected to one of the two projects described below. 

The first position is connected to the project “AI and entrepreneurial learning”. In this project, we take a particular interest in how entrepreneurs’ use of generative AI shapes the ways they learn from experience as they develop their ventures. Research on entrepreneurial learning has largely treated the transformation of experience into knowledge as a process taking place within the entrepreneur, who reflects, interprets feedback and decides how to act. Generative AI unsettles this assumption, as parts of reflection and sense-making are increasingly performed together with, or delegated to, a machine. This may broaden and accelerate learning, but it may also substitute speed for understanding. The project builds on and seeks to extend research on entrepreneurial learning and cognition, and aims to identify the mechanisms through which AI enables, constrains or reshapes how entrepreneurs transform experience into knowledge. Questions relevant to the project include, for example: How does AI change the ways entrepreneurs reflect on and make sense of their experiences? Under what conditions does acting on AI-generated input and feedback deepen entrepreneurs’ understanding, and when does it merely speed up action? What tensions arise when parts of the learning process are delegated to AI, and how do they challenge established theories of entrepreneurial learning? 

The second position is connected to the project “Under the radar: AI-driven ventures and the changing organisation of innovation in the life sciences”. In this project, we take a particular interest in AI-driven ventures in the life sciences that emerge and develop largely out of public view before they challenge much larger established firms. Such ventures are more than a technical or commercial phenomenon. They raise questions about how entrepreneurs pursue opportunities in knowledge-intensive and highly regulated settings, what established firms can and cannot see, and where new knowledge is created and who controls it. The project builds on and seeks to extend research on new venture emergence, science- and technology-based entrepreneurship, and the dynamics between new ventures and incumbents. Questions relevant to the project include, for example: How do AI-driven ventures in the life sciences emerge, organise and build legitimacy before they become visible to established actors? How do established life-science firms detect, interpret and respond to them? How does AI change where new knowledge is created and who holds it, and what does this imply for entrepreneurial opportunities: are they genuinely novel or mainly faster variations of what already exists? How do regulation and ethical concerns shape which AI-driven ventures and innovations reach patients? 

We welcome candidates with an interest in the questions outlined above. Applicants are encouraged to develop their own research questions, theoretical perspectives and methods within these broader themes. The PhD projects can be pursued using qualitative, quantitative or mixed-methods designs. The positions are connected to ongoing research at the Department and the PhD students will be embedded in a network of researchers in Sweden and abroad. 

Work duties  

Regulations concerning appointment as a PhD student can be found in the Higher Education Ordinance Chapter 5, 1–7 §§ and SFS 1998:80. For appointment to the position, you are required to be eligible for admission to the PhD (PhD) programme in Business Administration.

The PhD programme in Business Administration at Lund University is a four-year programme consisting of two parts: a course package comprising 90 ECTS credits, and a PhD thesis comprising 150 ECTS credits. The main task is therefore to devote yourself to your research project and participation in postgraduate courses.

As a PhD student you will mainly be working with your research project, but you can also be given more general tasks at the department, e.g. teaching, research or administrative work, in accordance with the regulations in SFS 1998:80. 

Eligibility/Entry requirements 

Admission requirements for the PhD programme:

  • General admission requirements: A master’s degree, and 240 completed ECTS credits of university studies. A person may also meet the general entry requirements if he/she has acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way in Sweden or abroad.
  • Specific admission requirements: At least 90 completed ECTS credits in a subject relevant to the research studies, including a degree project relevant to the research studies, equivalent to at least 15 credits. A person may also meet the specific entry requirements if he/she has acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way in Sweden or abroad. 

Requirements for the PhD posistion:

  • Very high proficiency in English, in speech and writing.
  • Ability to work independently. 

Meritous for the PhD posistion:

  • Courses/modules in entrepreneurship. 

Basis of assessment

The applicants will be assessed on the basis of their prospects of meeting the requirements for a doctoral degree (PhD) in Business Administration. Particular emphasis will be placed on the following:

  • Academic results, particularly on the master’s level.
  • Bachelor’s and master’s theses (with special importance attached to the master’s thesis).
  • Relevance and viability of the research plan.
  • Other results and distinctions which attest to the applicant’s ability to profit from the PhD programme.
  • Other knowledge and skills relevant to the thesis work and the subject of the programme. These can be demonstrated through the attached documents and/or a possible interview. 

Decisions on admission to the PhD programme are made by the Head of department after consultation with the Director of the PhD programme and, if necessary, additional co-assessors with special expertise in the applicant’s intended thesis area. 

Application procedure 

The application is to contain the following documents:

  • A complete application form, found at: https://www.lusem.lu.se/organisation/department-business-administration/doctoral-studies-business-administration
  • Letter of introduction (max 800 words), which contains a presentation of yourself and your qualifications as well as a brief explanation of why you are interested in the PhD programme at the Department of Business Administration.
  • Curriculum Vitae (2 pages)
  • Research plan of no more than 5 pages (max 2,000 words) stating the topic to be investigated, its positioning within entrepreneurship research, and the sources of data and methodology the candidate aims to use. The topic should be specific and clearly located within one of the two projects listed in the subject area section (see above). Please indicate which project the plan addresses.
  • Degree certificates of your Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees
  • A copy of your Master’s thesis
  • An executive summary (500 words) of your Master’s thesis
  • The names and contact information of two references, preferably active in academia.
  • Copies of certificates and copies of any other documents that you wish to include in your application. 

All submitted documents must be attested as to their authenticity. 

Your application should be written in English and sent as one pdf file to: application@fek.lu.se. 

Lund University welcomes applicants with diverse backgrounds and experiences. We regard equality, equal opportunities and diversity as a strength and an asset. 

Last day for applying is: 2026-12-01 

For further information please contact: 

Diamanto Politis, Professor

diamanto.politis@fek.lu.se

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Journalism, Digital Media: ESRC Welsh Graduate School for the Social Sciences (WGSSS) - Journalism, Digital Media and Democracy
jobs.department: Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences
jobs.description_html:
Media, Communications and Public Relations at Swansea has been consistently recognized for its excellence and is placed right at the top in UK league tables for various elements of its delivery. Priding itself on a strong sense of community, staff and students are involved at the cutting edge of the study of contemporary media and its impact. Our mix of esteemed practitioners and globally acknowledged scholars have expertise across a broad range of sub-themes within the Journalism, Democracy and Digital Media pathway.  

For example, while we attend to the traditional aspects of print and broadcast journalism and the way that these cover key areas such as politics, conflict, financial affairs, the climate crisis and sport, our expertise extends into alternative digital news media, fact checking, disordered information, hate speech, racism and misogyny. Colleagues have extensively researched social media and all its dimensions, the metaverse, virtual and augmented reality, the wider implications of surveillance and technological interventions into all elements of contemporary life. We have strong impact in the fields of digital access for minority groups and the ways that news and journalism are both governed and regulated, and overarching all of this, our film and TV studies scholars offer insight into how all such elements are represented to wider audiences. Our public relations scholars are research active in looking at both the corporate functioning and the more disruptive elements within that profession, and how organizations digitally manage and maintain crises and brand identities. We would welcome applications that tap into these themes and add new and important dimensions.    

Our strong links with the media sector itself - via our own Industry Panel – ensures the contemporary nature of our activities and provides a wide range of internship and work experience opportunities. In sum, studying a Media PhD at Swansea combines the benefits of accessing the most up-to-date experts in “media” in its widest sense with becoming part of a close-knit community of scholars who prioritize community and collegiality. Closing date: 4 December 2026, 17:00 | Expected start: 1 February 2027 | Duration: 3 years, full-time

Applications are invited for a three-year PhD studentship, funded by The Leverhulme Trust, in the Department of Psychology and Neuroscience at City St George’s, University of London. The successful candidate will be supervised by Dr Claudia Civai.

The project, Human contact as a costly premium: the consequences of new digital inequalities, investigates what happens when human contact becomes a service that only some people can afford.

As AI increasingly replaces human staff in high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance, people on lower incomes may be pushed towards AI-mediated services not by preference, but by cost. Across the UK and Italy, this interdisciplinary project combines large-scale surveys, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and behavioural and physiological measures to investigate whether unequal access to human contact affects people’s satisfaction, sense of agency, and ability to retain important advice.

The successful candidate will play an active role throughout the project. In the first year, they will contribute to a large-scale survey across the UK and Italy, developing skills in experimental design, pre-registration, and advanced statistical modelling. In years two and three, they will work on laboratory studies, leading the collection of fNIRS and behavioural data at research sites in the UK and Italy. Full methodological training and travel expenses will be provided.

The project offers an excellent opportunity to develop interdisciplinary research skills at the intersection of behavioural science, social psychology, and cognitive neuroscience, within collaborations involving London South Bank University and the University of Padua.

jobs.description_html:
Award Summary

100% of home (UK) tuition fees and an annual stipend at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 26/27)

Overview

Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is an established treatment for chronic neuropathic pain, typically considered for patients who have not responded adequately to more conservative therapies. Despite its clinical use, the mechanisms underlying its therapeutic effects and the reasons for loss of efficacy over time remain poorly understood. This PhD project will investigate how different SCS paradigms influence pain processing and neuronal activity, building on our ongoing research using clinically relevant preclinical models of neuropathic pain and SCS in rats.

The project will combine behavioural, molecular and neurobiological approaches to investigate how different stimulation parameters and paradigms influence neural recruitment and the mechanisms underlying analgesia. A particular focus will be understanding why treatment efficacy may decline over time, including the role of axonal homeostasis during high-frequency stimulation. The project will also develop and validate long-term stimulation models, extending stimulation from minutes to days to better reflect clinical practice and investigate sustained neurobiological adaptations. This will provide important insights into the long-term effects of SCS and strengthen the translational relevance of preclinical research. Ultimately, the findings will advance our understanding of how SCS works, why it sometimes fails, and how stimulation protocols can be optimised to improve the durability and efficacy of treatment for patients with chronic pain.

The supervisory team brings together complementary expertise in electrophysiology, pharmacology and experimental neuroscience across multiple species, supported by successful and well-established research laboratories. The project will offer excellent multidisciplinary training and the opportunity to work in close collaboration with Saluda Medical, a global leader in spinal cord stimulation technology.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Designing Photocurable Resins for High-Resolution DLP Printing of Ultrasoft Hydrogels
jobs.description_html:
Research organisation: University of Nottingham
Application deadline: 10 December 2026
Start date: October 2027 (or as soon as possible thereafter)
Funding: Fully funded DLA PhD studentship supported by EPSRC

Project Description

Cells sense and respond to the stiffness of their surroundings. Matrix stiffness influences cell spreading, mechanotransduction and stem cell differentiation. Many soft tissues, such as brain and liver, have moduli below 10 kPa. Hydrogels that replicate this softness within precisely defined 3D architectures are therefore valuable for tissue engineering and in vitro tissue models. Digital light processing (DLP) 3D printing can fabricate complex hydrogel structures rapidly and at high resolution. Achieving such resolution with very soft hydrogels, however, remains challenging. Their dilute, loosely crosslinked networks are prone to overcuring during printing. They also swell substantially after printing, which distorts fine features and alters the final dimensions and stiffness of the construct. As a result, many DLP-printable hydrogels are considerably stiffer than the tissues they aim to mimic.

This project will develop new resin formulations that enable high-resolution DLP printing of ultrasoft hydrogels. Working at the interface of polymer chemistry and additive manufacturing, the student will design reactive crosslinkers and photocurable resins, and establish clear links between resin chemistry, swelling behaviour, print fidelity and mechanical properties. Supervision by experts in polymer chemistry and 3D printing will provide broad training in synthesis, photopolymerisation, mechanical characterisation and DLP printing. This combination offers a strong foundation for a career in biomaterials or advanced manufacturing.

Eligibility and Application Process

Applications are welcomed from candidates with a background in Chemistry, Chemical Engineering, or a closely related discipline, and with a strong interest in sustainable chemistry and pharmaceutical formulation.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to contact: Dr Vincenzo Taresco: vincenzo.taresco@nottingham.ac.uk and Dr Yinfeng He: yinfeng.he@nottingham.ac.uk. Full supervisory team: Dr Vincenzo Taresco, Dr Yinfeng He, Dr Robert Owen and Prof Ross Denton.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Programmable Matter from Entangled Architected Materials (AE0088)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59, 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Robots, software and digital memory can be reprogrammed after they are built. Materials, by contrast, have mechanical behaviour that is fixed at manufacture. This PhD will investigate whether that behaviour can be reprogrammed after fabrication.

You will study architected entangled materials: networks of curved filaments whose stiffness and toughness arise from how the filaments interweave and contact one another. Fabrics and ropes are familiar examples. In these networks, small changes in contact and friction can produce very large changes in mechanical response.

The project will exploit this sensitivity by driving a weak deformation mode, orthogonal to the deformations caused by external loads, to reprogram the network. Ordinary loading does not activate this mode, so the network remains stiff and tough in service. Driving the mode deliberately changes the contact state and releases the network.

Potential applications include spacecraft trusses that can be reconfigured after launch, and wearable braces that stiffen to protect a joint and soften to allow movement.

Key objectives:

  • Understand how contact and friction govern stiffness and toughness in each state
  • Establish how driving a deformation mode that external loads do not activate changes the contact state
  • Determine the range of loading over which this mode remains inactive
  • Identify what limits the contrast in stiffness between the two states
  • The project is approximately 50% experimental, 40% computational and 10% theoretical.

You will join the AIM Lab, a new group in the Department of Aeronautics. As one of its first members, you will help shape the group.

You will develop expertise in the mechanics of slender structures, contact and friction, and the geometry of filament networks. You will fabricate specimens using multi-material 3D printing and a robotic fabrication cell, test them mechanically, and write simulation code to model them.

You will present at international conferences, including the annual meeting of the Society of Engineering Science and the Functionality through Nonlinearity conference. Imperial’s Early Career Researcher Institute provides training in research and career skills.

Overview

Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly central to offshore energy operations, yet their deployment remains constrained by limited endurance, energy density, and the ability to maintain station or perform interventions in harsh ocean environments. Offshore wind, subsea cables, and fixed/floating energy platforms require regular inspection and rapid-response maintenance, but current operations rely heavily on crewed vessels and ROVs-methods that are expensive, weather‑limited, carbon‑intensive, and inherently short-duration. 

This PhD project aims to develop a next‑generation endurant power and propulsion system enabling AUVs to achieve 500m+, 1000+ hours endurance and 2000+ miles operational range, unlocking persistent monitoring and immediate intervention capability for safety‑critical offshore energy infrastructure. Achieving this requires breakthroughs in both high‑energy‑density subsea battery systems and high‑efficiency electric propulsion, consistent with current research directions emphasising high energy density, intrinsic safety, and deep‑sea adaptability.  

The candidate will work with the industrial partner Walker Subsea.

The candidate will: 

  • Co‑develop system requirements based on real offshore inspection missions.
  • Integrate the battery and propulsion prototypes into an AUV platform.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Powering the Future: Terahertz Technology for Next-Generation Batteries
jobs.city: Coventry, University of Warwick, Warwick Salary
jobs.description_html:
From electric vehicles to grid-scale energy storage, the future of clean energy relies on breakthroughs in battery technology. This PhD will develop cutting-edge terahertz spectroscopy methods to unlock scalable manufacturing of next-generation solid-state batteries.

The project:

Solid-state electrolytes are attracting growing interest for next-generation solid-state batteries due to their improved thermal stability, reduced flammability, enhanced durability, and potential for higher energy density. However, manufacturing high-performance electrolytes remains challenging, as their microstructures must be carefully controlled and optimised to ensure good electrochemical performance, mechanical integrity, and impermeability. This challenge is compounded by the lack of rapid inspection methods capable of assessing microstructural homogeneity, which is increasingly important for product-scale electrolytes.

The PhD candidate will join a dynamic, interdisciplinary research team working at the interface of metrology, battery materials, and ceramic processing. Building on our previous demonstrations [1], this project will begin with the fabrication and characterisation of conventional electrolyte materials using emerging terahertz spectroscopy. The work will then progress to developing the technique further for measurements on product-scale electrolytes. In the later stages of the project, thermal control will be integrated to probe intrinsic conduction behaviour and link this to longer length-scale conductions, establishing a unified framework connecting microstructure and transport mechanisms.

In close collaboration with LiNa Energy, this project offers an exciting opportunity to contribute directly to innovations in solid-state battery manufacturing, advanced metrology, and quality control for next-generation energy storage devices.

[1]https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpowsour.2024.234050

Scholarship:

jobs.title: UKRI Funded PhD in Safe Artificial Intelligence
jobs.description_html:
Join our thriving multidisciplinary community and deliver projects focused on the safety of AI.

The Centre for Doctoral Training in Safe AI Systems (SAINTS CDT) is the UK’s first multidisciplinary PhD programme focused solely on the safety of artificial intelligence (AI).

Our vision is to train future leaders with the research expertise and skills to ensure that the benefits of AI systems are realised without introducing harm as the systems and their environments evolve.

The Centre for Doctoral Training in Safe AI Systems (SAINTS CDT) is the UK’s first multidisciplinary PhD programme focused solely on the safety of artificial intelligence (AI).

Fully funded PhD opportunity

SAINTS is part of the TechFirst pilot offering stipends of £30,000 for students eligible for home fee status. Join us and help grow the UK’s national capability in AI safety, part of the UK’s modern industrial strategy. Everyone is welcome if you are passionate about AI safety and looking to develop your research and innovation skills at doctoral level to further your career in safety-critical sectors such as transport, healthcare and national security.

As a postgraduate researcher with SAINTS CDT, you'll receive the following financial benefits:

  • A tax-free stipend £30,000* for your living costs (pro rata for part-time postgraduate researchers), which is paid to you in regular instalments. The amount of the stipend usually increases each year in line with inflation
  • Your annual tuition fees will be paid
  • Funding is available for you to attend research-related events and conferences

*You must have Home fee status to be eligible for the TechFirst stipend amount. Applicants who have International fee status are still welcome to apply but will receive the standard UKRI minimum stipend amount (£21,805 in 2026-27). The 2027-28 UKRI stipend amount will be confirmed in early 2027.

Applications are open until 12 noon GMT on Monday 11st January 2027.

The Programme

Our PhD in Safe AI takes a unique and purposeful approach. Postgraduate researchers with different backgrounds and experiences will train together.

Research will be focused on the lifelong safety assurance of increasingly autonomous AI systems in dynamic and uncertain contexts. It will build on methodologies and concepts in disciplines spanning AI, safety science, philosophy, law, sociology and health sciences.

You will also participate in a series of taught courses covering the technical, legal, ethical and societal underpinnings and implications of your research. These courses will give you the strong foundation you need for both your research and the next step in your career.

The PhD in Safe AI can be studied for four years full-time or eight years part-time.

Work directly with industry

The SAINTS CDT has an extensive network of over thirty partners, including major international companies, government organisations, regulators and charities.

Our partners will be closely involved in the research that you'll undertake throughout your PhD, and will provide you with opportunities to work in industry and gain valuable experience that will support your research development.

Some of our partners also expect to offer employment opportunities to SAINTS researchers when they graduate.

Location

You'll be based at the world's first Institute for Safe Autonomy at the University of York. It's an exciting and welcoming hub for innovation and collaboration with a modern and inclusive working environment. You'll benefit from world-class laboratories, collaboration spaces and expert colleagues working at the leading edge of their fields.

Entry requirements

Typically, you should have, or expect to obtain, one of the following combinations of academic qualification:

  • A first-class honours degree (or equivalent), OR
  • 2:1 in an honours degree and a Master’s degree (or equivalent)

We recognise that applicants may not have followed a traditional career path, and therefore relevant work experience or equivalent qualifications can be taken into account.

Your knowledge and experience should enable you to undertake doctoral research in your chosen area within the SAINTS CDT (e.g. computer science, engineering, mathematics, economics, health sciences, law, philosophy, sociology).

For more information about our entry requirements and details about how to apply, please visit the SAINTS CDT website.

Want to find out more or have a question to ask? Join us at one of our online applicant information webinars over November and December. Keep an eye out for dates and how to sign up on our website.

Contact us

If you have any questions, please email the SAINTS CDT administration team at saints-cdt-admissions@york.ac.uk

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Turbulence under Strain (AE0096)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59 on 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: Richard Feynman famously quoted ‘turbulence is the most important unsolved problem of classical physics’. Understanding and modelling turbulent flow physics will unlock a vast potential for optimising many applications of the energy and transportation sectors. While the last century has produced breakthroughs in our understanding of turbulent flows, these are confined in two extreme and polar-opposite regimes: when turbulence is highly or when it is lowly strained. Still, the physics of the in-between regime of intermediate-strain, which is critical for a wide variety of engineering and environmental applications, remains unexplored.

This project will focus on uncovering the physics of intermediate-strain turbulent wakes. Apart from being of interest from a fundamental perspective, such wake conditions are widely encountered in automotive, aeronautical and wind engineering applications among many others.

Various bluff bodies will be tested in the lab, carefully designed so that their near wakes produce average strain rates that vary from low to high levels. You will then document the failure of classical theories to describe intermediate strain regimes. The produced data-set will subsequently be utilized to develop a novel theoretical framework for intermediate strain turbulence, based on the concept of ‘simple transportation of energy’ recently proposed by the PI, and validated for the simpler case of homogenous decaying turbulence. The project will rely on laboratory experiments, conducted in the state-of-the-art wind tunnel facilities of the Aeronautics Department, and will utilize high speed particle image velocimetry to characterize 2D and 3D turbulent velocity fields.

The proposed work falls under the theme of the ERC project ONSET awarded to the PI and its successful conclusion could potentially lay the basis for the development of novel turbulence closure models for intermediate strain conditions, where current models are known to be inaccurate.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Real-time Data Assimilation for Multi-physics Flows (AE0095)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59, 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: Every model is wrong, and in engineering the errors matter. From aircraft wings to wind turbines and combustors, engineering systems are governed by fluid flows that interact with other physical processes, such as structural vibrations, acoustics and chemical reactions. On the one hand, physics-based models of these multi-physics systems are extrapolative – they provide predictions on phenomena that have not been observed. However, their parameters are uncertain, and their equations neglect part of the physics. On the other hand, measurements provide information on the true state of the system, but they are sparse and noisy. When operating conditions change rapidly, model errors grow, and forecasts lose accuracy precisely when they are needed most. Real-time data assimilation, which combines models with measurements, offers a way forward. However, most existing methods assume that the model is unbiased and they cannot cope with rapid changes in operating conditions, such as a gust hitting an aircraft wing or a sudden change in the load of a combustor. A fully-funded PhD studentship is available at the Department of Aeronautics, Imperial College London, to develop bias-aware data assimilation methods that estimate and correct model error as the dynamics evolve. The output of the project will be a model that learns from data any time that measurements are assimilated, without violating the physics. We will prototype the methods on low-order dynamical systems, and we will scale them up to higher-dimensional multi-physics problems.

You will gain experience in data assimilation and Bayesian inference, physics-constrained machine learning, and computational methods for multi-physics systems. You will employ high-performance computing facilities, present your work at international conferences, publish in peer-reviewed journals, and benefit from Imperial’s doctoral training programme and career support. These skills will prepare you for careers in academia, industry and research laboratories.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Generative Neural-Operator Surrogates for Real-Time Multiphysics Design (AE0094)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59 on 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: This PhD addresses a central bottleneck in engineering design: generating a candidate geometry is fast, but evaluating its physical performance is not. Neural operators can predict multiphysics fields in milliseconds once trained, and generative models can propose new geometries in seconds. Yet these two capabilities are rarely combined into a single, closed-loop system. Doing so would let a designer generate, evaluate and refine a component in real time, rather than waiting on costly simulation cycles. This has direct relevance to thermal management, electromagnetic components and multifunctional lightweight parts.

You will train neural-operator surrogates — Fourier Neural Operator and DeepONet-style architectures — on thermal and electromagnetic performance data, for example, from multifunctional metastructures. You will then embed these operators directly inside a conditional diffusion or transformer-based generator, so physics feedback becomes differentiable and near-instantaneous during generation, rather than computed afterwards. You will embed governing equation constraints as physics losses within the generative architecture, develop conditioning schemes letting users specify target performance directly, and validate designs computationally. You will quantify the trade-off between operator fidelity and generative design quality. You will test whether a single joint multiphysics operator (thermal and electromagnetic together) can replace two separate surrogates without losing accuracy. You will build towards an interactive design-exploration tool with sub-second feedback, benchmarking throughout against conventional solver-in-the-loop generative pipelines to prove where your closed-loop approach genuinely wins. You will work across both computational validation and, where feasible, experimental testing via 3D-printed prototypes, keeping the work tied to physically realisable structures rather than a purely theoretical exercise.

You will be supervised by Dr. Ajit Panesar and Prof. Rob Hewson, whose complementary expertise spans generative design, engineering optimisation, structural metamaterials and scientific ML, and you'll be working alongside a talented group of researchers in a dynamic, intellectually stimulating environment.

This project aims to advance how AI systems design, build, and refine interactive 3D games and virtual worlds, transforming high-level creative ideas into coherent, playable experiences.

Research Focus 

The PhD will investigate agentic AI systems that can plan complex creative tasks, use game development tools, and iteratively evaluate and improve their outputs. Moving beyond the generation of individual assets, the project will explore how AI can integrate 3D content, spatial layouts, game logic, and interactive behaviours into complete virtual environments. The project combines fundamental research in planning, spatial reasoning, and generative modelling with practical innovation in game development and interactive world creation. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Categorification and the Local Langlands Correspondence
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Professor Shaun Stevens

The representation theory of p-adic groups has been a highly active area of research over the last fifty years, motivated by the Local Langlands Correspondence/Conjectures and its deep connections to Number Theory. To begin with, only irreducible representations with complex coefficients were considered but, more recently, representations with coefficients in other rings or fields have been studied also. Moreover, to gain a better understanding, more importance has been given to trying to match the (derived) structures of categories on the two sides of the correspondence.

On the other hand, techniques from higher representation theory give a way to study these categories: for representations of p-adic general linear groups, this leads to a 2-representation of a certain quantum group – this is an example of a categorification of this quantum group, in which we understand its elements as functors. An analogue of this result is already known for finite general linear groups, and the project will begin by making this precise in the p-adic case. It will then aim to transfer information obtained by studying this 2-representation across the local Langlands correspondence, possibly by extending it to the relevant derived categories.

The project will be co-supervised by Shaun Stevens and Vanessa Miemietz.

Entry Requirements

The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 bachelor's degree in mathematics.

Start Date: 1 February 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Representations of P-adic Groups and Arithmetic
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Professor Shaun Stevens

The Local Langlands Correspondence has motivated a great deal of Number Theory and Representation Theory over the last fifty years. It connects representations of (roughly) the absolute galois group of a p-adic field to the representations of a matrix group G over the field. In the original formulation (now proved for several families of matrix groups G, including general linear groups) it considered only complex representations but, more recently, representations with coefficients in other rings or fields have been considered also. The correspondence results in a partition of the irreducible representations of G into L-packets (which are singletons for general linear groups), each of which is conjecturally characterised by an equality of local factors (L-functions and e-factors) – though a definition for such factors is only known for “generic” representations, of which there is (at least conjecturally) precisely one in each packet.

One of the difficulties in studying this is that the representations of G are (almost all) infinite-dimensional, so they are quite hard to get a handle on. One way for doing so, which has been very successful, is to restrict them to compact open subgroups K: we then look for representations of K whose presence in this restriction characterizes some property which representations of G might have; this property might be being “unramified”, ”tame”, “generic”,… Similarly, this restriction can be used to give very explicit descriptions of the representations of G, using arithmetic data. Such results also have interpretations via the Langlands correspondence, so consequences for the absolute galois group.

This project will be in the area of the local Langlands correspondence, exploring some of the problems raised above, or related questions.

Entry Requirements

The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 bachelor's degree in mathematics.

Start Date: 1 February 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Machine Learning-based Control of Reacting Flow Extreme Events (AE0092)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59, 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: The development of sustainable propulsion systems, based on hydrogen or sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs), is increasing the risk of extreme events occurring in these. These are rare events where the flow in the combustor suddenly takes extreme states far, potentially with grave consequences. Examples are flashback in hydrogen or thermoacoustic instabilities triggered by the varying SAFs properties. The safe and reliable operation of these future sustainable propulsion systems thus requires the ability to anticipate their occurrence through measurable precursors and the deployment of real-time mitigation based on those precursors.

Traditional methods have generally been unable to tackle this due to the turbulent nature of the underlying flows and the complex multiscale/multiphysics nonlinear interactions at the origin of such extreme events. Recent advances in differentiable solver and machine learning offer a pathway to enable such their mitigation and control.

In this project, you will develop a framework for the control of reacting flow extreme events that combines a differentiable reacting flow solver and a machine learning-based controller. The differentiable solver will provide short-term state dependency used by machine learning-based controller to obtain an optimal mitigation control preventing the reacting flow extreme event. This will be applied across various reacting flow applications, leveraging novel reacting flow actuators such spray water injection or electrically-driven fuel droplet control.

Research Group: You will join a research group on the European project CONTEXT, at the intersection of scientific machine learning and fluid dynamics, under the supervision of Dr. Anh Khoa Doan. You will also have the opportunity to interact with experts in turbulence and machine learning across the department, such as Prof. Luca Magri. Dr. George Rigas or Dr. Andrea Novoa.

Learning opportunities: You will develop expertise in reacting flow physics, machine learning for fluids and control, and high-fidelity simulations. You will have the opportunity of using cutting-edge facilities such as Imperial College HPC facilities.

Professional Development: You will have access to engaging professional development workshops in areas such as research communication, computing and data science, and professional progression through our Early Career Researcher Institute, and will have the opportunity to participate to international conferences.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: A Lagrangian Perspective of Entrainment into Wind-turbine Wakes (AE0091)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59, 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Wind turbines clustered together for reasons relating to land availability, onwards power transmission to the grid, and maintenance scheduling amongst others. Unfortunately, wind-turbine clustering is aerodynamically disadvantageous. Each turbine produces a turbulent wake that interacts with downstream turbines to reduce the efficiency of power generation and accelerate the accumulation of fatigue damage. Improved understanding of the spreading, and propagation of wind-turbine wakes is therefore essential to design more efficient wind farms.

Wakes increase in size with distance downstream, similarly to a plume of smoke expanding as it leave a chimney. The processes by which turbulent flows expand are, collectively, known as entrainment. Wind-turbine wakes are complex flows; they involve a background that is already turbulent (due to atmospheric processes) and contain multiple coherent motions such as the blade-tip vortices. All of these features complicate our understanding entrainment into wind-turbine wakes.

You will perform cutting edge experiments to directly observe entrainment, and how the wake’s coherent motions affect these processes, in a laboratory-scale wind-turbine wake from a Lagrangian perspective (i.e. one that moves with the flow), by undertaking state-of-the-art particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) measurements. Our research group has conducted groundbreaking research in recent years on turbulent entrainment and this is the next, exciting step in the journey.

A key feature of this PhD project is that it will run in parallel to a project running at DTU (in Copenhagen) aiming to produce reduced-order models of wind-turbine wakes accounting for the coherent motions and entrainment that you will study. This project will therefore grant you the opportunity to collaborate with one of Europe’s leading research groups in wind energy as well as travel between London and Copenhagen. You will also:

  • Gain hands-on experience of PTV and running experiments in a water facility that is well optimised for entrainment measurements,
  • Work in a research group that has taken a leading role in studying turbulent entrainment,
  • Be expected to write cutting-edge papers and present your findings at international conferences,
  • Gain access to Imperial’s network for professional development, helping you to make future career decisions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Structure-photodegradation-performance Relationship in Carbon Fibre-reinforced Thermosets (AE0089)
jobs.description_html:
Start date: As soon as possible

Application deadline: 23:59 on 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: The move towards more-sustainable transport requires lighter vehicle structures, so the high strength-to-weight and stiffness-to-weight ratios of fibre composite materials make them attractive in new applications in addition to their traditional use in aerospace. However, these composite structures are exposed to UV light, especially when used in aircraft and space applications. UV-induced photodegradation is known to damage the surface of composites through erosion and the formation of microcracks in the matrix, which can grow due to stresses on the structure. Thus, it is critical to use polymers that are highly UV-resistant for these applications, but which also possess the required mechanical and functional properties.

The objective of this project is to understand the UV degradation mechanisms of thermosetting epoxy polymers and how the structure / composition of the polymers affects their UV resistance in order to maximise their longevity and long-term performance. It is anticipated that the results arising from this PhD studentship will combine UV resistance data, and visual and chemical analysis with mechanical and fracture properties to build a map of the structure–property relationships for a given composite system. The identification of these structure–property relationships will enable the development of novel and more UV-durable formulations.

You will join the Department of Aeronautics at Imperial College London, benefiting from joint supervision by Professor Koon-Yang Lee (Aeronautics) and Professor Ambrose Taylor (Mechanical Engineering), alongside an industry research scientist from Syensqo.

You will develop specialist expertise in the analytical characterisation of composite materials, gaining hands-on experience in advanced composite manufacturing and analytical techniques in composite science and technology. Throughout your PhD, you will have access to state-of-the-art facilities at Imperial College London, including high-resolution microscopy, thermal analysis systems, UV/vis spectroscopy, FTIR, AFM, a Q-SUN test chamber and comprehensive mechanical testing facilities.

You will also have opportunities to present your research at national and international conferences, publish your findings in peer-reviewed journals and build professional networks with leading researchers and industry partners.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The Physics of Learning in Robotic Metamaterials
jobs.description_html:
Join us!

Are you a curiosity-driven scientist with a background in physics, engineering, applied mathematics or a related discipline? Join us to lead work at intersection of metamaterials, soft matter physics, and robotics. Look at https://binyshlab.com for some of our work.

This position revolves around the physics of active mechanical metamaterials and distributed robotic systems, combining table-top experiments with theoretical modelling. The project will focus on self-learning active mechanical networks but will be tailored to your interests and expertise.

What will you do?

Nature overflows with simple organisms–from starfish to bacteria–that function without a brain. In contrast to a conventional robot, which is centrally controlled and rigid, these living materials are mechanically soft, and spread actuation, feedback and computation right across their bodies, blurring the boundary between material and machine. Living systems are unconventional robots indeed.

Our work hints that key platforms to capture such material intelligence are ‘robotic metamaterials’–mechanical networks built from many sensors and actuators that locally communicate with one another to achieve collective functionality. These active networks could enable next-generation bioinspired robots that operate without central control, withstand massive damage and adapt to ever-changing environments.

In this PhD, you will lead research into robotic metamaterials that can adapt their dynamics to an environment after deployment. You will:

  • Develop and apply decentralized learning techniques to networks of active mechanical units to sculpt their dynamics and functionality and explore fundamental physical questions on the link between network structure and functionality.
  • Capture the nonlinear dynamics of these networks using theory and numerical simulations.
  • Design and perform table-top robotic experiments that implement your learning algorithms in unpredictable environments.

Who are you?

This PhD is ideal for a curiosity-driven scientist interested in (i) the intersection between materials and machines and (ii) What robotics can teach us about physics, and vice versa. You might be a physicist interested in robotics, a mechanical engineer interested in bio-inspired materials, or a computer scientist/mathematician interested in applied nonlinear dynamics and optimization. We seek an openness to combining table-top robotic experiments with simulations and theory, and an excellent MSc/MPhys/MEng degree (or equivalent).

How to Apply

Applicants should upload information via Birmingham’s Mechanical Engineering PhD portal via the 'Apply' button above specifying the title of the PhD position, and main supervisor (Jack Binysh). We aim to have you start in Early 2027.

In your application please include:

  • A cover letter in which you describe your motivation and qualifications for the position.
  • A CV which includes the contact information of two references.
  • A transcript of your degree grades.
  • A research proposal - Here, because this is an existing project, please feel free to use the job advert as a starting point, but do include any ideas you would be most excited to work on.

Funding is currently available to cover Home UK students, i.e. covering fees and providing a stipend at UKRI rates (current stipend: £21,805 p.a.) for 42 months. Strong international candidates should look at https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/study/international/fees/scholarships, and contact Dr. Binysh if they have a viable plan for international funding.

For relevant publications, details of research environment and our commitment to inclusivity, see https://binyshlab.com/positions/. Questions? Email Dr. Binysh in your own words at j.binysh@bham.ac.uk.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Formalising the Local Langlands Correspondence for GL₂(F) in Lean
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Christopher Birkbeck

This PhD project, based at our Norwich campus, offers a unique opportunity to work at the confluence of number theory, representation theory, and formal mathematics. You will undertake a single, ambitious research project: to begin the formalisation of the local Langlands correspondence for GL₂(F) in the Lean interactive theorem prover by leveraging AI agents. This correspondence is a cornerstone of the modern Langlands program, providing a deep and unforeseen bridge between harmonic analysis and number theory.

The primary goal of this project is to formalise the sophisticated mathematical objects required to state the main theorem. This will involve developing a computer-verified library for the two sides of the correspondence: (1) the representation theory of GL₂(F), where F is a non-Archimedean local field, including the theory of irreducible admissible representations; and (2) the intricate structure of two-dimensional Galois representations of the Weil group of F.

Once the definitions are in place, the second phase of the project will be to create a comprehensive framework to guide the formalisation of the proof itself, laying the groundwork for a long-term verification effort. This foundational work will be a landmark achievement in the digital formalisation of contemporary mathematics.

jobs.description_html:
Brushless Doubly Fed Machines (BDFMs) are emerging as a promising technology for offshore wind turbine generators due to their fractional-sized power converters, elimination of rotor brushes and slip rings, and simplified gearbox systems compared to high-speed generators. These features offer significant advantages, including lower capital and operational costs, increased reliability, and reduced maintenance demands which are key for the broader adoption of offshore wind energy. However, several challenges must be addressed, such as the machine's relatively low power density and power factor, high vibration levels, and complex magnetic field behavior.

This research project aims to propose design optimisations to enhance the performance of BDFMs and position BDFMs as a competitive alternative to direct drive and medium-speed permanent magnet generators, paving the way for more cost-effective and reliable offshore wind energy systems.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: AI-Driven Fault Diagnosis for Wind Turbine Generators
jobs.description_html:
Primary supervisor - Dr Abdi Jalebi Salman

Reliability is critical to the continued expansion of wind power, particularly for offshore installations, which already contribute around 10-15% of the UK’s electricity and are central to achieving net-zero targets and ensuring the resilience of national grid infrastructure. Preventive maintenance enabled by condition monitoring systems (CMSs) plays a key role in improving turbine reliability and availability while reducing operational costs and the levelised cost of energy. However, the drivetrain, comprising the gearbox, generator, and power electronics, remains a major source of failures, accounting for roughly one third of incidents and nearly half of maintenance costs in offshore turbines. Early and accurate fault detection in this subsystem is therefore essential.

Despite widespread deployment, existing CMS solutions are predominantly based on vibration measurements from accelerometers mounted on drivetrain components, and their performance remains limited. These systems often suffer from low fault detection rates, generate false alarms that reduce energy production, or fail to identify faults sufficiently early to avoid costly repairs. Moreover, they are largely ineffective at detecting electrical faults. The lack of commercially available CMS solutions based on electrical measurements is due to inherent complexity of interpreting electrical signatures of mechanical faults in real time. This creates a clear gap and opportunity for more advanced and integrated monitoring approaches.

This project aims to address the identified gap by developing hybrid fault diagnosis methods that combine analytical approaches based on drivetrain physical properties with AI-driven data analysis techniques to enhance the accuracy and effectiveness of fault detection and classification. The work will involve analytical studies, computer simulations, and finite element (FE) analysis, alongside experimental development and validation.

Entry requirements: The minimum entry requirement is 2:1 in Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Physics.

Mode of study: Full-time or part-time

Start date: 1st February 2027

Additional funding information: This is a self-funded project (Students worldwide).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Nonlinear Waves on Liquid Cylinders
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Prof. Mark Blyth

Inviscid liquid jets subject to surface tension and in the absence of gravity are known to be unstable under long-wave perturbations, a phenomenon described by the classical Rayleigh–Plateau instability. However, when vorticity and swirl are included, Erhard et al. (2022) have theoretically demonstrated the existence of nonlinear travelling-wave solutions on such jets — although their detailed properties remain unexplored. In this project, we will develop new computational methods to compute and characterize these novel wave solutions, with particular emphasis on solitary waves and on analysing their stability. We will also extend the study to related configurations, such as ferrofluid jets under vorticity and swirl.

The mathematical and numerical techniques developed during this work will deepen our understanding of nonlinear wave phenomena in fluid mechanics and contribute to the broader theory of interfacial flows.

jobs.description_html:
Start date: Between 1st August 2027 and 1st July 2028

Application deadline: 23:59 on 4th January 2027 (UK time)

Introduction: Aircraft condensation trails (contrails) are thought to be responsible for up to half of aviation's overall contribution to climate change, and eliminating them has become a priority for aviation sustainability. Understanding the exact consequences of a contrail in different circumstances remains a significant challenge - and one which you can help with. You will be tasked with investigating the chemistry of contrails - the role that these artificial ice clouds might have in modifying the atmosphere not by changing the climate, but by providing a surface on which atmospheric chemistry takes place. You will develop expertise in simulation of ice clouds and atmospheric chemistry-transport modelling using the Imperial High Performance Computing facilities, while also engaging with the challenges of informed decision making regarding aircraft design and aviation policy. Depending on how your research develops you can also expect to learn about satellite and in-situ evaluation of aviation impacts, possible technical mechanisms of impact mitigation, and the role of operational constraints.

Throughout your studies you will be a member of the Aerospace Environmental Impacts Simulation (AEIS) group and working within the Contrail Research Centre, part of the Brahmal Vasudevan Institute for Sustainable Aviation. You can expect constant exposure to debate, discussion, and collaboration with a broad group of researchers, all working towards a common goal and representing expertise from aircraft exhaust simulation through to satellite-based contrail detection. You can also expect to attend conferences and meet with international researchers working on atmospheric science and aviation sustainability. By developing the technical skills at the heart of quantitative environmental impact analysis, you will be able to contribute directly to the work of making aerospace truly sustainable.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Aeronautics: Electric Composites (AE0093)
jobs.description_html:
Introduction: This PhD puts you at the forefront of structural power composites (SPCs) — a WEF Top 10 Emerging Technology of 2025 — materials that simultaneously store energy and carry load. SPC promise a step-change weight savings for electric aircraft, EVs and satellites. Transitioning from device- to component-level fabrication in a trustworthy fashion would give industry the first credible route from lab-scale to flight- or drive-relevant components, and the chance to help unveil an Electric Composites future set to shape everybody's lives.

Within EleComp, a five-year EPSRC Programme Grant spanning Imperial, Bristol and Durham, your computational focus will be building physics-informed surrogate models and process simulations within a Bayesian-optimisation loop. This loop jointly searches design and process parameters, using active learning to get maximum insight from a minimum number of costly physical builds.

You'll trace the thread from manufacturing process to defects to performance — mechanical (stiffness, damage tolerance) and electrochemical (capacity, impedance, cycle life) — across routes from partners' established hand lay-up through to more adventurous AFP and continuous-fibre 3D printing. You'll iterate continuously against mechanical/electrical testing and characterisation data: data you generate, and data partners at Bristol and Durham share, to keep your models grounded in reality. You'll start on flat and near-flat coupons, where you can iterate fast. Then you'll push into genuinely uncharted territory: curved and ultimately cylindrical geometry. You'll ask the question nobody has yet answered — where do flat-trained models hold, where do they break, and how little curved data do you actually need to adapt them? You'll finish with a validated, geometry-transferable design-to-manufacture pipeline that's never existed before.

If you want a PhD at the genuine cutting edge of where machine learning, composites manufacturing and energy storage intersect, this is it. You'll be supervised by Dr Ajit Panesar and Prof. Emile Greenhalgh, working alongside the SPC and IDEA lab teams and, more widely, with leading academics (at Chalmers and KTH besides the core EleComp team) and industrial partners — helping to shape the Electric Composites future of tomorrow.

Applications are invited to undertake a PhD programme, in partnership with Airbus, to address key challenges in ensuring adoption of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) by understanding the thermophysical and thermochemical behaviour across conditions typical of fuel systems. This research will remove barriers to the adoption of SAF, both for current and future fuels.

Project overview

The research programme will use a mixture of computational, analytical, and machine learning approaches to model the heat transfer to fuels and their physical and chemical behaviour including changes in chemistry and physical properties. The interaction between fuel chemistry and physical behaviour will be investigated. If appropriate, experimental analysis to provide validation data will be acquired as part of the PhD, although where possible validation data will be taken from industrial and openly available literature. You will gain experience in computational, analytical, and experimental approaches across mechanical and chemical engineering applied in an aerospace industry context.

You will be based in the Mechanical and Aerospace Systems research group (previously known as the Gas Turbine and Transmissions research centre) within the Faculty of Engineering and will be part of a supportive team of 50 researchers, technicians, support staff, and academics. jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Characterising the Molecular Pathology of POLG-related Liver Disease in Alpers-Huttenlocher Syndrome
jobs.description_html:
Award summary

This PhD project is focussed on investigating the mechanisms underpinning liver dysfunction in childhood POLG-related mitochondrial disease, also known as Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome.

The award covers 100% of home (UK) tuition fees and an annual stipend of approximately £21,805 per year (UKRI Rates).

Overview

POLG-related mitochondrial disease is the most common inherited mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance disorder and is caused by pathogenic variants in the POLG gene, resulting in mtDNA depletion. Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is a childhood form of POLG disease that predominantly affects the central nervous system and liver, with patients developing epilepsy, hepatic dysfunction, or both. Acute liver failure is a particularly severe manifestation that most commonly affects infants and is associated with high mortality. Despite the clinical significance of hepatic involvement, the mechanisms underlying liver vulnerability in POLG disease remain poorly understood, and there are currently no disease-modifying therapies that prevent or treat liver failure.

To investigate the mechanisms underpinning POLG-related liver dysfunction in Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome, the molecular pathology of donated post-mortem liver tissue from children and adults with POLG disease will be characterised using quantitative untargeted proteomics and immunohistochemical techniques. Using POLG patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), hepatic organoids will be generated to investigate disease mechanisms and establish a platform for therapeutic screening.

The awardee will join the internationally recognised Newcastle Mitochondrial Research Group and will be affiliated with the Translational and Clinical Research Institute at Newcastle University and the School of Medicine at the University of St Andrews. The studentship will be based at Newcastle University with the opportunity to do a research placement at the University of St Andrews.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Enhancing the Otago Exercise Programme to Preserve Bone Health in Women with Osteopenia or Osteoporosis
jobs.description_html:
Project:

Exercise can preserve bone mineral density, but high-impact or heavy-load programmes may be unsuitable or unappealing for women with osteopenia or osteoporosis, particularly where weakness, impaired balance or fear of falling are also present. This PhD will develop a more accessible alternative by enhancing the established, home-based Otago Exercise Programme. Exercise bands will provide resistance throughout each movement, while high-speed contractions will aim to increase rate of force development and skeletal loading.

The PhD candidate will complete four linked studies: an evidence review; a laboratory electromyography comparison of traditional and banded Otago exercises; a feasibility and repeatability study in adults aged over 55 years; and a 12-month clinical study comparing usual NHS care, banded Otago and high-speed banded Otago in postmenopausal women with osteopenia or osteoporosis. Bone mineral density, measured by DEXA and blood based bio-markers, will be the primary outcome, supported by measures of strength, balance, falls, fear of falling and body composition.

The PhD candidate will gain experience in exercise prescription, surface electromyography, DEXA, clinical research, patient and public involvement, and mixed research methods while working with the University of Hull, Osprey charity and the local NHS Trust.

Applicants should hold at least a 2:1 honours degree, or equivalent, in sport and exercise science, strength and conditioning, physiotherapy, rehabilitation, biomechanics, human movement science or a closely related subject. A relevant taught MSc or Masters by Research is highly desirable. Applicants should demonstrate an interest in exercise for clinical or older populations, strong communication and organisational skills, and the ability to work sensitively with participants and clinical partners. Experience of exercise delivery, electromyography, DEXA, biomechanics, clinical research, systematic reviewing or statistical analysis would be beneficial, but training will be provided. For further details, please see the University's postgraduate admissions webpage. This

How to Apply:

Applicants should submit the University's online application and a personal statement explaining their motivation for doctoral study, interest in this project, relevant skills and experience, any training needs, and their understanding of the wider significance and future direction of the research. A separate research proposal is not required.

jobs.title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD Studentship with Network Rail: Low-carbon Cements for Low-risk Rail Infrastructure Applications
jobs.description_html:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk

The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance efficiency, safety and sustainability.

The extensive use of cement and concrete by Network Rail across its UK rail infrastructure combined with the high emissions associated with their manufacture, are fuelling opportunities for lower carbon alternatives. Cement-based binders are widely deployed in lower strength and/or lower risk applications in conventional rail infrastructure including ancillary applications and low-risk exposure classes. These could include concrete for walkways and kerbs, blocks and pavers, drainage channels and cable troughs, signal and fence bases, some platform components and concrete fill; and mortars and grouts for slope and subgrade stabilisation, erosion control, repairs and surface treatments.

These assets have varying manufacturing, design and performance criteria. Current standards, e.g. BS EN 197 and FLEX 350 already include a range of binary and ternary low carbon cements and alternative binders, while other low compositions are not yet covered. Poor workability, limited durability data and lack of a clear acceptance route are barriers to uptake. Lower risk assets enable tailored binders, including those using recycled railway, and other secondary materials, to be assessed.

A subset will be investigated based on initial mapping of cementitious binders and applications, and design and performance requirements. The project will combine advanced material characterisation and mix design development, early age performance and modelling, sensor technology and accelerated and long-term mechanical and durability testing. The aim is to deliver the performance and whole-life carbon evidence needed for uptake on the rail network.

For project-specific enquiries please e-mail Professor Abir Al-Tabbaa at aa22@cam.ac.uk.

For general enquiries, please email cdtcivil-courseadmin@eng.cam.ac.uk.

jobs.title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD studentship with Network Rail: Understanding Rainfall-induced Slope Failure Risk
jobs.description_html:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk

The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance efficiency, safety and sustainability.

Network Rail manage the UK's rail assets including many embankments and cuttings and possess a large amount of data from a variety of sources on their condition and performance. Failures of these slopes have a substantial impact on the rail network in terms of both safety and economic losses from speed restrictions and an understanding of the factors influencing the risk of failure is hence critical to focus remediation work on key locations within the network.

The project will aim to understand from available databases and modelling what processes and conditions drive the hotspots of failures seen around the rail network. These factors may include local geology and hydrogeologic conditions both from natural topology and the performance of drainage systems. As many of these failures are driven by periods of high rainfall, the effects of climate change on changing risks to the network will also be investigated. The project will use Network Rail data to identify common factors amongst clusters of slope failures and will then use Centrifuge and Finite Element modelling to investigate why these factors are critical and the influence of future climate changes on risk. This understanding will then allow machine learning or AI models to be used to identify risk hotspots within the network and to focus remediation efforts on these locations.

jobs.title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD Studentship with Network Rail: Infrastructure System Management in a Changing Climate
jobs.description_html:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk

The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance efficiency, safety and sustainability.

Climate change and shifting patterns of extreme weather are impacting risk profiles of transport assets, requiring re-evaluation of investment strategies to maintain reliable services. This research will investigate how environmental and operational thresholds for key rail assets can be scientifically defined, quantified and integrated into long-term climate adaptation planning. The main aim of the study is to develop methods to identify tipping points arising from climatic stressors such as extreme heat, high-intensity rainfall, soil moisture variation, and compound weather events. This will require an interdisciplinary systems approach and data analysis to explore historical asset/network performance. The insight will then be used as a starting point for evaluating future performance. 

This project is not about advancing fundamental physics or engineering models of a specific asset type, but rather, understanding how the data available via Network Rail can be modelled to support identification of thresholds or tipping points for the railway infrastructure system. It is envisaged that the project will evaluate how threshold-based insights can enhance the timing, prioritisation and appraisal of adaptation options within existing decision frameworks used by Network Rail and national transport bodies.

For project-specific enquiries please e-mail Dr Kristen MacAskill at kam71@cam.ac.uk. For general enquiries, please email cdtcivil-courseadmin@eng.cam.ac.uk.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Microbiomes for Sustainable, Low-Input Agriculture
jobs.description_html:
Primary supervisor - Dr Myriam Charpentier

Can we harness beneficial soil microorganisms to grow productive crops with less fertiliser?

Modern agriculture relies heavily on nitrogen and phosphorus fertilisers, but their intensive use has significant economic and environmental costs. Plants naturally interact with diverse soil microorganisms such as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi that can improve nutrient acquisition, soil function and resilience. Understanding how crops recruit and interact with these beneficial microorganisms could therefore provide new opportunities for more sustainable agriculture.

Building on recent discoveries from our laboratory, the student will investigate how wheat genetics can be exploited to enhance beneficial interactions between crop roots, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and additional soil microbiome, and whether these tripartite interactions can improve crop performance under reduced-fertiliser conditions.

You will combine field experimentation, crop phenotyping, plant-microbe biology and microbiome approaches to investigate how wheat genotype and nutrient management influence beneficial microbial associations. You will assess crop performance and nutrient-use efficiency, characterise fungal and bacterial communities associated with roots, and identify microbial functions linked to improved crop performance under reduced-input conditions.

Based at the John Innes Centre, you will work within a collaborative research environment bringing together expertise in plant-microbe interactions, wheat genetics, crop physiology, field experimentation, microbiome science and microbial genomics across JIC, NIAB and the Earlham Institute.

This interdisciplinary PhD is ideal for a student interested in plant science, microbiology, crop genetics, bioinformatics or sustainable agriculture who wants to translate fundamental biological discoveries into approaches for reducing agricultural inputs while maintaining crop productivity.

This studentship offers the opportunity to undertake a 4-year PhD research project whilst enhancing professional development and research skills through a comprehensive training programme provided by the UKRI-BBSRC Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership (NRPDTP). You will join a vibrant community of world-leading researchers.

Our partners value diverse and inclusive work environments that are positive and supportive. Students are selected for admission without regard to gender, marital or civil partnership status, disability, race, nationality, ethnic origin, religion or belief, sexual orientation, age or social background.

Entry requirements

At least UK equivalence Bachelors (Honours) 2:1. English Language requirement (Faculty of Science equivalent: IELTS 6.5 overall, 6 in each category).

Mode of study
