The studentship includes payment of Home level tuition fees (directly to the University), a stipend to cover living expenses (2026/7 stipend rate: £21,805), and a Research Training Support Grant of £5,000 p.a. for each year of the studentship. This award is open to Home Fee Status applicants only.

jobs.title: Doctoral Fellowships in Maternity Disparities
jobs.description_html:
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Inequalities Challenge: Maternity Disparities Consortium (MDC) is proud to announce its doctoral fellowships competition. We are seeking the next generation of researchers to help us tackle persistent inequalities in maternity. 

The MDC brings together a UK wide collaboration of universities, NHS trusts, councils, charities, and industry partners. You can find information about our consortium members here. Our goal is to improve outcomes for women and babies before, during, and after pregnancy through inclusive, evidence-based research.

Capacity Development 

The MDC capacity development programme aims to build the next generation of maternity disparities research leaders, strengthen the workforce to deliver and sustain impact across the UK.

The Consortium focuses on growing long-term research capacity and expertise, especially within underrepresented disciplines, professions and underserved communities; inspiring and supporting the next generation of researchers with the right skills mix to work across clinical, practice and research sectors.  

The Opportunity 

We are offering up to 8 funded salaried doctorates across a range of potential projects at universities across our Consortium. We are specifically looking to grow research capacity among underrepresented disciplines such as midwives, health visitors, neonatal nurses, social care practitioners and community pharmacists.  

  • Start: June 2027 
  • Duration: Up to 3 years (Full-Time) or 4 years at 0.8WTE (Part-Time) dependent on project, please see individual project pages. 

Funding:  

  • Full salary, including national insurance and superannuation, based on your current full time equivalent (fte) salary, up to a salary of £68,000fte (100% direct costs only). 
  • Active clinician or practitioner applicants, or applicants that are registered practitioners employed in a local authority setting, can claim up to 20% clinical or practice time within the award 
  • Full PhD tuition fees, at UK home rate 
  • £5,000 contribution towards research, travel, training and consumables. 

Who is a MDC doctoral fellowship for? 

To be eligible for this scheme you should be an active clinician or practitioner or a registered practitioner based in a local authority setting. Applicants must hold a substantive contract in a clinical / local authority practice role. 

For this award, we define ‘active clinicians or practitioners’ as people who hold a contract of employment in the UK who are either: 

  • Registered UK health, public health or social care professionals  
  • Doctors or dentists registered with the General Dental Council or General Medical Council 
  • Health and care professionals (HCPs) (which includes nurses, midwives, allied health professionals, regulated clinical and practitioner psychologists, pharmacists, and healthcare scientists) registered with one of the national regulatory bodies, including the: 
    • Nursing and Midwifery Council 
    • Health and Care Professions Council 
    • General Dental Council 
    • General Medical Council 
    • General Optical Council 
    • General Osteopathic Council 
    • General Chiropractic Council 
    • General Pharmaceutical Council 
    • Pharmaceutical Society of Northern Ireland 

Fixed term contracts of employment of any duration are acceptable but honorary contracts or bank work are not.  

We define ‘registered practitioners based in local authority settings’ as people who are:  

  • Registered UK health, public health or social care professionals, registered with a national body including:  
  • Social Work England, Northern Ireland Social Care Council, Scottish Social Services Council, Social Care Wales 
  • UK Public Health Register 
  • Health and Care Professions Council 
  • Nursing and Midwifery Council 

And hold a contract of employment in the UK with either a: 

  • local authority  
  • provider of local authority commissioned services, or a 
  • non-profit organisation, such as a charity that provides services on behalf of a local authority, or that otherwise supports a local authority in meeting its objectives 
  • fixed term contracts of employment of any duration are acceptable but honorary contracts or bank work are not 
  • non-profit organisation, which provide services on behalf of a local authority, or that otherwise supports a local authority, do not need to be commissioned or funded by that local authority, but the support does need to be co-designed with, or at the very least acknowledged and signposted by, the local authority or authorities in question 

We welcome applications from individuals passionate about maternal health equity and particularly from areas that are underrepresented in maternity disparities research. We are committed to building a supportive, inclusive, and caring research community. We particularly encourage applications from: 

  • People from underrepresented ethnic backgrounds. 
  • People with disabilities, neurodivergent conditions, and long-term health requirements 
  • Candidates of all genders, ages, and beliefs. 

Each project has a supervisor, theme lead and capacity development lead listed on the project page. We encourage you to contact them to ensure the project is a right fit for you. 

Frequently asked questions 

I am a registered practitioner, but I currently work in higher education and do not have active employment in practice. Am I eligible?

This scheme is specifically for active clinicians, practitioners, or registered practitioners based in a local authority setting. Applicants must hold a substantive contract in a clinical / local authority practice role. 

Doctoral Fellowships in Maternity Disparities

For more information, please click on the 'Apply' button above, Please note, you may apply for a maximum of two projects.

Accessibility & Support 

We want you to perform at your best. You may contact individual supervisors when asking for more details about the projects and your suitability for the project. General enquiries about the recruitment process and MDC, including if you require any reasonable adjustments for the application process or the interview (such as alternative formats, extra time, or specific technological needs), please contact nihr.mdc.capacitydevelopment@newcastle.ac.uk.  

NIHR and DHSC have a duty as a public body to promote equality of opportunity.  We will contact all applicants throughout the application period with an Equality Monitoring Form. Monitoring ensures that all applications to NIHR MDC Programmes are treated equally in terms of gender, ethnicity and/or disability. Information will be anonymised and stored separately from your application, only be used for the purpose of monitoring equal opportunities and be kept securely and in confidence. 

Closing Date: 5pm 11th January 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship Archaeobotany of Zambezi Valley
jobs.description_html:
We invite applications for a 3-year funded PhD studentship starting in April 2027 under the co-supervision of Dr Alexander Weide and Professor Stephanie Wynne-Jones as part of the ZAMBEZI project. This PhD studentship is funded as part of an ERC Advanced Grant project. 

Zambezian Entanglements in the South-Central African Iron Age (ZAMBEZI) is a 5-year project based on fieldwork in Zambia and Zimbabwe. The project centres on renewed excavations at the site of Ingombe Ilede, Zambia, and exploration of the broader region, including further sites in Zambia and northern Zimbabwe. As such, ZAMBEZI will be generating new data for some key sites through which the archaeology of this region is known and offers the opportunity to rethink second-millennium lifeways and connections in this place. The project is a collaboration with the National Museum of Zambia. 

We are looking for a highly motivated applicant to join the project. The selected applicant will be jointly co-supervised by the PI of the project, Professor Stephanie Wynne-Jones, and Dr Alexander Weide, with additional input from other members of the Department and McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, and external researchers depending on training needs. 

The successful applicant's research will focus on plant use, agricultural practice and landscape change, using data from flotation of material from excavations at Ingombe Ilede and neighbouring sites.

Applicants must meet the requirement for a PhD in Archaeology (see details here: https://www.postgraduate.study.cam.ac.uk/courses/directory/aaarpdarc) and be familiar with the archaeology of south-central Africa. 

The successful applicant will become part of the ZAMBEZI project and be based at the McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, University of Cambridge, which also hosts a large community of researchers working on a wide range of global archaeology and heritage. 

The studentship will provide a stipend covering maintenance and fee costs. See: https://www.postgraduate.study.cam.ac.uk/finance where a successful applicant is not a citizen of the UK, immigration health surcharge and visa fees will be covered. Additionally, fieldwork costs and selected conference attendance, as well as maintenance payments for the duration of parental leave are all covered.

How to make an application

Applications should be submitted for the PhD in Archaeology via the Applicant Portal (via the above 'Apply' button). Dr Alexander Weide and Professor Stephanie Wynne-Jones should be identified as your preferred supervisors and you must state that you are applying for the ZAMBEZI project in the "proposed title" section. jobs.title: PhD Studentship Zooarchaeology Later Pastoralism
jobs.description_html:
We invite applications for a 3-year funded PhD studentship starting in October 2027 under the co-supervision of Professor Paul Lane and Dr Lizzie Wright, as part of the Landscape Historical Ecology and Archaeology of Ancient Pastoral Societies in Kenya (LHEAAPS) project. This PhD studentship is funded by a UKRI Frontier Research Grant.

The LHEAAPS project aims to investigate the origins and evolution of Pastoral Iron Age societies in north-central Kenya through integrated analysis of patterns of human and livestock mobility, dietary practices, exchange networks, and responses to periods of known drought and increased rainfall over the last c. 1800 years. Through the innovative use of diverse bioarchaeological, archaeological and zooarchaeological approaches, the PhD project is intended to contribute to the reconstruction of diets, animal economies and herd management strategies (including seasonal and longer-term mobility of livestock) via combined zooarchaeology and isotopic analyses. The study will contribute to wider syntheses and analyses aimed at demonstrating the value of understanding these pastoralist pasts as paths for planning more sustainable futures for the region’s contemporary pastoralist societies. In doing so, the project aspires to respond to calls to build long-term sustainability and resilience into social-ecological systems in sub-Saharan Africa through provision of deep histories of human-environment interactions and holistic approaches to the reconstruction of past and present human responses to climate-induced socioecological vulnerability.

We are looking for a highly motivated student to join the project. The selected student will be jointly co-supervised by the PI of the project (Professor Paul Lane, University of Cambridge) and Dr Lizzie Wright (Assistant Professor in Zooarchaeology), with additional input from other members of the Department and McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, and external researchers depending on training needs.

The successful applicant’s research will focus on reconstruction of the animal economies and herd management strategies associated with Pastoral Iron Age sites across north-central Kenya, assessing changes and continuities over time in terms of dietary breadth, mobility strategies and related factors. In order to do this a combination of zooarchaeological (analysis of species composition, body part representation, mortality, pathological and metric data), and isotopic analyses will be employed.

Candidates must meet the requirement for a PhD application in archaeology (https://www.graduate.study.cam.ac.uk/courses/directory/hsarpdarc/requirements), and have (or expect to obtain by July 2027) an MA, MSc or MPhil degree in archaeology, archaeological science or a cognate discipline, with evidence of a sound grounding in and specialist knowledge of zooarchaeology. Ideally, applicants will have knowledge of East African Holocene archaeology and/or on the archaeology of pastoralist economies, and practical field experience in researching the archaeology of pastoralism.

For further details and how to apply please click the 'Apply' button above.

For informal enquiries, please contact Professor Paul Lane and Dr Lizzie Wright via email: pjl29@cam.ac.uk and eew39@cam.ac.uk

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Sustainable Aviation Fuel Thermochemical Modelling
jobs.description_html:
Sustainable aviation fuel thermochemical modelling

Applications are invited to undertake a PhD programme, in partnership with Airbus, to address key challenges in ensuring adoption of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) by understanding the thermophysical and thermochemical behaviour across conditions typical of fuel systems. This research will remove barriers to the adoption of SAF, both for current and future fuels. 

Project overview

The research programme will use a mixture of computational, analytical, and machine learning approaches to model the heat transfer to fuels and their physical and chemical behaviour including changes in chemistry and physical properties. The interaction between fuel chemistry and physical behaviour will be investigated. If appropriate, experimental analysis to provide validation data will be acquired as part of the PhD, although where possible validation data will be taken from industrial and openly available literature. You will gain experience in computational, analytical, and experimental approaches across mechanical and chemical engineering applied in an aerospace industry context.

You will be based in the Mechanical and Aerospace Systems research group (previously known as the Gas Turbine and Transmissions research centre) within the Faculty of Engineering and will be part of a supportive team of 50 researchers, technicians, support staff, and academics. The group has a dynamic research culture with a programme of seminars, writing, and social events with a research office hub providing a quiet working environment with social and meeting spaces.

You would be expected to spend part of the PhD period based in Bristol at the Airbus site and will receive supervision support and training from both the university and Airbus. This research will support the path to net zero flights and there may be opportunities to become involved in practical aspects of fuel system design and testing during the PhD.

Candidate requirements 

We are looking for an enthusiastic and self-motivated person with a rigorous approach to research.

  • You should have or be expected to gain a high 2:1, preferably a 1st class honours degree in chemical, mechanical or aerospace engineering or a chemistry or computer science related degree
  • A good knowledge and/or experience in heat transfer is essential, as is the ability to work well in a team
  • Prior experience in the areas of computational fluid dynamics, chemistry, machine learning, or computational heat transfer will be an advantage.

Eligibility and funding

Due to funding restrictions this studentship is only available to UK (home fees) citizens.

The PhD studentship will cover fees and tax-free stipend of £24,000 p.a. for four years.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in the Landscape Archaeology of East African Montane Systems
jobs.description_html:
We invite applications for a 3-year funded PhD studentship starting in October 2027 under the co-supervision of Professor Paul Lane and Dr Stefania Merlo, as part of the AFRI-CAN project. This PhD studentship is funded by ERC Synergy grant No. 101224449.

The AFRI-CAN project (– Lead PI Professor Rob Marchant, University of York) explores the interlinked interactions of human systems and mountain ecosystems understood as mountain socioecological systems by combining state-of-the-art modelling, interdisciplinary insights and valuation assessments to co-produce pathways for sustainable mountain futures. Focussed on six contrasting East African mountain settings, the AFRI-CAN project aims to investigate how communities interact with nature, how ecosystems evolve, and which pathways could support sustainable and resilient mountain futures.

We are looking for a highly motivated applicant to join the project and contribute to Work Package 1. The selected applicant will be co-supervised by Professor Paul Lane and Dr Stefania Merlo with additional input from other members of the Department and McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, and external researchers that are part of the AFRI-CAN project, in particular Dr Daryl Stump, at the University of York.

The successful applicant’s research will focus on developing detailed historical land-use and land cover map of landscape change across the mountain study sites over the past 6,000 years through the integration of archaeobotanical, faunal and material culture data and historical maps with a particular focus on forestry and forest management. The doctoral student will play a central role in collating and assessing existing historical and archaeological records from the MAEASaM (Mapping Africa’s Endangered Archaeological Sites and Monuments) project and other data sets (e.g. the Pandora repositories), as well as conducting supplementary targeted archaeological fieldwork relating to land use activities across the target study sites and synthesising detailed archaeobotanical, faunal and material culture data relevant to the sites. This will include analysing historical maps, aerial photographs and remote sensing and integrated historical data across the study sites to develop finer-resolution maps of land-use and landcover for the past 150 years.

Applicants must meet the requirement for a PhD in Archaeology (see details here: https://www.postgraduate.study.cam.ac.uk/courses/directory/aaarpdarc), have (or expect to obtain by July 2027) an MA, MSc or MPhil degree in a relevant discipline and possess the following additional skills:

  • Expertise in landscape archaeology, historical geography or landscape history preferably in an African context (Essential)
  • Familiarity or experience in the using databases and geospatial analysis and mapping (Essential)
  • Experience with using historical maps and remote sensing imagery to identify archaeological sites (Essential) and create Land Use Land Cover maps (Desirable)
  • Experience with synthesising archaeological and historical datasets (Desirable)
  • Experience in conducting archaeological field surveys (Desirable), ideally in an African setting

For further details and how to apply please click the 'Apply' button above.

For further information and informal enquiries, please contact via email either Professor Paul Lane (pjl29@cam.ac.uk) and/or Dr Stefania Merlo (sm399@cam.ac.uk)

jobs.institution: Trinity College Dublin, The University of Dublin

The Trinity Centre for Asian Studies (TCAS) invites applications for a fully funded 4 year doctoral research position in Southeast Asian Studies to begin September 1, 2027. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Modelling and Mitigating the Impacts of Climate Change in Historic Buildings
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Jack Panter

The southern/eastern UK climate is showing a rapid and significant increase in the prevalence, duration, and severity of hot, dry weather. One surprising impact is on our historic houses and cultural heritage: in the National Trust’s portfolio (a key example being Blickling Estate, Norfolk), interior temperatures

are placing significant heat-stress on staff and visitors, leading to site closures, and low humidity is degrading their collections. In response, Blickling Estate aims to become a pioneer in experimentally analysing and computationally modelling the climate impact on internal temperature and humidity, and developing new cooling and humidification interventions. A large research gap is ripe for exploring: while modelling buildings in urban environments is experiencing significant research interest, similar modelling in a historical context is almost wholly unexplored. Thus, this is a unique challenge at the intersection of engineering, climate science, culture, and health.

You will join UEA’s Thermofluids Laboratory, and use state-of-the-art experimental and computational techniques to understand, model, and propose solutions to the heat and humidity challenges at Blickling Estate. This project will also involve time on-site at Blickling gathering experimental data and testing solutions. The project has the following aims:

  • Develop the first thermo-fluid digital twin of Blickling Hall to model how the local geography and climate, air flows, materials, and building layout influence internal temperatures and humidity; explain which factors impact internal conditions; and predict response to future weather/climate events.
  • In collaboration with Blickling Estate, develop and explore a range of interventions aimed at cooling the building and maintaining appropriate humidity.
  • Perform laboratory and on-site experimental testing of trial interventions, supported by the thermo-fluid model, to ultimately understand and explain efficacy.

Ultimately, the successful outcomes of this project will likely lead to national impact on the future of UK buildings heritage in the face of climate change.

Entry Requirements

The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 bachelor's degree in Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, Physics, Applied Physics, Applied Mathematics, Computer Science, Chemistry, or Environmental Science.

jobs.title: AstraZeneca funded Non-clinical PhD Studentship (Fixed Term) in Improved 2A Peptides for Co-translational Separation of a Polyprotein
jobs.description_html:
Applications are invited for a 4-year PhD studentship starting on 1 October 2027 and based in the Department of Pathology, University of Cambridge, and the AstraZeneca Discovery Centre at Cambridge. The student will be working on a collaborative project jointly supervised by Prof. Andrew Firth at the University of Cambridge and Dr Giovanni Ciotta at AstraZeneca and will have the opportunity to work across the two sites. The project focuses on manipulating peptide-bond skipping sequences to aid protein engineering.

2A peptides mediate co-translational separation of a polyprotein via a mechanism known as "ribosome skipping" or "StopGo". These ~20 amino acid peptides adopt an unusual conformation within the translating ribosome that prevents peptide bond formation at a specific site but instead promotes release of the nascent peptide followed by continuation of translation. These sequences have proved to be exceptionally useful in biotechnology because they allow the introduction of all components of a pathway or multi-subunit complex in a single step, with stable stoichiometric co-expression from a single promoter. However, 2A peptides have some caveats - including ribosome drop-off, ribosome pausing/stalling, and some amount of separation failure - which constrain their functional utility. We have identified new classes of 2A sequences, some of which have improved properties compared to traditional 2A peptides. This PhD project will contribute to our work investigating these new 2A sequences and optimising them for biotechnological applications.

The UCam team has expertise in molecular biology including ribosome profiling, ribosome structure and function, cell biology, cryo-electron microscopy, and bioinformatics. The AZ team has expertise in cell therapy, CRISPR/Cas9 technologies, and viral vectors. The PhD project will focus on molecular biology techniques but there will also be opportunity for bioinformatic skill development and there may be scope to obtain structural biology experience. At the AstraZeneca site, the student will focus on implementing optimised sequences in specific biotechnological applications, e.g. in cell therapy.

For full details and application process please click the 'Apply' button above.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The Long, the Short and the Sticky: Finding the Mass of Natural Polymers by NMR
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Matthew Wallace(opens in a new window)

Polymers extracted from natural sources are ubiquitous in modern life, from texturing agents in foods to cell encapsulants in biomedicine. In addition to the structure and sequence of the monomers, the molecular mass i.e. chain length of polymers is crucial in determining their performance in these applications. However, mass determination of natural polymers is extremely difficult due to the tendency of the chains to self-associate and form gels, even at low concentrations. Common techniques such as size-exclusion chromatography assume polymer molecules behave as non-associating spheres. However, aggregation can severely distort measurements and irreversibly contaminate expensive equipment. Our inability to determine polymer molecular mass severely hinders our ability to use natural polymers for targeted applications, where extraction and processing steps must be carefully designed to obtain the correct mass fractions and properties.

In this project, you will develop and apply advanced nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) methods to determine the chain length and aggregation state of a range of natural polymers, including those extracted from seaweed by our industrial partner. Through advanced experimental and pulse sequence design, in collaboration with Dr Rob Evans (UoManchester), you will develop first-of-their-kind models linking the Brownian motion of polymers with their macroscopic diffusion along concentration gradients at high dilution. You will thus create a unique toolset for the self-consistent determination of the overall mass distribution that could be extended to other aggregation-prone macromolecular systems such as synthetic nanoparticles for cancer therapy. Your work will provide a turning point in our ability to characterise macromolecular sizes by NMR, overcoming critical limitations of chromatographic approaches and current NMR methods that consider Brownian motion (self-diffusion) alone.

Training: You will develop a diverse and highly competitive skillset spanning NMR spectroscopy, mathematical modelling, data analysis and complementary analytical techniques including dynamic light scattering and chromatography.

Entry requirements: The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 Bachelor's degree in Chemistry, Pharmacy, Pharmacology, Physics, or a related discipline.

Mode of study: Full time

Start date: 1 October 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Historical Genomics of the Declining Red Squirrel in Britain
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Anders Bergström

The red squirrel in Britain is one of the most iconic examples of a declining population. It has suffered greatly since the introduction of the invasive grey squirrel in the late 1800s, but even before then it was struggling due to hunting and deforestation. However, already since the late 1700s, people have tried to counter the decline by bringing in new red squirrels from continental Europe. How all these past processes have affected the genetic make-up, fitness and ancestry of British squirrels is poorly understood.

This project will study the rollercoaster history of the red squirrel in Britain using historical DNA. By tracing the genetics of the red squirrel over the past few hundred years, the project has two goals:

1) To provide general insights into the genetics of population decline and rescue, broadly applicable across organisms.

2) To reconstruct the specific history of the widely cherished red squirrel, to potentially help future efforts to conserve it.

The project will use historical DNA techniques to sequence genomes from squirrels in museum collections, to directly analyse how genetic diversity, inbreeding and genetic load has changed over time, and evaluate the effects that the many translocations had on populations. The project will also address how much native British squirrel ancestry persists today, to test whether the many introductions has led to a complete loss of native ancestry (‘genetic swamping’).

The student will receive broad training in molecular biology, historical DNA, genomics, bioinformatics and population genetics. The student will take part in journal clubs and departmental seminars, present their work at conferences, and develop skills in critical thinking and science communication.

The ideal candidate will have a background in a biological science (e.g. genetics, molecular biology, zoology, evolution, ancient DNA), and have strong interests in genomics, wet-lab work, data analysis, and evolution.

Entry Requirements: The minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 Bachelor's degree in Biology, Genetics, Zoology, Ecology, Biochemistry, or Archaeology.

Mode of study: Full time

Start date: 1st October 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Dynamics Driving Photoswitchable Molecules using Laser Spectroscopy
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. James Bull

A PhD position is available in laser spectroscopy at the University of East Anglia, supervised by Assoc. Prof. James Bull and supported by an EPSRC grant. The project will investigate the excited- and ground-state dynamics of molecular photoswitches, which undergo light-driven structural changes with applications in photomolecular motors, smart materials, and photopharmacology.

The research will examine how molecular structure and environment control photoisomerisation, excited-state relaxation and photochemical efficiency. These dynamics ultimately define light-driven molecular function. Experiments will be conducted in both the gas phase and condensed phase, combining photoisomerisation action (PISA) spectroscopy, time-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy, with condensed-phase ultrafast spectroscopies. Comparing the dynamics in isolated (gas phase) molecules with those in solution will reveal how solvent polarity, hydrogen bonding and viscosity influence excited-state lifetimes, relaxation pathways, branching ratios and photoisomerisation quantum yields.

The project will use custom-built vacuum instrumentation and advanced ultrafast laser systems to characterise molecular isomers, probe short-lived intermediates and uncover the mechanisms underlying photoswitching. Many of the experimental capabilities in our laboratory are unique worldwide, providing opportunities to study reactive species and photochemical processes that are difficult to access using conventional techniques. The ultimate aim is to establish structure-dynamics relationships that guide the rational design of more efficient and functional molecular photoswitches.

The successful candidate will receive comprehensive training in laser spectroscopy, ultrafast experimental techniques, vacuum instrumentation and data analysis, working alongside experienced rearchers.

Further details are available at www.eigenket.org (opens in a new window). Queries and further discussion on the project is welcome.

Entry requirements: A 2:1 or 1st Bachelor's degree in Chemistry or Physics.

Mode of study: Full Time

Start date: 1st October 2027

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Quantum-Resilient Security for Safety-Critical Vehicular Systems
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr Hassan Malik

The rapid growth of connected and autonomous vehicular systems is transforming modern transport infrastructure. However, advances in quantum computing are expected to undermine the security of current cryptographic methods. This creates a pressing need for robust and future-proof security solutions for safety-critical, real-time vehicular communication systems.

This PhD project aims to develop quantum-resilient security approaches for connected vehicular systems. The research will investigate the suitability of post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) techniques for dynamic and resource-constrained vehicular communication infrastructures operating within emerging 6G-enabled networks. A key focus will be on understanding the trade-offs between security strength, computational overhead, and communication latency in time-sensitive environments.

The project will combine system modelling, simulation, and algorithmic implementation to evaluate PQC schemes under realistic vehicular conditions. Beyond performance analysis, the research will explore adaptive and lightweight strategies to enable efficient key management and secure communication in highly dynamic settings. It will also investigate optimisation techniques for resource-constrained platforms and identify practical design principles for integrating quantum-resilient security into deployable vehicular systems.

The expected outcomes include novel approaches and frameworks for deploying efficient, low-latency, and scalable security mechanisms tailored to vehicular applications. The research will support the secure operation of autonomous transport systems and strengthen the resilience of vehicular communication networks.

The broader societal impact lies in improving the safety, reliability, and trustworthiness of connected transport systems. By enhancing the resilience of vehicular communication, the project contributes to safer mobility and reduced vulnerability to cyber threats.

The student will gain interdisciplinary expertise in cybersecurity, networked systems, and applied cryptography, with opportunities for collaboration with academic and industry partners.

Entry Requirements

A minimum of a 2:1 honour degree (or international equivalent) in a relevant discipline. Candidates should have a strong background in programming and/or networking. Prior knowledge of cybersecurity or cryptography is desirable but not essential.

Mode of Study

Full time

Start Date

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Clean and Safe: Developing Antimicrobial Formulations for Food Preservation and Hygiene
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Yan Fen Lee(opens in a new window)

Foodborne pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes can be present in up to 12% of raw fish, posing serious food safety risks, including listeriosis, which can be life-threatening if left untreated. Listeria is particularly difficult to control because it can grow at refrigeration temperatures and form biofilms that persist on equipment and surfaces in food processing plants, protecting it from desiccation, heat, and standard cleaning and disinfection agents.

This exciting PhD project aims to design and optimize a commercial product to reduce microbial contamination in the seafood industry. Supervised by Dr Yan Fen Lee (UEA) and Dr Matthew Gilmour (Quadram Institute), you will use natural, food-safe ingredients to formulate a multipurpose antimicrobial disinfectant for use within seafood processing plants to control Listeria and other microbes. You will also incorporate the disinfectant into ice blocks/flakes to control microbial growth during shipping and storage. The project will make a significant real-world contribution towards minimising seafood spoilage, food safety risks and expensive wastage, and supporting a more sustainable and resilient seafood industry.

You will have opportunities to train and work in different research laboratories at UEA and the Quadram Institute, and will gain practical experience and highly transferable skills in areas such as microbiology, formulation science, antimicrobial resistance, and genome sequencing. There will also be opportunities to gain experience in the commercial aspects of research translation at Norwich Research Park. Training in scientific writing, communication, and career development will be supported through local and international conferences, seminars, group research discussions, and institutional training programmes.

Motivated, self-starting candidates with a background in (micro)biology, applied chemistry or a related discipline are welcome to contact Dr Yan Fen Lee (yan-fen.lee@uea.ac.uk) for more information.

Entry requirements: A 2:1 Bachelor's degree in Biological sciences, microbiology, chemistry, biotechnology, biochemistry, or food science.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Digital Twins for waste reduction in Industry 5.0
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor: Dr. Mohsin Raza

Reducing industrial waste is a key challenge in achieving sustainable manufacturing and advancing the vision of Industry 5.0. Manufacturing processes can generate significant waste through material inefficiencies, defective products, equipment failures, excessive energy consumption, and suboptimal production planning. Digital twins, integrated with artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and advanced data analytics, offer opportunities to monitor manufacturing operations, identify sources of waste, and support proactive, data-driven interventions.

This PhD project will investigate the development of intelligent digital twin frameworks to predict, monitor, and reduce waste in manufacturing processes. The research will explore how near real-time data from industrial sensors, machinery, and production systems can be integrated into digital twins to identify 2inefficiencies, detect anomalies and predict product defects, to optimise the use of raw materials and reduce waste. AI and machine learning techniques will be investigated to support waste prediction androot-cause analysis.

The project will explore simulation-based approaches that enable manufacturers to evaluate alternative production scenarios and assess their potential impact on waste generation before implementing changes in real-world environments. Relevant sustainability indicators may be incorporated to measure improvements in material utilisation and overall waste reduction. The research will further investigate key metrics to understand waste patterns and make informed operational decisions.

The successful candidate will contribute to innovative research addressing industrial waste and environmental sustainability. The project aims to develop intelligent digital twin solutions that help manufacturers minimise waste, improve resource efficiency, in line with Industry 5.0. The project will offer opportunities to develop innovative digital twin solutions, publish research in leading academic venues, and explore practical applications.

The standard minimum entry requirement is a 2:1 bachelor's degree.

Bocconi University invites applicants for 8 fully funded PhD positions within the Legal Studies doctoral program. Fellowships amount to € 27,000 gross per year for three years. Students with fellowship are exempt from the payment of tuition fees for the duration of the three-year program. 

The International and European Law curriculum seeks to foster world-class research on any topic within the two broad subject areas of international law and European law. Potential fields of interest include, but are not limited to, general public international law, international trade law, international investment law, international cultural heritage law, international criminal law, private international law, European economic law, European trade law, European internal market law, European external relations law, European Citizenship, comparative and European constitutional law, EU governance, EU fundamental rights, and European social law, privacy and media law. Interested students will become part of  the Bocconi European Studies Lab (BLEST - https://www.blest.unibocconi.eu/ ), a center for interdisciplinary research in the field of European matters, and might co-operate with the Institute for European Policy Making (IEP, https://iep.unibocconi.eu/).  

The Business and Social Law curriculum aims to promote excellence in study of business law with an approach combining an interdisciplinary perspective, an international orientation and the analysis of the specific fields of the law covered by the program (e.g. corporation, securities, competition, commercial contracts, bankruptcy, IPRs, labor law, white collar crime). The study of law and economics and social sciences complements the study of business law. 

Bocconi University is part of CIVICA, the European University of Social Sciences (civica.eu), a network of 10 European universities (Science Po, European University Institute, Hertie School, London School of Economics and Political Science, Stockholm School of Economics, Central European University, and SNSPA School of Governance, National University of Political Studies and Public Administration, SGH Warsaw School of Economics). Beside the courses offered by the Bocconi PhD in Legal Studies Program, students can choose from a rich portfolio of courses offered by our partners. PhD students are encouraged to take part in exchanges and activities (including targeted summer and winter schools) within the CIVICA network. Furthermore, Bocconi has several exchange programs with partners outside the CIVICA network. 

During their second and third years, students are expected to actively engage in department life, with opportunities to serve as Teaching Assistants where available. 

Students are encouraged to network with PhD students from other departments and universities and with speakers at our guest seminar series and other events. 

The program aims to create a vibrant community of young researchers fully integrated into the life of the Department and in this way to contribute to forming the next generation of research leaders. Successful applicants will spend the first part of the program at Bocconi following a set of tailored courses on legal and interdisciplinary research methodologies and specialized seminars on selected topics. Students are subsequently encouraged to spend a period abroad as visiting researchers at foreign universities, taking full advantage of the opportunities offered by the CIVICA network and by the other partner institutions in international research centers or international organizations. The PhD in Statistics and Machine Learning at Bocconi University is a rigorous, internationally oriented four-year doctoral program taught in English, the working language of Bocconi's international research community. It provides in-depth training in modern Statistics and Machine Learning, with strong foundations in probability and an emphasis on integrating theory, statistical modeling, and computation. 

The program features two years of structured coursework, following the model of leading US PhD programs. The first year provides rigorous foundational training in Statistics, Probability, and Machine Learning, and concludes with the Summer School in Advanced Statistics and Probability. The second year offers specialized, research-oriented courses focusing on advanced topics and recent developments in the field. Alongside this coursework, students begin working on original research problems, develop their research interests, and identify an advisor. Hours: full time

Closes: 27 November 2026

Are you planning to start an Accounting and Finance PhD in October 2027? Don’t miss the opportunity to apply for one of the University of Liverpool Management School’s 4-year Graduate Teaching Fellowships (GTF).

Receiving one of our GTF gives you the funds to launch your academic career, while you gain valuable teaching training and experience to become a rounded scholar:

  • £21,805 annual maintenance grant* (for four years)
  • Full coverage of PhD programme fees (for four years)
  • HE teacher training and practice.

This means that as well as pursuing your PhD research, you’ll also be involved in a fixed number of teaching hours during your time with us.

In year one, alongside your specific PhD research modules, you’ll complete a short teacher training programme by the University of Liverpool.

As well as gaining a formal HE teaching qualification, you’ll learn key pedagogical skills for the academic job market, primarily through shadowing mentored classroom involvement.

During the remainder of your PhD, you’ll have the opportunity to put your research skills into practice while completing your doctoral research thesis.

Who is this for?

These studentships are open to full-time PhD students worldwide.

You’ll need a UK master’s degree, or international equivalent, in accounting and finance or a related discipline, preferably at merit or above, plus demonstrable quantitative and programming skills.

How to apply

Before formally applying, you must express your interest in a GTF position by completing this form before Friday 27 November 2026 at 5pm (UK time), an submit a strong research proposal in areas including, but not limited to:

  • Asset pricing and investment
    • Empirical asset pricing and performance evaluation
    • Investment technology, ethics and strategy
    • Equity and other asset classes
    • Financial econometrics and machine learning.
  • Corporate finance and accounting
    • Corporate governance and shareholder value
    • Corporate finance, networks and insider trading
    • Market-based accounting research and corporate transparency
    • Sustainability, corporate social responsibility (CSR) and environmental, social and governance (ESG).
  • International financial markets and the macroeconomy
    • Sovereign debt and international monetary policy
    • Time series analysis of macro and financial indicators
    • Impact of social media on financial markets.
  • Financial technology (FinTech)
    • Payment technologies and the future of money
    • Explainable artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services
    • Integration of FinTech and big data in financial markets and sustainable finance.

You’ll also need to submit:

  • A personal statement
  • A copy of your highest degree transcript
  • A curriculum vitae (CV).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Fatigue Failure of Target Graphite
jobs.description_html:
Research Studentship in Graphite Composite Materials for High-Power Neutrino Targets

Project title: Fatigue Failure of Target Graphite

3.5-year DPhil studentship 

Project title: Fatigue Failure of Target Graphite

Supervisors: Prof Dong (Lilly) Liu (Oxford), Dr Kavin Ammigan (Fermilab)

The Department of Engineering Science at the University of Oxford invites applications for a fully funded D.Phil. project investigating fatigue failure and degradation mechanisms in graphite materials used as proton-beam targets for next-generation neutrino facilities. The project is supported by Oxford and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab) and is closely linked to international neutrino programmes including DUNE. The research will develop new fatigue-testing methodologies for target graphite, investigate crack initiation and propagation under cyclic loading, and characterise the relationships between microstructure, thermal properties, irradiation damage and mechanical performance. Experimental work will involve advanced characterisation techniques including X-ray tomography, FIB-SEM tomography, Raman spectroscopy, thermal conductivity measurements, high-temperature mechanical testing, ion irradiation, and synchrotron experiments at Diamond Light Source. This project will work closely with Dr. Chris Densham's group at Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) to support targets design.

Eligibility

This studentship is funded jointly by the Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory and is open to all students. The award covers Home tuition fees and a full stipend.

Award Value

Course fees are covered at the Home rate. The stipend (tax-free maintenance grant) is c. £21,805 for the first year, and at least this amount for a further two and a half years.

Candidate Requirements

Prospective candidates will be judged according to how well they meet the following criteria:

  • A first-class or strong upper second-class degree (or equivalent) in Engineering, Materials Science, Physics, Mechanical Engineering, Nuclear Engineering or a closely related discipline.
  • Strong interest in materials behaviour under extreme environments and experimental research.
  • Excellent written and spoken English communication skills.
  • Ability to work effectively within an international multidisciplinary collaboration.

The following skills are desirable but not essential:

  • Experience in mechanical testing, fracture mechanics or fatigue analysis.
  • Experience with materials characterisation techniques.
  • Data analysis and scientific programming (e.g. Python, MATLAB). 
  • Interest in particle accelerator, nuclear or energy applications.

Application Procedure

Informal enquiries are encouraged and should be addressed to Prof Dong (Lilly) Liu (dong.liu@eng.ox.ac.uk).

Candidates must submit a graduate application and satisfy the University of Oxford admission requirements for the DPhil in Engineering Science.

Please quote 27ENGMM_DL in all correspondence and in your graduate application.

jobs.description_html:
This is a project focused on how AI will provide a seamless service to mobile users of tomorrow. It is expected the student will have a background in AI with a curiosity on wireless networking.

Machine learning that occurs over a distributed network is attractive to reduce latency, ensure data and compute is sovereignly hosted, and utilise available edge computation resources. There are many challenges when the demand is spatially and temporally mobile, and when the inference is computationally heavy. This PhD studentship will advance the research in AI on Radio Access Networks (AI-on-RAN) by exploring how to optimise distributed and mobile inference of large language models by adapting how tokens, memory, and network bandwidth is used in real time.

The outcomes are expected to shape how future AI algorithms are designed, as well as how future computation and communication resources are invested in 6G telecommunication networks.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: SCALE-Decode: Unlocking Growth Workflows in UK SMEs
jobs.description_html:
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) underpin UK employment and innovation, yet many struggle to turn early success into sustainable growth. Rising demand can expose informal routines, disconnected systems, founder dependence and employee overload. Managers may see delayed delivery or lost sales without understanding how constraints travel across the firm. Research and policy treat issues separately, while generic AI lacks context. SCALE-Decode examines how responsible AI can reveal growth workflows, diagnose bottlenecks, and build an AI system to support managerial actions.

Work Package 1 (months 1-12) will map and explain SME scale-up workflows. Manager and employee interviews, walkthroughs, task diaries, process documents and privacy-preserving event logs, where suitable, will be integrated through qualitative analysis, Business Process Model and Notation and process mining. Cross-case comparison will distinguish symptoms, including delay and rework, from underlying causes such as centralised approvals, capability gaps and poor information transfer. Stakeholder validation will refine three deliverables: a Scale-up Workflow Framework, anonymised maps and a bottleneck taxonomy. Together, they will help firms and advisers trace local constraints across an organisation and strengthen workflow-centred scaling theory through credible evidence.

Work Package 2 (months 10-24) will build SCALE-Decode, a secure AI system to help SMEs scale by reconstructing workflows, diagnosing scaling bottlenecks and generating feasible action plans. A knowledge graph will connect activities, dependencies, organisational conditions, evidence and interventions. Four AI components will gather information, produce editable maps, diagnose constraints, and generate and critique actions. Each recommendation will identify its evidence, prerequisites, expected benefit, cost, effort, risk and uncertainty. Managers will correct maps and approve recommendations. Technical, adversarial, usability and unseen-case testing will assess fidelity, traceability, feasibility and unsupported claims. Deliverables comprise a validated prototype, documentation and responsible-use guidance.

Work Package 3 (months 22-36) will evaluate feasibility, usefulness and implementation in SMEs. A longitudinal field study will compare AI-assisted diagnosis with existing approaches and track workflow understanding, decision quality, action completion and selected operational indicators. Usage records, surveys and interviews will show why recommendations Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council Doctoral Landscape Award are accepted, adapted or rejected and whether outcomes vary with workflow maturity, digital readiness or owner-manager dependence. Case studies will examine employee capability and wellbeing, recognising that gains must not depend on work intensification. Deliverables will include an evaluation dataset, comparative findings and implementation evidence, establishing where SCALE-Decode adds value, where human expertise remains essential and which conditions support responsible adoption.

Work Package 4 (months 36-42) will integrate findings and translate them for research and practice. Outputs will include academic papers, reusable workflow passports, sector templates, checklists, an adviser toolkit, policy brief and public-engagement materials. Practitioner workshops will refine resources and inform future development. This package will convert evidence into usable guidance for SMEs, advisers, growth hubs, policymakers and technology providers.

Funded by: EPSRC Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - From Fan to Father: Exploring the Role of Football Fan Communities in Supporting New Fatherhood
jobs.description_html:
We are pleased to announce the opportunity for a funded PhD project within the Faculty of Business and Law. The project will explore the role of football fan communities in supporting new fathers as they start their fatherhood journey. While many men aspire to greater involvement in childcare, they often feel excluded from traditional parenting support, which is frequently oriented towards mothers. The project will explore whether football fan communities, which provide strong social bonds and a sense of belonging for many men, can act as sources of support during early fatherhood.   

While scholarship has explored how parenthood impacts sports fandom, this has often prioritised the voice of mothers. This project will use qualitative research methods to explore the transformative potential of sports fan communities to support new fathers in their parenting roles and practices. The project has potential to make a significant impact, informing practice within sports clubs and governing bodies. 

Objectives

The project will explore the role of football fan communities as sites of social support during the transition to first-time fatherhood. Specifically, the project is organised around three interrelated strands of inquiry: identity transformation, social support, and masculinity and belonging.

  • To explore how first-time fathers negotiate and reconstruct their identities as both football fans and parents during the transition to fatherhood.
  • To identify what forms of support (e.g., emotional, informational and practical) football fan communities provide to first-time fathers, and how these forms of support are experienced by fathers themselves.
  • To explore how football fan communities shape, reinforce or challenge understandings of masculinity and fatherhood during the transition to first-time parenthood. 

Funding

This studentship is open to home and international applicants. Home and international tuition fees will be covered for the duration of the 3-year award. 

The student will receive a standard stipend payment for the duration of the award. These payments are set at a level determined by the UKRI, currently £21,805 for the academic year 2026/27.

Candidate requirements

Essential: 

  • An undergraduate degree (UK first or upper-second class honours, or equivalent) or Masters degree in sport management, marketing, sociology or related disciplines.
  • An interest in issues surrounding parenthood, sport and fandom.

How to apply

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - (Re)claiming and (Re)shaping Place: The Economics and Geography of Women’s Football Stadiums
jobs.description_html:
We are excited to announce the opportunity to apply for a funded PhD project within the Manchester Metropolitan University’s Faculty of Business and Law. The project will examine how stadium infrastructure arrangements contribute to the development of women’s football and the places in which the game is experienced. Using comparative case studies and mixed methods, the research will explore how stadiums influence supporter attachment, identity and legitimacy, and how these processes relate to attendance and economic outcomes.

The project offers an opportunity to contribute to the rapidly expanding field of women’s football research while engaging with leading research communities in sport policy, place management and applied sports economics.

Objectives

The project has four main objectives:

  • To develop a conceptual framework explaining how stadium infrastructure contributes to placemaking in women’s football.
  • To examine how different infrastructure arrangements shape attachment, identity, and legitimacy.
  • To investigate the relationship between placemaking, supporter attachment, and socioeconomic outcomes, including attendance and supporter spending.
  • To generate evidence-based recommendations for clubs, governing bodies, and policymakers making future infrastructure decisions.

Funding

Candidate requirements

  • Knowledge of women’s football, professional football structures, or the commercial and organisational development of women's sport would be an asset.
  • Ideally, the candidate will have relevant academic background in at least one of the following disciplines: human geography, sport management, sports economics, or a closely related discipline.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Legal Geographies of Vehicle Dwelling
jobs.description_html:
Applications are invited for a funded PhD studentship with the Manchester Law School at Manchester Metropolitan University. This socio-legal research project will explore the everyday legalities and mobilities of vehicular dwelling.   

Vehicular dwelling sits uneasily within legal and spatial categories designed around fixed forms of residence. As people increasingly live, travel and work from vehicles, they move through legal and jurisdictional spaces, encountering a range of legal processes: parking and traffic regulation; insurance; social care; health; employment; education; planning and waste management, each overlaid by a longstanding legal tension around the public/private divide. Drawing on legal geography and mobilities scholarship, this project understands vehicular dwelling as a form of everyday mobility through which law, movement and dwelling are continually negotiated. 

Exploring ‘van life’ as a specific form of vehicular dwelling, this project expands on the aspirational and/or touristified framing of this way of life to scrutinise inequities, immobility and systemic legal inadequacies faced by vehicle dwellers. 

Objectives

This project aims to examine how mobile forms of dwelling are governed and regulated.

Research Objectives: 

  • To map the plural legal and regulatory frameworks encountered through vehicular dwelling. 
  • To understand vehicle dwellers' everyday experiences of these legal and regulatory frameworks and how they shape mobility practices. 
  • To understand what these encounters reveal about the normative assumptions underpinning law and its privileging of fixed forms of dwelling. 

Funding

The student will receive a standard stipend payment for the duration of the award. These payments are set at a level determined by the UKRI, currently £21,805 for the academic year 2026/27.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Board Approaches to Workforce Engagement, Employee-Perceived Effectiveness, and Sustainable Corporate Efficiency in UK Firms
jobs.description_html:
This project intends to examine how workforce engagement mechanisms recommended by the UK Corporate Governance Code relate to sustainable corporate efficiency through employees perceived effectiveness. The Code recommends that boards engage with their workforce through one or more of three mechanisms: a workforce director, workforce advisory panel, or designated non-executive director. These provisions reflect the Financial Reporting Councils view that effective workforce engagement can contribute to long-term sustainable growth.

However, given the UKs long-standing shareholder-primacy model and differences in how these mechanisms enable employees to communicate with boards and influence strategic and monitoring decisions, whether they shape employees perceived effectiveness and, in turn, sustainable corporate efficiency remains under-explored.

The project intends to address this gap by combining primary survey data on employees perceived effectiveness with secondary firm-level data on engagement mechanisms and sustainable corporate efficiency.

Objectives

The project aims to examine how workforce engagement mechanisms recommended by the UK Corporate Governance Code relate to sustainable corporate efficiency and whether employees perceived effectiveness of engagement explains this relationship.

The objectives are to:

  • Assess whether employees perceived effectiveness of workforce engagement differs across the Code-recommended mechanisms.
  • Examine the association between different workforce engagement mechanisms and sustainable corporate efficiency.
  • Investigate whether employees perceived effectiveness of workforce engagement mediates the relationship between the engagement mechanism adopted and sustainable corporate efficiency.

Funding

This studentship is open to home and international applicants. Home and international tuition fees will be covered for the duration of the 3-year award. 

The student will receive a standard stipend payment for the duration of the award. These payments are set at a level determined by the UKRI, currently 21,805 for the academic year 2026/27.

Candidate requirements

We particularly encourage applications from candidates from the Global South, Black and Minority Ethnic (BME) backgrounds, and other groups currently underrepresented in the doctoral research community.

Prior experience in quantitative research and data analysis using statistical software such as Stata, R or EViews would be particularly advantageous.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship - Digital State Capitalism in International Business: Geopolitics, Digital Sovereignty and Techno-Nationalism
jobs.description_html:
This PhD explores how dynamic geopolitical rivalry expressed through digitalisation strategies and techno-nationalism changes the relationship between states and international businesses. It examines how governments seek technological independence and how businesses respond to new opportunities, restrictions and pressures. 

You will compare countries with different political-economic systems to investigate emerging forms of ‘digital state capitalism’, or how states shape digital markets to pursue economic, security and political goals. Your findings will help businesses and policymakers understand the consequences of digitalisation strategies for international trade, innovation and business decision-making. 

Through comparative case studies, policy analysis and business and media data, you will develop skills in research design, critical analysis and communicating complex findings. You will draw on university databases and digital resources, supported by supervisors specialising in international business and state–business relations. 

Objectives

The study asks: 

  • How are geopolitical rivalries transforming how states use digital technologies to influence international business? 
  • How do states use regulatory, financial, infrastructural and organisational mechanisms to pursue different digitalisation strategies that seek to increase their technological autonomy? 
  • How do these mechanisms and resulting forms of digital state capitalism vary across different political-economic systems? 
  • How do MNEs respond to these interventions, and what are the consequences of their internationalisation strategies? 
  • What are the consequences and outcomes for international trade, investment, and innovation?

Funding

This studentship is open to home and international applicants. Home and international tuition fees will be covered for the duration of the 3-year award.  

The student will receive a standard stipend payment for the duration of the award. These payments are set at a level determined by the UKRI, currently £21,805 for the academic year 2026/27. 

Candidate requirements

Essential:

  • Excellent research and communication skills
  • Intellectual curiosity, diligence, and perseverance
  • Good academic writing and analytical skills, with the ability to think critically about complex political-economic issues
  • Engage critically with theories and concepts
  • Investigate complex real-world data

Desirable: 

  • Experience with qualitative and/or quantitative research methods.
  • Familiarity with international political economy, digital governance, or related fields.
  • Proficiency in a second language
